The free-schedule (fs) ProVerif group is separate from that parallel roster. `make -C beaconcrypt-core check-proverif-fs` runs it serially, one query per ProVerif process, with its own per-target timeout (`PROVERIF_FS_TIMEOUT`, 1800 s) and address-space cap (`PROVERIF_FS_ADDRESS_SPACE_KIB`, 10 GiB); `verify-in-shell` and `verify-proverif-in-shell` run it after `check-proverif`. One pass takes a little under three hours and must run alone on the machine. A failed target keeps its ProVerif log at the path its error message names, and setting `PROVERIF_FS_LOG_DIR` keeps the logs of every target. Its results and their meaning are in [Free-schedule ProVerif registration](#free-schedule-proverif-registration-fs-registration), [Free-schedule ProVerif records, Server to Beacon](#free-schedule-proverif-records-server-to-beacon-fs-records-s2b) and [Free-schedule ProVerif records, Beacon to Server](#free-schedule-proverif-records-beacon-to-server-fs-records-b2s).

For CI and reviewed generated artifacts, use:

```sh
make -C beaconcrypt-core check-proverif-transcript-fidelity
make -C beaconcrypt-core check-generated
make -C beaconcrypt-core check-inventory
```

The transcript-fidelity target checks the canonical interface against compiled core behavior, adapter wiring, symbolic structure, and all required mutations; the generated check runs the extraction-backed suite and rejects tracked or untracked extraction drift; and the standalone inventory command checks monitored trust-boundary membership and fingerprints. The dedicated formal-verification workflow distributes the equivalent transcript-fidelity, Lean/VCVio, per-scenario ProVerif, and inventory checks across independent jobs, then reports the established aggregate status only when every component passes. Together, those commands make the proof reproducible and prevent a covered transcript fact, query, monitored trust-boundary file, or generated file from silently disappearing or changing without an explicit baseline update. The synchronization gate establishes only its enumerated deterministic facts; it does not prove the complete handwritten process model faithful, discharge the reviewed symbolic assumptions, or establish primitive or protocol computational security.

## Safe summary wording

In ordinary language: the proof gives strong evidence that selected core
bookkeeping follows its specification and that a simplified protocol resists
an active network attacker for the particular exchanges modeled. The guarantee
depends on real cryptography, surrounding code, storage, and deployment
preserving the assumptions; those parts are not proved end to end.

For an audit or security statement that needs exact scope, use:

> ProVerif proves the maintained ideal-model queries using the exact two production HKDF domains, shared symmetric-HKDF prefix semantics, authenticated-context structure, disjoint tagged-key encodings and an explicitly named ML-KEM public-key-binding assumption. Four historical exact registration-origin correspondences remain explicit alias-negative controls. HB-89 instead proves projected session and exact authenticated-record agreement for the modeled schedules, without asserting unique response encodings; the computational bridge remains open.

> Beaconcrypt formally verifies selected extracted PQXDH and symmetric-ratchet
> control functions for exact transcript construction, checked state
> transitions, bounds, and logical key lifecycle. A complementary ProVerif
> model proves fixed-trace secrecy and injective authentication properties
> against an active symbolic network attacker. Replicated attacker-owned
> beacons can submit valid self-signed registrations; the server can commit
> their responses and the attacker can recover their routed canary without
> exposing the five honest-session canaries. The model also
> precisely documents two named deleted-key secrecy results at one snapshot,
> cached-key exposure, and absence of post-compromise security. These guarantees
> are conditional on ideal cryptographic assumptions, faithful adapters and
> handwritten modeling, correct application recipient routing, high-level
> non-rollback execution, and the stated replay-owner and compromise scope; the
> complete application and primitive implementations are not formally verified.
> Separate bounded honest-only passive-classical and passive-quantum scenarios preserve the five selected canaries and have explicit progress and Ed25519/X25519 recovery controls. The passive-quantum classification treats ML-KEM as opaque and is a symbolic dependency result, not a QPT or QROM theorem. A bounded active-quantum man-in-the-middle instead recovers the initial task, records the selected replacement ML-KEM public key and exact response ciphertext in its recovery witness, and violates both honest registration-origin and authenticated-bundle agreement, so active post-quantum security is explicitly refuted.
> The production symbolic KEM theory assumes ML-KEM public-key binding or strong cross-key shared-secret collision resistance, which generic IND-CCA does not imply. `get_registration_bundle` returns `Some` at most once per live Beacon object and exposes no same-identity ML-KEM rotation through that method; caller-constructed bytes through public secret accessors are outside this claim. In an isolated non-production multi-epoch control, the strong theory preserves exact key/ciphertext agreement and the new-session canary after old-key compromise, while a deliberately weakened public re-encapsulation theory exposes the accepted root and canary and breaks agreement. A future same-identity rotation design would need explicit replay semantics plus either the binding assumption or cryptographic binding of the selected KEM key into the authenticated handshake transcript.
>
> For the symmetric ratchet, production stores one affine `ConcreteRatchetKernel` with direct fixed-width chains and a sequence-tagged cache. Typed initial, per-step KDF, seal, and open phases make publication explicit: sends retain advancement even when sealing fails, while receives publish only after successful opening. The target is consumed separately from the 50 skipped-key slots. Lean proves unconditional panic freedom for the complete default extraction; constructs terminating receive executions; checks exact cached/future staging and publication, exhaustion, rejection neutrality, replay, and retry; and preserves structural validity through arbitrary finite mixed histories. Canonical entries additionally preserve the unchanged ideal ratchet relation under fixed interpreters, with exact positive-target receive correspondence when the callback implements ideal decryption. Authenticated equal-root initialization and complete directional lifecycles preserve paired sessions. Restoration proves structural guarantees for arbitrary supplied material and canonical guarantees under trusted persistence provenance. HB-59 and HB-60 provide separate source/finite-model synchronization checks. Semantic interpretation by the Rust adapter, primitive correctness/security and output noncollision, parser and codec fidelity, compiler correspondence, concurrent ownership, crash handling, and physical erasure remain external. `PersistentServer` supplies generation/head CAS and loser fencing under a trusted payload-integrity, provenance, linearizability, durability, and rollback-resistance contract; snapshots have no cryptographic authentication or encryption.
>
> A dedicated state-neutral receive trace rejects a forged future frame twice from the exact same receiver state, later accepts the authentic target while publishing only its skipped key, rejects replay, and accepts delayed delivery. A separate exact capacity leg advances from sequence 1 to sequence 52 with 50 skipped keys, consumes sequence 52 separately, rejects sequence 54 while the cache is full, consumes cached sequence 51, and then accepts sequence 54 while publishing sequence 53. Explicit compromise after rejection discloses the unchanged live chain and empty cache: future material is exposed because it remains derivable from that chain, not because rejection retained anything. The predecessor F* artifact proves general rollback, preparation, publication, replay, retry, and capacity properties for the callback-bearing source snapshot; current Lean proves complete positive-target ideal receive correspondence, arbitrary-state rollback and termination, exact cached/future publication, structural and canonical finite lifetimes, replay, and retry. HB-60 checks the two finite ProVerif traces against current core planning/publication and exact query text. The traces supply concrete cryptographic and exact-schedule witnesses; byte-level parsing, semantic adapter-driver fidelity, and arbitrary successful receive schedules remain outside them.
>
> Lean `CommitmentSurface` proves the exact fixed-width production transcript, its injectivity, and the pointwise theorem that two distinct accepted explanations of one fixed payload produce an explicit collision witness for arbitrary pure hash and AEAD-open functions.
> Lean machine-checks factor-one reductions from the direct full-control modified-CTX commitment game and the stronger raw-payload misattribution game to BLAKE2b-512 collision advantage, dedicated factor-one wrong-sequence, wrong-sender, and cross-session record-opening specializations, exact equality between the current generated 229-byte transcript builder and the ideal CTX preimage, and Boolean component-level privacy preservation relative to modified nonce-AEAD IND$ and a classical public ROM. The Lean sender result is below the beacon's earlier pinned-sender check and cross-session interpretation relies on associated-data provenance, while the source/model representation bridges, numerical ROM and BLAKE2b-512 bounds, PPT/runtime preservation, adapter hashing/provenance, Hax/Rust semantics, compiler correspondence, ordinary-integrity preservation, concrete ChaCha20-Poly1305/BLAKE2b privacy, and protocol-level multi-key privacy composition remain open or assumed.
> A supplementary differential ProVerif control gives the base AEAD two distinct valid openings: CTX makes the double-open event unreachable, and removing CTX makes the same query produce a witness.
> The resulting real-world strong-commitment claim remains conditional on BLAKE2b collision resistance, correct libsodium behavior, production field provenance, and adapter/compiler correspondence.

Statements such as “the whole implementation is proven secure,” “all application messages are proven confidential,” “the cryptographic primitives are verified,” “F* proves replay or rollback impossible across replicas,” “the complete CTX implementation and BLAKE2b security are formally proved end to end,” or “beaconcrypt is post-quantum secure against active attackers” are not supported by the current proof corpus.

## Complete Lean extraction panic freedom

`PanicFreedom/API.lean` gives an unconditional normal-return theorem for every one of the 279 non-helper `RustM` operations in the current default production extraction. Each theorem quantifies over the extracted operation's complete argument list and concludes `∃ result, operation arguments = RustM.ok result`. Ordinary `Err`, `None`, exhausted counters, failed authentication, cancellation, and defensive rejection count as normal returns. The theorems require neither valid-state assumptions nor correct cryptographic responses. They therefore cover malformed typed control, restoration, and pending-phase values as well as states constructed through the public API.

The checked proof families cover constructors and accessors, static assertions, control transitions, bounded searches, byte encodings, initial and step KDF response splitting, all four receive loops, restoration, pending validation, cached and future publication, and every first-order send/receive phase. The final `ReceiveKdf.resume_total` theorem discharges staged-slot bounds, counter additions and subtraction, and the final pending validator for arbitrary represented continuations and responses. `PanicFreedom/Bytes.lean` additionally proves the exact 76-byte partition: key bytes 0 through 31, next-chain bytes 32 through 63, and nonce bytes 64 through 75.

`scripts/check_lean_panic_freedom.py` derives the operation set and argument binders from the generated `Extraction/Funs.lean`. Its manifest supplies theorem names only; it cannot supply weaker propositions or extra hypotheses. The checker requires an exact operation-set match and reproduces the aggregate module byte for byte. `make check-lean` runs this gate and its regression checks before compiling the aggregate certificates. Generated loop bodies and closure machinery are internal helpers whose safety is discharged through their callers; the remaining 100 pure declarations do not carry `RustM` failure outcomes. The checker pins the complete reviewed eleven-file ideal model set, including the previously reviewed HB-88 response-encoding witness and HB-95's authorized sequence-one transition and admission theorem. The original ten-file `27ff282` digest was stale; the current digest preserves sorted path-and-content hashing, includes the three Lean-port elaboration-only theorem-body rewrites, and retains the rejection tests for added or edited model files. No model definition or theorem statement changes in the toolchain migration, and all 279 extracted-operation certificates remain unchanged.

This is a complete panic-freedom proof for the default extracted core boundary, with the extraction and Lean/Aeneas library semantics remaining trusted. It does not cover adapter execution, cryptographic primitive implementations, compiler behavior, allocation failure or process termination, or test-only feature surfaces absent from this extraction. Panic freedom is separate from behavioral refinement. The semantic modules described below additionally prove cached material correspondence, complete future staging/publication, arbitrary finite operation histories, and paired-session preservation against the reviewed ideal models.

Fresh locked Lean extraction reproduced every generated file without changes. The complete workspace mutation suite passed all 1,164 cases: 814 caught, 350 unviable, zero missed and zero timed out. Core unit and transcript-fidelity tests passed (77 and 13 tests); Rust formatting and all-feature workspace Clippy passed, with pre-existing Clippy warnings. The required locked aggregate verification was attempted and stopped in regenerated F* `split_initial_ratchet_kdf_output` on its index-addition obligation before reaching Lean. That pre-existing aggregate failure remains recorded as historical evidence. The later completed declaration audit supplied the Lean replacements, and the predecessor F* artifacts are archived at Git commit `a79817c`.

The final locked `make check-lean` gate passed, including all nine coverage-checker regressions and the full 3,110-job Lean project build. The reviewed trust-boundary inventory passed. The complete 269-contract dependency audit found 19 contracts without axioms and 250 using only Lean's standard `propext`, `Classical.choice`, and `Quot.sound`; none depends on placeholders or additional assumptions. This completes the extracted-core panic-freedom milestone.

## Lean semantic migration: cached publication and fixed interpreters

`Refinement/RatchetCachedPublication.lean` closes the cached material-array gap. `publish_cached_receive_exact` proves the exact physical transformation, including the case where the target already occupies the last slot: the old last slot becomes empty, the target receives the old last material when distinct, and every other slot is unchanged. `KernelRefines.cached_publication` combines that equation with the checked control swap-removal result. It proves both directions of correspondence with the ideal filtered skipped-key store, preserves both chains and the send counter, and proves the entire unused suffix remains empty. `CachedOpenRefines.finish_success_refines` then derives the actual `ReceiveOpen.finish` result, ideal plaintext/removal result, and complete post-state relation without assuming a publication equation or final `CachedPublicationRefines` relation. Initial kernel validity and successful ideal decryption remain the appropriate semantic premises.

`Refinement/RatchetInterpreter.lean` gives one fixed pure request interpreter a precise mathematical meaning through the total extracted 76-byte decoder. Its `withInterpreter` instance retains the existing ideal model's AEAD operations and correctness law and instantiates its KDF fields with the decoded chain and material. `interpretedResponse_refines` and `interpreter_request_refines` derive response refinement from that definition and the extracted request fields. This proves conformance to the chosen pure interpreter; it does not prove a concrete HKDF implementation correct or change the ideal model files.

`Refinement/PqxdhConcreteSession.lean` connects both extracted initial start/resume drivers to complementary role kernels under a shared fixed 64-byte interpreter. It proves exact half selection, empty zero-counter kernel relations, directional chain equality, and matching canonical message material at every index. `authenticated_registrations_establish_concrete_session` composes equal authenticated root inputs with an arbitrary fixed root derivation and the shared interpreters. `PqxdhSurface.lean` adds 40 direct raw-byte proofs for tag round trips, constructed bundle validation, rejection and result shapes, registration binding, allocation, authentication inversion, and complete honest registration execution. These match the weaker raw-input F* premises without assuming primitive-model representations. The declaration-level PQXDH audit covers all 68 historical declarations, including the paired lifecycle guarantees proved in `PqxdhSessionLifecycle`.

`Refinement/RatchetReceiveLoopExact.lean` proves exact bounded future publication: it copies precisely the specified staged interval into the live array, clears precisely that staged interval, and preserves unrelated cells, chains, and control. It also proves acceptance of a staged window satisfying the validator's explicit slot conditions. `Refinement/RatchetFutureRefinement.lean` defines the canonical future-phase invariant and proves that every correctly decoded nonfinal response actually produces the next KDF phase while preserving exact consecutive control entries, absolute staged slots, canonical material, request fields, and remaining derivation bounds. `RatchetFutureAdmission`, `RatchetFutureFinalization`, `RatchetFutureTrace`, `RatchetFuturePublication`, and the relative structural counterparts now complete initialization, terminal validation, publication, and whole-operation receive refinement.

`RatchetFutureAdmission.lean` proves that a canonical kernel, future wire target, and available skipped-key capacity cause the actual `begin_receive` operation to construct the initial canonical KDF phase. `RatchetExecution.lean` defines counted KDF prefixes and complete executions whose edges are equations about extracted operations. It proves prefix composition and determinism of both phase execution and the whole entry-point result under fixed interpreters. The later `RatchetFutureTrace`, `RatchetReceiveIdeal`, and `ByteTraceRefinement` results below establish existence, ideal-state preservation, and complete observable correspondence; the execution relation alone would not discharge those obligations.

## Lean future publication and concrete commitment correspondence

`RatchetFuturePublication.lean` proves the full material publication step from the completed private transaction invariant. The extracted copy loop preserves every existing skipped key, publishes exactly the newly derived skipped keys in the appended control slots, leaves all slots above the live prefix empty, installs the canonical final receive chain and counter, and preserves the send state. Consequently, any accepted callback result re-establishes the complete `KernelRefines` relation. A separate theorem uses ideal decryption to identify the delivered plaintext and ideal receive poststate. Neither result assumes that publication succeeds or that its output already refines the model. The ideal models are unchanged.

`CommitmentSurface.lean` closes the raw F* commitment obligations: exact production input bytes, six-field transcript injectivity, a left inverse and injectivity for the full-width little-endian sequence encoder, and an explicit hash-collision witness from two distinct accepted openings. The delivery theorems apply to ciphertexts produced by that interpretation; the replay theorem permits arbitrary ciphertexts. They do not verify the surrounding library, actual cryptographic algorithms, or provenance of externally restored state. ## Public-HKDF counterexample and secret-input replacement

`PqxdhPublicKdfCounterexample.lean` attacks the existing game itself: the adversary queries one public address, locally computes the fixed source output, and compares the answer. Lean checks zero randomness queries, at most one complete-stream query, real acceptance probability one, and random acceptance probability `1 / card(Vector UInt8 76)`, namely `2^-608`. The exact advantage is their absolute difference and is proved at least one half. Local computation is public and efficient when HKDF is efficient; the query theorem does not machine-check PPT/runtime preservation. This refutes a negligible bound for that public game, not production secret-root security. Existing ROM inequalities and their proofs are preserved, with their unsupported computational interpretation corrected.

`PqxdhSecretInputKdf.lean` samples one joint public-context/secret-input pair and gives an observer the context and the honest 32-byte root. The comparison world replaces only that root with independent uniform bytes. The observer can evaluate public HKDF on any guesses in both worlds. Context is arbitrary and may leak IKM or PRK; these are absent only as separate arguments, and any context leakage belongs in the extraction obligation. `SourceRootCorrect` is the functional equation identifying the source root with the first 32 bytes of `HMAC(PRK, INFO_PQ || 0x01)`, where `PRK = HMAC(0^64, IKM)`; it is neither a primitive secrecy assumption nor a proof of libsodium internals.

`sourceRootAdvantage_le_extract_add_hmac` proves a coefficient-one bound by two explicit primitive gaps. The Extract game exposes the entire PRK together with the joint sampler's public context; its reduction expands that supplied PRK and runs the root observer. This is a stronger primitive observation than the final root and is not an assumption equivalent to protocol secrecy. Its smallness remains an unresolved computational extraction obligation for the actual input/transcript distribution. A 256-bit hidden coordinate cannot give statistical uniformity over a 512-bit PRK; the desired bound must be computational. The second gap is the ordinary HMAC PRF experiment with an independent uniform 64-byte secret key. The reduction makes at most one challenge HMAC query, at the exact root Expand message. Distributional lemmas commute independent samples and prove the first half of a uniform 64-byte block is exactly uniform, allowing the triangle inequality to identify the games. No public-HKDF random-table term or ROM-guess term appears in this new bound.

The `zeroSaltPatched` controls change a keyed family only at the public all-zero key. Lean proves that fixed-salt Extract becomes constant for every IKM, while the whole keyed oracle is unchanged at every other key and a uniform 64-byte key hits the exceptional key with probability `2^-512`. These structural/probability controls explain why ordinary uniform-key HMAC PRF security does not automatically justify fixed-salt extraction, even for secret high-entropy inputs. They are not an attack on actual HMAC-SHA-512, and no unproved general PRF hybrid bound is claimed for the countermodel.

The new root experiment contains no adaptive external signing, converted-DH, decapsulation, compromise, persistence or other-session oracle. A justified prechallenge context can represent earlier observations, but later interactions need a larger interface and reduction. Extending this result to both RFC 5869 blocks, both domains and the shared 64/76-byte prefixes is a separate next step. Connecting it to authenticated target selection and challenge-blocked KEM decapsulation, then evolving correlated chains, remains open. It therefore cannot be substituted as if it were the old initialized-chain capstone.

## HB-111: authenticated-root composition

This milestone integrates the complete native authenticated-root reduction and derives its source, continuation and primitive-endpoint resource bounds. The final verification receipt is maintained in [the authenticated-root record](impl/authenticated-root-composition.md). HB-110 is reserved for the separate paused evolving-KDF work.

The authenticated-root experiment now includes original identity, prekey, ML-KEM and one-time generation; the three original signatures; arbitrary candidate selection; the selected Server's actual root and response builder; and the complete adaptive native scheduler before and after registration. An internally selected unchanged, unrevealed, unconsumed candidate receives the root hybrid. Changed signed fields under the same unrevealed identity incur one explicit forgery term. Other accepted keys, revealed identities and rejection keep their actual common continuation. The theorem has no premise that the adversary selects an honest candidate.

For that same experiment, the final comparison has the following explicit shape, where every reduction is displayed in the checked statement:

`Adv(actual, consistent uniform roots) ≤ Adv(joint identity weak-EUF reduction) + Pr(ordinary KEM correctness error) + Adv(ordinary one-key IND-CCA reduction) + Adv(actual secret-input Extract-family reduction) + Σ j<qRoot Adv(indexed uniform-key HMAC reduction j)`.

The identity advantage is the existing joint Ed25519/X25519 interface, including the permitted converted-DH use of the same seed. This is an explicitly stronger joint-use contract than ordinary Ed25519 EUF-CMA alone. The Extract endpoint is also explicit: it retains the actual public context and 128-byte source DH coordinates, the fixed 32-byte `FF` prefix, and one shared uniform 32-byte KEM contribution in the exact 192-byte root input. It compares the complete 64-byte Extract value against its consistent ideal family. That family, `PqxdhCorrelatedExtractFamily`, is a generic adaptive game over an arbitrary client: one hidden uniform 32-byte string `s` in the KEM shared-secret position is sampled once, and each 128-byte query `m` is answered with zero-salt HMAC-SHA-512 of `FF^32 || m || s` in the real game and by a lazily sampled random function in the ideal game. It is an additional, non-standard split-key PRF assumption keyed through the message input; it is not implied by the HMAC PRF assumption, which places the secret in the key position, or by extractor results for high-entropy inputs. The bound charges its advantage for the explicitly constructed reduction, as it does every other advantage term, which does not make the game adversary-specific; the [assumption list](#cryptographic-assumptions) gives a plausibility note and related literature. Expand uses the separately constructed ordinary HMAC reductions and preserves repeated-input correlations. The production 32-byte root is the actual first-32 projection. All public HKDF evaluations remain the fixed production computation, and no distinguishable public-HKDF/random-table advantage is used. The CTX hash is not real in this experiment: the actual game models BLAKE2b as a programmable classical random oracle, lazily sampled and shared by the CTX commitment and the KDF callbacks, which the adversary can also query directly.

The ordinary KEM correctness error is charged once for the complete continuation, including repeated native finishes that encounter the same challenge ciphertext. The proof neither infers perfect correctness from IND-CCA nor assumes every encapsulation is good. The selected KEM secret remains inside the private source and CCA interpreters. The ordinary CCA reduction receives the challenger-supplied shared secret and confines it to private root routing. The protocol post callback receives neither that supplied secret nor the selected KEM secret key; it receives its original selection, optional response and permitted oracle replies. Public postchallenge decapsulation blocks the challenge ciphertext, while matching private native roots use the opaque shared handle. Common and rejected branches keep their original unblocked interface.

### Intrinsic and common-branch query accounting

`PqxdhPhase2SharedBounds.collect_total` counts twelve source-shaped preparation callbacks, including decapsulation before the four DH calls. `afterInputs_total` charges the temporary-secret erasure after admission. `prepare_total` combines these into thirteen callbacks. `afterRoot_total` charges initial64, application access and the existing native raw receiver's 53 KDF/hash/opening callbacks. `tail_total` adds the one private root callback for 56 tail callbacks, including optional failure. `owner_total` gives the full 69-callback cap for every finish attempt. `collect_decapsulation` and `prepare_decapsulation` prove that only the original collected decapsulation occurs. `afterRoot_no_root` excludes another private-root callback from the remaining initializer, application and raw work. `tail_root` and `owner_root` give a cap of one private-root request per finish attempt. `owner_decapsulation` gives the corresponding cap of one decapsulation. `PqxdhAuthenticatedRootCommonBounds.selectorLift_total` preserves the complete logical source query count under the public lifting, while `selectorLift_roots` proves that lifting cannot request an opaque target root. `coins_total` preserves the exact native-builder coin count, and `coins_roots` excludes target-root requests from those coins. `completed_total` charges the full adaptive common schedule on a rejected registration; `accepted_total` adds the actual builder cost on accepted common candidates. `completed_roots` and `accepted_roots` prove that both branches stay outside the target-root channel. `completed_bounds` and `accepted_bounds` produce the complete conservative class ledger from those same programs.

Writing `T = (64 + 5*qAux) + sourceSchedulerBill(qLocal, postBudget)`, each common observer class is bounded by `T`, with zero opaque roots. The source interpreter separately charges identity creation at 32 uniform calls, yielding the conservative ordinary uniform cap `34*T` and base/decapsulation caps `T`. The weighted scheduler bill includes every attempted native finish at `69*(max(qLocal,64)+1)` before source identity interpretation, as well as the original record/public/reveal classes. Local and builder auxiliary costs are explicit all-query, all-state budgets. No post-registration no-create assumption is imposed. A completed root-failure branch can use an ordinary encapsulation during preparation and then an unused outer challenger encapsulation; both must remain in their respective final bills.

For the generic endpoint's actual root client, let `U = qKeygen + (uPre + qBase*bPre + qDecap*dPre + qEncap) + (uPost + qBase*bPost + qDecap*(dPost + privatePost))`. The client has uniform cap `U` and root cap `1+privatePost`. Each indexed HMAC reduction has uniform cap `U+64*(1+privatePost)` and at most one challenge query; each corresponding real or random HMAC game has total uniform cap `64+U+64*(1+privatePost)`. The source-specific pre/post, CCA, Extract, actual-source and challenger ledgers are the separate consuming statements described below.

`PqxdhPhase2PostSchedulerBounds.publicWork_bound` preserves the exact public CCA classes and excludes private-root capabilities from public forwarding. `auxiliary_bound` charges actual local auxiliary sampling at `max(qLocal,64)` while proving that it makes no selected-key base, decapsulation or private-root requests. `routed_step` separately identifies the original selected-key decapsulation, private-root and costed local callback positions. `handles_step` preserves these classifications under the private KEM-handle translation. `targetFinish_bound` combines those concrete costs with the intrinsic owner bounds: `69*max(qLocal,64)` uniform calls, zero selected-key base calls, at most one selected logical decapsulation and at most one private root per attempted finish. `target_step` extends the ledger to all original record/reveal, forwarded identity/source, public CCA and native finish requests. `target_bound` accumulates it over the entire adaptive source scheduler and complete split state. `uniform_bill` expands the result into `qCoin+64*(qSend+qRaw+qHash)+33*qSource+qPublicUniform+69*max(qLocal,64)*qFinish`. `base_bill` gives `qPublicBase`, `decapsulation_bill` gives `qPublicDecapsulation+qFinish`, and `root_bill` gives `qFinish`. `fullPostBounds` packages these exact source-derived caps for the component interface. No honest-key, successful-finish, correctness or opaque post-program budget premise establishes these counts.

The final component route conservatively adds the separate private-root and public-decapsulation caps, producing a postchallenge selected-decapsulation allowance `qPublicDecapsulation+2*qFinish`. `PqxdhAuthenticatedRootBudgets.lean` closes the resource premise of the authenticated-root composition. The certificate keeps three separate resource coordinates for each actual prekey sampler, one-time sampler, ephemeral sampler, optional native encapsulation and total encapsulation. They therefore cover rejection, optional failure, arbitrary subsequent scheduling and every attempted finish.

Let `D = qWrite + SourceSchedulerBounds.bill(qLocal, preBudget)` and `T = (64 + 5*qAux) + SourceSchedulerBounds.bill(qLocal, postBudget)`. The certificate transparently defines `uPre = 32 + uPrekey + uOneTime + 2*D + uEphemeral + max(uNativeEncapsulation,uTotalEncapsulation) + 34*T`, with the precise parenthesization of `prepare_caps`. The base preparation count is `bPrekey + bOneTime + D + bEphemeral + max(bNativeEncapsulation,bTotalEncapsulation) + T`, and the logical-decapsulation preparation count is the same expression with the corresponding decapsulation coordinates. The maximum includes the total encapsulation on an eligible root-failure branch. The ordinary challenger encapsulation is still separately charged outside preparation.

The postchallenge definitions are `uPost = (64 + 5*qAux) + PostSchedulerBounds.bill(qLocal, uniform, postBudget)`, `bPost = postBudget(base)`, `dPost = postBudget(publicDecapsulation) + postBudget(finish)`, and `privatePost = postBudget(finish)`. The existing post uniform bill expands to `qCoin + 64*(qSend+qRaw+qHash) + 33*qSource + qPublicUniform + 69*max(qLocal,64)*qFinish`. The builder's actual coins are separate from this post schedule. Define `Q = 1 + privatePost` and `U = qKeygen + ((uPre + qBase*bPre + qDecap*dPre) + qEncap) + (uPost + qBase*bPost + qDecap*(dPost+privatePost))`. `prepare_bounds` consumes the checked source-prefix and common-dispatch bounds, including both source samplers and all common/rejected continuations. `localCoins_bounds` proves that real builder coins are only public uniform requests. `targetAccepted_bounds` then executes the actual builder before the complete native target scheduler and derives all four postchallenge classes. `resume_bounds` discharges every completed/pending mode and every optional initial-root outcome. `sampler_bounds` packages the resulting actual prepare/resume inequalities with the separately stated primitive sampling bounds into the existing `SamplerBounds` structure. ### Scope and validation

This result concerns one source-generated KEM-backed authenticated Server root and its complete permitted adaptive native continuation. It does not prove Beacon-side pinned-Server Phase2 authentication, a replicated multi-session symbolic/computational composition, evolving-chain secrecy, or global adaptive raw-record origin. Current-chain descendants and additional global reveal/target-selection obligations remain in the separately paused work. Snapshots, persistence and restoration are outside this proof. No complete raw-response origin or computational assigned-ID agreement is claimed here. The established sequence-one initial admission remains unchanged; the former later-record registration relabel witness is now an omitted-policy diagnostic, while the separate X25519 encoding-alias witness remains valid.

Permanent contracts retain correct primitive implementations, exact joint identity and Extract-family security interfaces (both additional, non-standard assumptions listed under [cryptographic assumptions](#cryptographic-assumptions)), fixed source/primitive correspondence, compiler and native adapter assumptions, and the existing physical-erasure boundary. No primitive algorithm or implementation security proof is attempted. No symbolic free-constructor injectivity is inferred from a weaker primitive name. The experiment does use the BLAKE2b random oracle: it models BLAKE2b as a programmable classical random oracle, lazily sampled and shared by the CTX commitment and the KDF callbacks, which the adversary can also query directly. That is an explicit idealization of this experiment, not a consequence of BLAKE2b collision resistance. The later common symbolic/computational experiment must still identify all idealizations it uses.

The milestone contains nineteen new modules and 121 guarded statements beyond the retained thirteen-module, 63-statement HB-109 source-scheduler port. Every new theorem has a checked dependency guard allowing only `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`. Independent semantic review covers the exact source, theorem statements, assumptions and all resource consumers. Four declarations in the generated joint-EUF ledger use a bounded 1,000,000-heartbeat elaboration allowance matching its imported predecessor; no logical assumption or verification gate changes. The owned locked environment previously passed the baseline-plus-HB109 Lake build with 3,436 jobs. The unchanged Rust/build/binding/schema input manifest passed formatting, Clippy, 297 workspace tests, both no-default role builds and 17 transcript-fidelity tests. The complete final Lake, locked Make, inventory and publication receipt is recorded in [the milestone guide](impl/authenticated-root-composition.md). No Rust source changed, so mutation, Go and Python suites are not repeated for this proof-only work.
