Public HKDF and current/skipped-key reads retain explicit source classes even when they add no randomness. This finish experiment uses its existing finite owner family; the source-ordered growing registry, prechallenge creation/disclosure composition and enclosing global budgets are later consumers.

Fifteen modules and 110 statements cover the [saved Post compiler](impl/selected-post-compiler.md), [its disclosure behavior](impl/selected-post-disclosure.md), [source-derived saved descriptor scope](impl/saved-descriptor-receive-scope.md) and the [pending receive](impl/selected-pending-receive-compiler.md), [complete owner](impl/selected-pending-owner-compiler.md) and [role](impl/selected-pending-role-compiler.md) compilers. They preserve complete native replies, cache behavior, rollback, sequence checks, original Server AD/peer lookups, Beacon reinstallation and LIVE observation timing. At most one dynamic component call is made by each compiled pending operation; private lookups and all prefix/backend work remain separately billed. An unavailable selected-key argument does not prove independence of the supplied context.

The [initializer and occurrence package](impl/initial-installation-receipts.md) adds 37 of those statements. Literal retained Beacon and supplied Server initialization produce the actual zero-state constructor and directional reachability under the fixed interpreter. The complete first Builder/Post program retains attempted-initializer evidence even if a later step fails; its successful-install map is distinct. Attempt ordinals increase in source order, with cap 1+qPost. Local tokens do not identify cryptographic sessions, and the old Boolean coordinate marker is preserved with its original meaning. Existing arbitrary roles receive no invented origin. Successful installation-to-current-path preservation and the eleven-field Phase-1 session projection remain subsequent consumers.

Twelve modules and 136 statements give the actual [authentication observer](impl/selected-authentication-observer.md), [accepted-record event](impl/selected-accepted-record-event.md), [confidentiality observer](impl/selected-confidentiality-observer.md), [complete receive receipts](impl/selected-complete-receive-receipt.md), [role attribution](impl/selected-role-receipt-attribution.md), [seal receipts](impl/selected-seal-production-receipts.md) and [chronological source audit](impl/selected-source-production-audit.md). The [acceptance classification](impl/selected-acceptance-source-origins.md) and [functional plaintext correspondence](impl/selected-plaintext-source-origins.md) use the actual returned optional plaintext. All accepted positions are classified as known material, a fresh selected tuple winning the ordinary observer, or a matching earlier selected cryptographic production. For a match, the same earlier entry supplies plaintext, AD, sequence, sender and decoded payload, using the existing functional AEAD correctness contract. No secretly recovered plaintext is inserted into an adversary's target, and equality of tuple bytes does not identify sessions or installations.

The [selected-key protocol production event](impl/selected-protocol-production-event.md) ranges over every accepted position and both finite role families in the same audited run. Its missing-inner-production event, outside the explicit known-route case, implies the existing ordinary all-attempt winner with coefficient one. The independent uniform selected-key experiment used here models BLAKE2b as a programmable classical random oracle, lazily sampled in one cache shared by the selected-key and known-key CTX commitments and the adversary's direct hash queries. In that experiment, with empty initial component state and qSeal < 2^96, the bound is the constructed validation IND$ advantage plus qHash/2^128, twice the sum of the indexed ordinary INT advantages over i < qRaw, and qRaw/2^512. There is no additional raw-attempt or role-selection factor at this selected-key layer. Four component query classes and the original source fallback are explicitly bounded; source private derivations still pay up to 51 per raw receive. The production selected-key sampler, allowed disclosures, key aliases, successful wire publication, full session origin and global selection remain separate. An earlier failed writer is a cryptographic production, not a successful wire publication.

Four modules and 31 statements establish [retained directional paths](impl/retained-source-directional-paths.md), [native counter order](impl/native-source-counter-order.md), [actual source cycles/meetings](impl/retained-native-source-cycles.md) and [paths in the exact nonce-event history](impl/nonce-history-source-paths.md). All use the same complete fixed private responses, actual source counters, optional writers and original record/read continuation. The nonce-history consumer uses the effective selected/parent table and existing event list, with exact pre-call Server/Beacon lookup evidence. It derives path certificates from explicit initial source certificates and never transfers a support-only replay into a probability equality. Equal roots and cross-owner aliases remain explicit cases. Actual installation intervals, strict ordering within those intervals and the source KDF probability reductions are still needed before repeated inputs are a small loss.

The final common computational-symbolic experiment, complete saved outer continuation, source-ordered dynamic creation and compromise schedule, production key/context nonexposure, global target selection and all advertised symbolic event correspondences remain open consumers. The exact-joint fixed-salt Extract endpoints (the Extract games listed under [cryptographic assumptions](#cryptographic-assumptions)), the explicit unbounded related-DH Extract-family advantage and the BLAKE2b random-oracle idealization are unchanged; a list of these components is not an end-to-end security theorem. Primitive implementations, snapshots, persistence and restoration remain outside the active proof.

## Audit remediation A: alias-robust registration response control

Audit remediation A corrects one ProVerif control that production refutes. Until this change, `main-registration-controls` required `inj-event(BeaconAnyCommitted(main_transcript)) ==> inj-event(ServerCommitted(main_transcript))` to be TRUE. `BeaconAnyCommitted` is emitted in `HonestBeacon` immediately beside `BeaconCommitted`, on the same 18-field `establishment_transcript` value, and also in the `MainLaterBeacon` branch on that branch's 18-field transcript. That transcript contains the raw server ephemeral encoding and the complete response. The [production counterexample](#production-counterexample-to-exact-registration-origin) shows that an attacker can flip the public high bit of the Server's ephemeral key: X25519 ignores that bit, so the root and the authenticated record are unchanged and the Beacon completes, but the raw field and the response it records differ from the ones the Server issued. The exact query is therefore false for production for the same reason as the three historical exact queries, yet it was a required control. It had also never been run under the alias theory: `check-phase2-x25519-alias.py` selected only the three `BeaconCommitted` and `BeaconRegistrationCompleted` queries, so its TRUE result came only from the canonical single-encoding theory.

The required control is now the projected query `inj-event(BeaconAuthenticatedRegistrationCompleted(main_agreement, main_sequence, main_payload, main_frame, main_claimed)) ==> inj-event(AuthenticatedRegistrationRecordSent(main_agreement, first_sequence(), main_payload, main_frame, main_claimed))`. It says that every Beacon completion, on either scheduling branch and whatever sequence the Beacon recorded, is injectively matched by a Server event that sent a sequence-one authenticated record. The matching event has the same HB-89 eleven-field authenticated session projection, the same complete authenticated payload and decoded frame, and an assigned ID equal to the Beacon's claimed outer ID. This is the property the exact query was meant to state: a genuine later record cannot replace the registration response. The Server sends such a record as `AuthenticatedRegistrationRecordSent` at sequence three, so the frame a completion would have accepted appears only in a sequence-three event and has no matching sequence-one event. Unlike the exact query, the projected one does not compare the raw ephemeral encoding, raw KEM ciphertext, ordered root input or complete response bytes. HB-89 keeps these as diagnostic fields outside authentication equality; the actual root, the associated data and the authenticated frame are still compared. The high-bit flip changes only such fields, so it does not falsify the projected query, as the alias checker below confirms. `main-registration-controls` still has ten queries, and the other nine results are unchanged.

The exact query moved verbatim to `exact-registration-origin-queries.pvl` as the fourth historical control, and `check-phase2-x25519-alias.py` now selects all four historical exact queries. It requires all four TRUE in the canonical X25519 theory and all four FALSE in the high-bit alias theory, each with a reconstructed public-bit-flip delivery trace. For the `BeaconAnyCommitted` query this is the first alias-theory run; ProVerif 2.05 reports it FALSE with a sequence-one trace in which the attacker delivers `x25519_flip_high_bit` of the Server's ephemeral key. The checker's projected set now also includes the new main-registration control, so it requires four projected queries TRUE under both theories: the three from `queries.pvl` and the new one. The alias checker runs the one-session `phase2-x25519-alias-control.pv` process, with one honest Beacon and one Server on the sequence-one branch. The replicated baseline with the later branch checks the new query in the canonical theory only, through `main-registration-controls`.

The ProVerif alias theory models only the documented high-bit alias, but production accepts a larger class of equivalent ephemeral encodings. Adding a point of order 2, 4 or 8 to the ephemeral point leaves every clamped X25519 output unchanged, because clamped scalars are multiples of the cofactor. For example, replacing the u-coordinate `u` by `1/u mod p`, which adds the order-2 point, gave identical nonzero outputs for 20 of 20 random scalar pairs in an RFC 7748 check run for this remediation, and libsodium rejects only small-order inputs and all-zero outputs. Like the high-bit flip, these encodings change only the raw ephemeral field, which the projected query does not compare, so they are one more reason why the historical exact queries are not production properties. The computational event planned for Milestone B therefore identifies two ephemeral encodings when they give equal outputs under every scalar, as the `SameDhReplies` premise of `Model/Pqxdh/ResponseEncodingAlias.lean` does, rather than only up to the high bit.

The gates changed with it. `check-results.awk` requires the projected query TRUE in `main-registration-controls` instead of the exact one. `beaconcrypt-core/proofs/check-inventory.sh` requires four historical query bodies in `exact-registration-origin-queries.pvl`, exactly one copy of the moved exact query there, no `inj-event(BeaconAnyCommitted(` in `main-registration-control-queries.pvl` or `queries.pvl`, and exactly one copy of the new projected control. `beaconcrypt-core/tests/proverif_transcript_fidelity.rs` pins a fourth historical query-body hash, requires the projected control once among the controls and the exact query once among the historical queries, and rejects any `BeaconAnyCommitted` correspondence among the controls. The alias checker's self-test now rejects six raw-result and seven projected-result negative controls, including a relabelled `BeaconAnyCommitted` result and a projected result with the wrong sequence.

This remains symbolic agreement over the retained-value projection in the ProVerif model and its modeled schedules. It is not a computational authentication result: it does not bound the probability that a real adversary makes the Beacon accept a registration response the Server did not send, and it does not show computationally that the Beacon authenticates the Server. That result is the subject of Milestone B of the [remediation plan](impl/audit-0b4039e-remediation-plan.md). The historical exact 18-field correspondences remain alias-negative controls, not production properties. No protocol, wire-format or production Rust change is made.

## Audit remediation D: a jointly satisfiable hypothesis instance for HB-111 and HB-112

The audit found that nothing in the repository showed that the hypotheses of the two headline computational theorems can hold at the same time (finding F6). A theorem whose premises are inconsistent is true for a vacuous reason, so this matters even though every premise looked satisfiable on its own. `Computational/PqxdhHypothesisWitness.lean` now builds one concrete instance and applies both theorems to it with every premise proved rather than assumed. `hb112_instance` applies `PqxdhAuthenticatedEvolvingSecrecy.bound` to the owner `.beacon 0` at record 1, and `hb111_instance` applies `PqxdhAuthenticatedRootBudgets.authenticated_native_root_bound` with both of its conclusions, because its `RootFields` premise is proved as well.

The instance is deliberately trivial and insecure. It has one server and one generated beacon, the empty base oracle, `Unit` for every auxiliary type, a KEM with constant key generation, encapsulation and decapsulation, identity primitives whose signatures never verify, an adversary program that makes no query and a continuation that returns false, so every resource budget in the certificate is zero. Its HKDF is built from a toy HMAC (the first 64 bytes of message followed by key) by zero-salt Extract and the first two RFC 5869 Expand blocks, which is exact HKDF for every production output length. The HKDF prefix law, `SourceFullCorrect` and `SourceRootCorrect` are proved for that construction over any HMAC, so they do not depend on the toy HMAC. The module therefore shows only that the premises are jointly consistent; it says nothing about security, about the size of either bound, or about an adversary that interacts with the protocol.

The module also settles how the ideal model's perfect-correctness KEM law `decap_encap` relates to these results. ML-KEM-768 does not satisfy that law, but neither headline statement reads the KEM fields of `Pqxdh.Crypto`: their KEM is the separate `kem` parameter, whose failures are charged through the explicit correctness-error term. `actual_withKem` and `rootActual_withKem` prove by `rfl` that replacing only the KEM fields and their laws in the source leaves the actual games of HB-112 and HB-111 unchanged, so production can supply any perfectly correct placeholder for those fields. The same `rfl` transfer fails for the HB-112 ideal game, whose prepared prior appears in types through support-indexed subtypes. This does not affect the use of the theorem: it holds for every choice of those fields, and the ideal game is an intermediate object of the bound rather than a statement about production. The model-level and refinement-level agreement theorems that do use `decap_encap` keep their stated scope, as `PQXDH_IDEAL_MODEL.md` now records.

## Audit remediation D: bridged headline statements

The audit found that the HB-111 and HB-112 experiments run a Lean model of the source in which ten extracted functions are replaced by hand-written definitions, related to the extracted code only by separate lemmas that the headline theorems never mention (finding F5). A reader of the headline statement alone could not tell which of those equations hold. `Computational/PqxdhHeadlineBridges.lean` restates both headline theorems with the proved equations attached, so that citing the restated theorem cites the bridges too.

`authenticated_native_root_bound_bridged` repeats HB-111's statement, with the same hypotheses and both conclusions, and conjoins nine bridge equations: the Lean `prepare` equals `server_prepare_commit`, the Lean publication matches `server_commit`, the Lean Phase-1 start matches `beacon_start`, the Lean Beacon publication matches `beacon_commit`, the consumed identifier is the output of `registration_id`, the Lean seal and open hash inputs are the output of `build_commitment_transcript` (for 153-byte associated data and 16-byte tags), the Lean send returns what `SendSeal.finish` returns, the Lean payload split matches `OpenFrameContext.from_frame`, and on the accepted branch the experiment equals a run of the extracted `server_accept`, using only HB-111's own `RootFields` premise. `evolving_bound_bridged` repeats HB-112's bound with the first eight of these. The `_full` versions add a bridge for `validate_init_kex`: for every fixed-width Phase-1 bundle, the extracted validation accepts exactly when the four Lean parsers accept, with the same fields, and rejects with `InvalidKeyEncoding` otherwise; bytes of the wrong width are rejected by the parsers and have no extracted bundle, so width handling in `InitKex.from_encoded` is outside this bridge. For HB-112 the `_full` version also adds the accepted-branch acceptance bridge, which needs HB-111's `RootFields` premise and the server identity map as additional hypotheses.

The module also defines experiments that execute the extracted acceptance on the accepted branch instead of the Lean stand-in, and proves that each has exactly the same output distribution as the original experiment under the `RootFields` premise, so the unchanged bounds hold for them as well. That meets the rule of executing the extracted function for acceptance; the other stand-ins still run as Lean definitions and are covered only by the conjoined equations.

What remained unbridged in this module are the record-opening phases `begin_open`, `OpenCommitment` and `OpenAead`, and `finish_frame_read`. The record-opening phases are now bridged by `PqxdhOpenBridges` (next section). `finish_frame_read` is the check that decoding consumed the whole input; it belongs to frame decoding, which is outside the proof: messages are arbitrary byte strings that each side knows how to decode, so the experiments keep the frame decoder as a free function. The frame decoder, router, writers, auxiliary services, primitives and initial role states also remain free parameters, and `DecoderAgreement` and `SourceWiring` are still not premises. The bridged statements therefore certify a Lean model whose correspondence to the extracted core is proved function by function; record opening is related through a hand-written transcription of the unextracted `execute_open`, and none of these statements verifies the Rust adapter.

## Audit remediation D: record-opening bridge

The first bridging pass left record opening unbridged. In the HB-111 and HB-112 experiments a hand-written Lean program opens each protected record: it splits the payload, queries the commitment hash, compares the digest with the supplied commitment and queries the AEAD. Production instead runs extracted phases (`begin_open`, the `OpenCommitment` transcript, erasure, supplied-commitment and resume steps, and `OpenAead.request` and `finish`), and the adapter function `execute_open` in `beaconcrypt/src/ratchet.rs`, which is not extracted, composes them with the libsodium calls. `Computational/PqxdhOpenBridges.lean` links the two.

Because `execute_open` is not extracted, the module transcribes it by hand as the Lean function `executeOpen`. The transcription calls the extracted phases in the same order as the Rust code. It sends the commitment hash and the AEAD opening to the primitive interface the experiments already use, compares the digest by length-checked byte equality, which is what `libsodium_rs::utils::memcmp` computes (primitive law PL-11 together with the wrapper's length check), and lets the transcript erasure write any array, where production writes zeros. That this transcription matches the Rust function is checked by review, not proved; it is recorded as adapter-level trust in OR-10 of the trusted-boundary inventory. The constant-time behaviour of the comparison and the physical effect of zeroization are not modelled.

Bridge B12 (`open_bridge`) says that for every opening capability of the experiments whose payload and associated data can be represented as a Rust byte slice and a 153-byte array, the extracted payload admission `OpenFrameContext.from_frame` returns normally. If it rejects, the payload has at most 80 bytes, a length the experiments' frame check already rejects, and the experiments' opening step makes no query and returns the entry state. Otherwise the experiments' opening step, and separately its opening callback, are equal as programs to `executeOpen` run on the same ratchet entry and prepared receive with the admitted context. Equality as programs means that the two agree for every hash and AEAD reply, including a failed hash, a mismatched commitment, a failed AEAD and success, and for a capability without material, and that the extracted phases never fail on these inputs. The only side conditions are the representation conditions, which hold for every payload of at most `Std.Usize.max` bytes and every 153-byte associated data. `authenticated_native_root_bound_bridged_open`, `authenticated_extracted_root_bound_open`, `evolving_bound_bridged_open` and `evolving_extracted_bound_open` restate the four existing bridged headline theorems with B12 conjoined, under the same hypotheses; no premise is added. A check of the constants reachable from the statements confirms that `begin_open`, the four `OpenCommitment` functions and `OpenAead.request` and `finish` now occur in them; `finish_frame_read` does not.

Several gaps remain. The experiments still run the hand-written opening; B12 is a conjoined equation, not a change of experiment. Production's capability carries the admitted frame context while the experiments' carries the decoded frame. The next section proves that the extracted receive driver gives both context types capabilities with the same ratchet entry and prepared receive, and relates a hand-written transcription of the adapter loop `decrypt_message_with_ratchet` to the experiments' receive driver. In HB-112 the kernel is published by a symbolic step after the callback, so for HB-112 only the callback equality concerns the opening. `finish_frame_read`, which checks that decoding consumed the whole input, is not bridged: it belongs to frame decoding, and messages are arbitrary byte strings that each side can decode, so the experiments keep the decoder as a free function and no serialization-library behaviour is used.

## Audit remediation D: receive-context bridge

B12 left a gap before the opening step. The experiments and production obtain the opening capability from the same extracted receive functions, `begin_receive` and `ReceiveKdf.resume`, but they attach different contexts to it. The experiments attach the decoded frame and associated data (`OpenContext`); production attaches the payload views admitted by `OpenFrameContext::from_frame` (`OpenFrameContext`). B12 compares capabilities with the same ratchet entry and prepared receive, but nothing showed that the two contexts lead to such a pair. Production also drives these functions from an unextracted loop in `decrypt_message_with_ratchet` (`beaconcrypt/src/ratchet.rs`), and nothing related that loop to the experiments' receive driver. `Computational/PqxdhOpenContextBridge.lean` addresses both.

The extracted receive functions never inspect the context; they only store it. `begin_receive_map` and `resume_map` unfold the extracted code to prove this: running the functions with a context transformed by any function gives the same complete result, including failures and every rejection, except that the stored context is transformed. So, for any sequence of KDF replies, if the receive with the experiments' context reaches an opening capability, the receive with production's context reaches one with the same ratchet entry and prepared receive (`open_transfer`, `open_frame_context_transfer`). `opened_record_bridge` combines this with B12. The experiments' own driver `RawCtxOwnerOracle.receive` behaves the same way: with a transformed context it issues the same KDF queries, and its opening query is on the transformed capability (`oracle_receive_map`).

Because `decrypt_message_with_ratchet` is not extracted, the module transcribes its post-decoding part by hand. `executeDecoded` compares the sender key identifier with the expected one and calls the extracted `from_frame` admission. If either check rejects, it returns the unchanged kernel and no plaintext. `executeReceiveFrom` then calls the extracted `begin_receive`, and `executeReceive` runs the loop. A rejection returns its kernel. A KDF request goes to the experiments' KDF interface (production calls `ratchet_hkdf` here), and the reply is passed to the extracted `ReceiveKdf.resume`. An opening capability goes to `executeOpen`, the transcription of `execute_open` from B12. Production takes the kernel out of its slot before the loop and puts the returned kernel back; the transcription models this by taking the kernel as an argument and returning the kernel to reinstall. Review, not proof, establishes that these transcriptions match the Rust function, and the same holds for the list-of-replies model used by `opened_record_bridge`. This is recorded as adapter-level trust in OR-10 of the trusted-boundary inventory.

`receive_loop_bridge` proves that the transcribed loop started with production's context equals the experiments' receive driver started with the experiments' context. It requires that `from_frame` admits production's context for a byte slice and a 153-byte array representing the frame's payload and associated data. `decoded_receive_bridge` extends this to the checks. For every decoded frame, the transcribed checks and loop equal the part of the experiments' raw receive `RawCtxWholeOwner.rawReceive` that runs after decoding and before the result is published. The checks agree for three reasons: the sender comparisons are the same; the extracted admission rejects exactly the payloads of at most 80 bytes, which is the experiments' length condition; and a 153-byte array meets the experiments' associated-data length condition. Both equalities hold as programs over the experiments' KDF, hash and AEAD queries. They therefore hold for every reply, including rejection before or after KDF replies, a failed hash, a mismatched commitment, a failed AEAD and success. The only side conditions are B12's representation conditions. The same equalities also hold before the primitive interface is embedded into the receive adapter (`receive_loop_native`, `decoded_receive_native`), including at the interface of the HB-111 target opening site `PqxdhBeaconPhase2Shared.afterRoot` (`decoded_after_root`). No security premise is added, and no headline theorem is restated.

Several gaps remain. The empty-input rejection is not transcribed. Frame decoding is outside the proof, including the check that decoding consumed the whole input and the sequence number read from the frame: messages are arbitrary byte strings that each side knows how to decode, the bridges quantify over the decoded frame, and no serialization-library behaviour is used. This module does not address whether `ratchet_hkdf` answers the KDF query correctly (OR-07). The transcriptions, the kernel take and put, and the serialization of operations on one owner remain adapter-level trust. The experiments still run their hand-written programs. The bridges are separate equations rather than a change of experiment, and they are not conjoined with the headline theorems. HB-112's experiments use `RawCtxWholeOwner.rawReceive` in `PqxdhBeaconPhase2Publication.afterRoot`, but they also receive through a symbolic chain owner with the driver `RawCtxPendingOwnerQueries.calls`. Existing theorems relate that driver to `RawCtxChainReceive.execute` (`RawCtxPendingOwnerQueries.receive_call`) and, under realization premises, to `RawCtxOwnerOracle.receive` (`RawCtxChainRealization.receive_native`). This module does not compose them with `receive_loop_bridge`.

`PqxdhReceiveHeadlineBridges` puts these bridges into the headline statements, as audit finding F5 asks. `ReceiveBridge` is the conjunction of `ContextBridge` with the native-interface statements `decoded_receive_native` and `decoded_after_root`, and the four theorems `authenticated_native_root_bound_bridged_receive`, `authenticated_extracted_root_bound_receive`, `evolving_bound_bridged_receive` and `evolving_extracted_bound_receive` state the corresponding record-opening restatement of `PqxdhOpenBridges` together with `ReceiveBridge`, under the same hypotheses. A check of the constants reachable from their statements confirms that they now also reach `ReceiveKdf.impl.request` and the transcriptions `executeDecoded` and `executeReceive`. The added conjunct is a proved equation between hand-written transcriptions of adapter code and the experiments; it does not change the experiments or verify the Rust adapter.

## Audit remediation B: server authentication (in progress)

Milestone B proves that a Beacon completes registration only with a response that an honest Server session derived (audit finding F1). The reviewed route R1 adds one idealization, zero-salt HKDF-Extract on 192-byte inputs as a programmable random oracle, and one hardness assumption, a Gap-DH-type assumption on X25519 treated as a black box; partnering is by identical root derivation, and the design grounded in the Rust implementation is in `doc/impl/audit-0b4039e-remediation-plan.md` section 6. Only the first stages are built so far, and no server-authentication theorem is stated yet.

`PqxdhExtractRomSeparation` defines the patched HMAC `romHmac hmac table`, which answers from `table` on the zero key and 192-byte messages and is the real HMAC everywhere else (`eval_other`). It proves that the idealization touches nothing else the protocol computes: the ratchet's Extract inputs are 32 bytes and the PQXDH root input is 192 bytes in the extracted types (`ratchet_input_ne`, `root_input_eq`), every HKDF-Expand keeps its real value for every table (`expandRoot_same`, `expandFull_same`), and the 76-byte and 64-byte production ratchet responses equal HKDF over the patched HMAC (`production_ratchet_unchanged`, under the existing functional contracts `SourceFullCorrect` and the ratchet prefix contract of the production source bundle). That production makes exactly two kinds of zero-salt Extract call, on the root input and on 32-byte ratchet inputs, is adapter-level trust citing `beaconcrypt/src/pqxdh.rs:46-58` and `beaconcrypt/src/ratchet.rs:86-98`.

`PqxdhServerAuthAssumptions` states the X25519 class law as a named premise: if two peer inputs give the same X25519 output under one scalar, they give the same output under every scalar. It holds for clamped X25519 because equal nonzero outputs mean the peers differ by negation and a small-order point, and equal zero outputs mean both peers have small order. It is a functional contract like the existing `dh_comm`, not a hardness assumption, and it is satisfiable by a non-degenerate toy function while ruling out functions that ignore the scalar. With it, a reduction that holds neither the Server seed nor the Beacon's prekey scalar can decide whether two peers give the same DH value by evaluating both under a scalar it holds (`static_iff`, `scalar_iff`). The module also names the Gap-DH term `serverGapDhAdvantage` as the advantage in the existing game `PqxdhJointGapDh.game`; no new hardness game is defined. The game's decision services answer on every 32-byte input the X25519 function accepts, so this is a Gap-DH-type assumption rather than one implied by textbook Gap-DH; its plausibility pointers are Signal's PQXDH specification, Okamoto and Pointcheval (PKC 2001) and Abdalla, Bellare and Rogaway (CT-RSA 2001), and the twist-inclusive form rests on the twist security of Curve25519 (Bernstein, PKC 2006; RFC 7748). The owner approved two further functional contracts on 2026-09-30, both stated in the same module: `X25519ScalarSpread` (for a fixed peer, a nonzero X25519 output comes from at most 64 scalar strings, which bounds the chance that two Server sessions reach the Beacon's root input) and `NonzeroHonestDh` (X25519 with an honest public key is never all-zero, used only by the negative controls).

`PqxdhExtractRomFamily` builds the random oracle that the experiment will use. `romImpl` answers the adversary's public HMAC queries with the real function outside the zero-key, 192-byte slice (`rom_public_real`) and from a lazily sampled table inside it (`rom_hit`, `rom_miss`), and it answers the honest root derivations of the Server and the Beacon from the same table (`rom_derive_hit`). Every table read is logged, the table only grows, and the answers never depend on the log (`rom_history_append`, `rom_cache_mono`). An honest derivation and the adversary's zero-key query at the same bytes read the same entry, whichever comes first (`rom_side`, `derive_then_public`, `public_then_derive`), and a root request is one table read followed by the real 47-byte root Expand, which never falls in the table (`rom_root`, `rootExpand_outside`). The answers agree with the patched HMAC of `PqxdhExtractRomSeparation` for any table extending the final cache (`rom_public_patch`, `rom_derive_patch`).

`PqxdhServerAuthKeySchedule` bounds the key schedule that turns a table entry into the first ratchet keys. Its output is the 108 bytes the Server and the Beacon use first: the 76-byte ratchet step of the first half of the 64-byte initializer, derived by the production HKDF from the 32-byte root Expand of the entry, together with the second half of the initializer. `keySchedule_bound` shows that for any distinguisher, telling this output for a uniform entry from 108 uniform bytes is at most the sum of five advantages of reductions built from that distinguisher: the root Expand as an HMAC PRF, the initializer's zero-salt Extract of the uniform root, the initializer's Expand, the step's Extract of the uniform first half, and the step's two-block Expand. The only premise is the functional contract `SourceFullCorrect`, and `fromRoot_model` checks that the output bytes are the model's `ratchetOut` and `rootChains`. `keySchedule_bound_context` gives the same bound when side information is sampled before the entry.

`PqxdhPhase2LocalMatching` prepares the step that charges the second kind of win, where the Beacon accepts a partner's root but a different key identifier, payload or associated data, to first-record CTX integrity. The Beacon's accepted fields are the key identifier of the registration reply, the plaintext after its 8-byte key-identifier prefix, and the associated data built from the pinned Server identity and the Beacon's own identity (`acceptedFields`, following `beacon.rs:462-484` and core `pqxdh.rs:616-628`); the partner's sealed fields are read the same way from its sequence-one seal (`sealedFields`, `server.rs:463-477`). `accepted_of_match` shows that if the accepted record opens as a record that the partner sealed with the same nonce, associated data and encoding, the two field triples are equal, so an accepted tuple that differs from every partner seal is a CTX forgery (`fresh_forall`, `won_of_attempt`). The native provenance lemmas (`local_opening`, `consumer_opening`, `consumer_matching`) tie the key that opened the accepted record to the receive material the run reached from the Beacon's installed kernel, which the later CTX step identifies with the partner's first-record key. `joint` shows that all premises of `accepted_of_match` can hold together, and `relay_fields` shows that an honest relay gives equal fields. The frame decoder stays a free function, and the only primitive facts used are AEAD correctness and the 16-byte tag length.

`PqxdhServerAuthExperiment` defines the server-authentication game. The game samples the Server's identity seed and all of the target Beacon's secrets itself and publishes the Beacon's Phase 1. The adversary gets the registration methods of the public Rust `ProviderServer` trait as two oracles: accept (`get_shared_secret`, `server.rs:332-422`) validates a Phase 1 message, consumes its registration identifier and derives a root, and returns a session handle; build (`build_registration_response`, `server.rs:424-502`) consumes a pending session, assigns the next key identifier, seals the sequence-one record under a payload the adversary chooses, and returns Phase 2. It also gets the target Beacon's single finish, the patched HMAC of route R1, the BLAKE2b random oracle, and a reveal of any installed Server session. A reveal returns only the kernel installed after the sequence-one seal, which is proved to be the kernel advanced by the first send, holding neither the initial send chain nor the sequence-one key (`reveal_post_registration`, at every reachable state). The game logs every derivation and every seal, and freezes a snapshot of the log at the Beacon's acceptance. A Server session is a partner when it derived the same 192-byte root input as the Beacon (`partner_iff_root_input`, at run level against the extracted `server_accept` and Beacon builder). The adversary wins if the Beacon accepts and, in the snapshot, no session is a partner (W1), partners exist but none sealed the accepted key identifier, payload and associated data (W2), or two sessions are partners (W3). `win_le_games` splits the win probability into the events the later stages bound, and the invariant `GameInv` records the facts they need: the finish is atomic, every seal comes from a session that derived a root, a session seals at most once, and a finish can succeed only once (`finish_single_shot`). The module lists twelve adversary restrictions with their justification, among them no Beacon secret reveal (no key-compromise impersonation is claimed), no reveal of a pending session (the Rust token is opaque), and record oracles omitted because a reveal lets the adversary compute them. Win and the other events do not depend on the derived roots kept in the log (`win_erase`), which the key-factoring stage uses.

`PqxdhServerAuthNegativeControl` checks that the experiment can be won when it should be and is not won by honest behaviour. `negative_control`: if the Server's identity seed is revealed to the adversary before the finish, an explicit adversary that never queries the Server builds its own Phase 2 for the target Beacon, using the seed, its own ephemeral key and encapsulation, the public random-oracle HMAC and BLAKE2b, and makes the Beacon accept with no partner session (W1) with probability at least one minus the ML-KEM correctness error. `relay_not_win`: an honest relay that passes the Beacon's Phase 1 to the Server, builds the response and delivers it wins with probability at most the KEM correctness error, and `relay_live` shows that this relay does reach the Beacon's acceptance with probability at least one minus that error, so the upper bound is not vacuous. The premises are the existing functional contracts (deterministic decapsulation, the ChaCha20-Poly1305 body-length contract), the approved nonzero-honest-DH law, and abstract codec laws saying that each side reads back what the other writes and that writers succeed on messages below a size limit; no hardness assumption is used. A toy instance satisfying all premises at once, with zero KEM error, is checked outside the library and will be added with the witness stage.

## Audit remediation C: first-record integrity for a protocol-derived key

HB-112 shows that one protocol-derived key is indistinguishable from uniform while in use, and the HB-127 record endpoints bound forgeries for an independent uniform key. Nothing connected the two, so no statement said that a record protected by a key the protocol actually derives cannot be forged (audit findings F7 and F9). Eight new modules build that connection for the first record that Beacon `b` sends after an honest registration. The first six reach an end-to-end inequality whose right-hand side still contains two explicit game terms, and the last two bound those terms, so the final inequality `PqxdhFirstRecordStopTagged.first_beacon_record_integrity_stop` contains only reduction advantages and explicit statistical terms. A ninth module, `PqxdhFirstRecordReplay`, extends the event with replays at the same bound.

The event is stated through the adversary's own view, because the HB-112 hybrid chain carries only the adversary's final bit. `PqxdhFirstBeaconRecordIntegrity.forgeryPost` wraps any post-registration adversary, logs its transcript, and outputs its bit together with `Forged`: the Server peer created by the registration accepted a sequence-1 record whose decoded frame differs from every sequence-1 record that any honest sender returned earlier. Logging adds no oracle query, so the adversary's resource certificate carries over. The counted probability is the HB-112 target event for that adversary on the branch where Beacon `b`'s honest session exists: `b` published record 1 from the selected root and the selected chain was never disclosed.

The chain of steps is as follows. `PqxdhFirstRecordTarget` specialises HB-112's first-record bound to one fixed target and splits both the real and the key-last ideal game exactly into their completed and pending branches, charging the completed branch once more with the authenticated-root reductions. `PqxdhSelectedFirstRecord` proves that the key-last ideal's native continuation, run with the target step fixed to a key, nonce and next chain, is exactly the selected-key compiled run of the saved post interpreter under an explicit state projection, with no premise for the actual prepared callbacks. `PqxdhFirstBeaconRecordIntegrity` moves from that run to the stopped source interpreter and then to the executable CTX client, keeping the undisclosure of the selected chain through the coupling. `PqxdhFirstBeaconRecordCtx` compiles the Server's registration builder into the same CTX client, moves the key draw first, charges the case where the two halves of the uniform initializer response are equal (2^-256), and applies the existing adaptive authentication bound with raw and seal budgets derived from the certificate. `first_beacon_record_integrity` then bounds the pending-branch forgery probability by HB-112's target loss, the completed-branch root loss, the CTX terms (the IND$ advantage of the constructed validation reduction, qHash/2^128, twice the sum of the INT-CTXT advantages of the constructed indexed reductions, and qRaw/2^512), 2^-256, and two game terms. Public HKDF stays real and every existing assumption term stays explicit; BLAKE2b is the programmable random oracle of the CTX games.

Two game terms remained after that step. `gapGame` is the probability that the compiled run ends with the forgery bit set while the ordinary CTX observer does not win. `PqxdhFirstBeaconRecordCanonical` bounds it by 2^-256 for a corrected event. The original event compared decoded frames. Messages are arbitrary byte strings that each side knows how to decode, and the record writer and frame decoder are free functions of the experiment, so nothing guarantees that the bytes an honest sender returned decode; if they do not, while another byte string decoding to the same frame is accepted, the original event counts a genuine record as forged. The canonical event `CanonicalForged` instead counts an accepted sequence-1 record only if the writer's encoding of its decoded frame is not the byte string an honest sender returned, so re-encodings of genuine records are never counted (`sent_reencoding_not_counted`). With it, `first_slot_hidden` proves without any premise that the Server peer's first-message slot stays hidden until consumed, and `gap_le` shows that a canonical forgery the observer does not win happens only in the initializer-alias case. The only added premise is `ReadWritable`: the writer produces bytes for every frame the reader returns. It is a property of the abstract message model (a frame one side can decode is a frame the other side can write), relates two environment functions, and involves no probability, adversary or secret; no property of a serialization library is used or proved. The event can miss a real forgery only if the writer maps two different frames to the same bytes. `first_beacon_record_integrity_canonical` therefore bounds the canonical forgery probability by HB-112's target loss, the completed-branch root loss, the CTX terms, 2^-256 twice, and the one remaining game term, `stopGame`.

`stopGame` is the probability that a second seal under the selected key and nonce happens while the selected chain is still undisclosed. `PqxdhFirstRecordNonceStop` reduces it to a repeated sending-chain input, and `PqxdhFirstRecordStopBound` moves it to the source-only run and proves that no Beacon other than the freshly generated one can finish on the selected response, because only that Beacon holds a generated KEM handle. The theorem also takes a named hash-budget premise on the existing preparation program (`PrepareHashBudget`, shown satisfiable) and a numeric side condition that the total query count is below 2^96.

`PqxdhFirstRecordStopTagged` bounds the remaining probability. For Beacon `b` the selected sending chain is `target`, the second 32 bytes of the uniform 64-byte initializer block; the first 32 bytes are independent of it. The proof runs the source-only game with a tagged interpreter in which each chain is either known bytes or the one hidden selected chain. The tagged interpreter never reads `target`: it answers private derivations on the hidden chain with the programmed replies, and it records every known chain from which it derives in a log. Openings, sealings and public HKDF are the real ones, because they do not read the private table. A coupling shows that the actual run and the tagged run agree until a logged known chain equals `target`, and that a second use of the selected chain while it is undisclosed cannot happen without such a collision (`stop_tagged`, `post_triple`). At the start of the run, only the freshly generated Beacon holds a generated KEM handle (`PqxdhFirstRecordStopBound.front_only`), so no other Beacon can reach the selected chain through the initializer. Because the tagged run never reads `target`, `target` can be drawn after the run (`delayed_bound`), and the chance that it equals one of the logged chains is at most the log length divided by 2^256. By the existing per-operation derivation bounds, the log gains at most one entry per send and at most 51 per raw receive or finish attempt, plus one for the send of the first Server builder (`build_log`, `run_log`). `source_stop_bound` therefore bounds the source-only term by (1 + qSend + 51 (qRaw + qFinish)) / 2^256, where the budgets are the adversary's query budgets for sends, raw receives and finish attempts, and `canonical_stop_bound` instantiates them with the post budgets of the adversary's resource certificate. `first_beacon_record_integrity_stop` substitutes this into `first_beacon_record_integrity_canonical`. Its premises are exactly those of that theorem, and no premise is added: the query budgets come from the certificate, and the bound involves no probability premise.

For replay (F7), `PqxdhFirstRecordReplay.first_beacon_record_integrity_replay` bounds a larger event by the same right-hand side and under the same premises as `first_beacon_record_integrity_stop`: a canonical first-record forgery, or a reacceptance at the registered Server peer. A reacceptance is an accepted Server raw receive at that peer whose decoded frame has the sequence number of a frame the peer had already accepted; every accepted exact replay of an accepted record and every second accepted sequence-1 record is one (`replay_reaccepted`, `second_first_reaccepted`), and reacceptance is excluded at every sequence number, not only the first. The proof follows the actual game's Server raw receive through the routing and the frame decoder into the extracted receive driver running on the stored peer state. Admission, the skipped-key cache and publication are extracted code, and only the key-derivation and opening replies come from oracles, so no free environment function decides acceptance. For arbitrary oracle replies, routing, decoder and writer, the peer's receive control stays structurally valid and has consumed every accepted sequence number, a consumed sequence number is rejected with the state unchanged, and no other query kind replaces or resets the peer (`receive_result`, `compiler_tracks`, `logged_invariant`). Hence no reachable transcript of the pending branch has a reacceptance, for every adversary and whatever its final bit (`no_reacceptance`), the reacceptance-only proxy's HB-112 difference is zero (`reaccepted_zero`), and adding reacceptance to the event changes no probability (`replay_canonical`). That no later operation re-installs the peer holds by construction of the game's post interface, which has no Server registration, snapshot or restore query after the first builder. The event uses the sequence number of the frame that the decoder returns, which is the target the driver checks, and not the sequence field of the opening reply, which is an arbitrary oracle answer at the level where the adversary's queries are answered. The single-step driver fact `replay_not_counted` is unchanged. The replay statement covers only the Server peer registered by the first Server builder. Confidentiality of the record, Server-owned targets and records after the first are not covered by the integrity statements.

### First-record confidentiality (S7)

`PqxdhFirstRecordConfidentiality.first_record_confidentiality` is a left-or-right confidentiality statement for the same record: the first record that Beacon `b` sends after an honest registration hides which of two equal-length plaintexts it carries. The experiment is the HB-112 actual game with every secret sampled inside, run with the wrapper post `confPost adversary b β`. The adversary has the whole post-registration interface (sends and raw receives of every Server peer and Beacon, reveals, selectors and Beacon finish attempts). It also has one challenge query, which takes two plaintexts `m0` and `m1` and returns the record produced when Beacon `b` sends `m_β`. `confGame β` is the accepted pending leaf of the HB-112 actual game for record 1 of Beacon `b` with this post. It counts the runs in which the adversary outputs `true` and all of the following hold: the challenge is fresh, record 1 of Beacon `b` is published from the selected root, and the selected chain and the record key are undisclosed. Restricting to this leaf is the honest-session condition: in the other branches Beacon `b` has no honest partnered session and the adversary may know its root. The notion is single-challenge adaptive left-or-right confidentiality of one honest session's first record in the full multi-party protocol, with state reveals and replayable-CCA-style receive suppression. The theorem bounds `|Pr[confGame false] - Pr[confGame true]|`.

The wrapper and HB-112's event impose the following restrictions inside the experiment. None of them is a premise about the adversary.

- Equal lengths. A challenge with `|m0| ≠ |m1|` is refused without any request, because a CTX record reveals the length of its plaintext.
- One challenge, sent as Beacon `b`'s first send. Only the first acceptable challenge is forwarded, and only if no send of Beacon `b` was requested before, because the statement concerns the single key that HB-112 selects: the key of record 1 of Beacon `b`.
- Fresh challenge. The adversary's bit counts only if the challenge returned a sequence-1 record and no adversary send of Beacon `b` returned a sequence-1 record (`Fresh`). This makes the challenge the record whose publication HB-112's event requires, and it excludes only runs in which the challenge did not become that record.
- Receive replies. After the challenge, a Server or Beacon raw-receive reply whose decrypted plaintext equals `m0` or `m1` is reported to the adversary as a failure; the receive itself still takes effect (`suppress`, `screen`). The suppression is by plaintext because receives take abstract byte strings and the proof does not reason about their encoding. It also hides unrelated records that carry `m0` or `m1`, which is harmless because every other plaintext a receive can return was chosen by the adversary or comes from a ciphertext the adversary built. Beacon finish replies are not screened; runs in which a finish opens with the selected key are charged to `collGame` below. The raw receive oracle returns plaintexts, so delivering the challenge record, or a replay of it, would reveal β. This is the restriction of replayable CCA security (Canetti, Krawczyk and Nielsen, CRYPTO 2003), with the failure reply in place of a separate symbol, and which replies are suppressed does not depend on β. It replaces the plan's wording that the target record is not delivered: delivery is allowed, and the restriction also covers other records that carry `m0` or `m1`.
- Undisclosed selected chain and record key, and publication from the selected root. These are HB-112's event. Revealing the selected chain gives the adversary the record key; that chain is Beacon `b`'s sending chain before the challenge and the Server's matching receiving chain before it receives record 1. Revealing the record key itself does the same. A Beacon that finished on a response the adversary chose has a root the adversary knows.

A left-or-right bound needs every step in both directions, so the proof runs the first-record integrity chain both ways. `PqxdhFirstRecordTarget.pending_bound` moves each side to HB-112's key-last ideal. An instrumented copy of the compiled post (`insImpl`) records three things: the origin and publication transcript, whether Beacon `b`'s first send used the selected hidden material, and whether a Beacon finish opened a record with the selected key. The C5 steps then reach an ordinary CTX client: the Server builder, the key-first reordering and the initializer half-alias term 2^-256. The CTX privacy bound (`AdaptiveCtxDynamicKnownBounds.selected_privacy`, the core of `privacy_bound`) compares that client's selected-key game with its random view (`source_random`). The two random views are equal (`random_views_equal`). In the random view a selected seal returns a uniform body and tag of the plaintext's length. The two clients run identically until the adaptively chosen challenge (`Pre`). After it they differ only in the challenge plaintext and in replies that agree once `m1` is identified with `m0` (`Twin`). Such clients have the same output distribution in the random view (`randomView_pre`, `client_pre`). The argument would fail if the challenge were not a hidden selected seal. `hiddenGap_zero` shows, from an origin invariant of the compiled run (`all_run`, `gap_free`), that the confidentiality event forces the challenge to use the selected hidden material, so that term is exactly zero.

For each β, the bound contains the following terms:

- the CTX privacy loss `twinLoss` of the constructed client: the IND$ advantages of the constructed validation and view reductions, qHash/2^128, twice the INT-CTXT advantages of the constructed indexed reductions, and qRaw/2^512;
- HB-112's first-record target loss and completed-branch root loss for the post `confPost adversary b β`;
- the stop bound (1 + sends + 51 × (raw receives + finish attempts)) / 2^256 of `PqxdhFirstRecordStopTagged.stop_bound`, with the post budgets of the certificate for that wrapper post;
- the two game terms described below.

Added once overall is 2/2^256. The premises are HB-112's premises. In addition, for each of the two wrapper posts the theorem takes one resource certificate, one `PrepareHashBudget` premise and the side condition that the query count is below 2^96. `first_record_confidentiality_budget` restates the bound with the adversary's own per-kind budget, counting each challenge as one Beacon `b` send (`conf_query_bound`, `confCertificate`), so the stop terms become 2 (1 + sends + 51 × (raw receives + finish attempts)) / 2^256. `single_output` and `single_true` show that the counted event is reachable, and `unscreened_reveals` is a negative control: without the receive screening, the reply to opening the challenge record determines β. `ReadWritable` is not needed. Records are byte strings that each side knows how to decode, and no serialization-library property is used.

Two game terms per bit were explicit in `first_record_confidentiality`. Both are now bounded: `keyGame` below and `collGame` in the next subsection, and `first_record_confidentiality_complete` states the bound without any game term.

`collGame` is the probability, in the selected-key CTX game, that the confidentiality event holds and some Beacon finish opened a record with the selected key. A finish parses the plaintext it opens, so its behaviour could depend on β if it opened the challenge record. For that reason such runs are split off rather than compared. Such an opening requires a finish to derive a chain equal to the hidden selected chain `target`. The marked Beacon receives on the other half of the uniform initializer block, every other finish derives from values that do not depend on `target`, and a finish makes at most 51 derivations. The planned bound reuses `PqxdhFirstRecordStopTagged`. Its tagged log already records every chain from which a finish derives, so `delayed_bound` and `run_log` apply unchanged. The coupling, however, must also track the concrete finish's derivations, which `PqxdhFirstRecordNonceStop.sourceObserved` does not record. The event includes the confidentiality event because that coupling holds only while the selected chain is undisclosed.

`keyGame` is the probability, in the key-last run with a uniform record key, that the first-record event and the absence of hidden disclosure hold while the record key equals one of the values the adversary revealed. `PqxdhFirstRecordKeyBound.key_bound` bounds it. The proof first moves from the key-last run to the instrumented compiled run (`keyRun_le`), paying the nonce-repeat stop term once more, which `PqxdhFirstRecordStopTagged.stop_bound` bounds. In the compiled run the record key is used only by the selected CTX operations, and a reveal of a hidden slot stops the run with no reply and leaves only a nonce marker in the history, so every revealed value that could equal the key is a candidate computed without the key (`keys_hit`). The number of candidates is bounded from the adversary's certificate: the prepared history is bounded by `PqxdhInitialPreparedSourceCaps.prepared_history`, the builder keeps it, and each compiled post request adds at most one observation (`ins_history_run`), which gives `candidateCount` (the initial reveal observations, the preparation cap and the post budget). A key-free client that returns its candidates is then moved, with the key kept, to the canonical CTX game (`RawCtxPrefixKeyOrder.complete`, `schedule_interpretation`, `real_schedule`), and `RawCtxSelectedKeyProbes.candidate_bound` bounds a hit by `recoveryLoss`: twice the sum of the IND$ advantage of the constructed validation reduction, the guessing term (qHash + candidates)/2^128 and the INT-CTXT advantages of the constructed attempt-indexed reductions. The initializer half alias adds 2^-256. `first_record_confidentiality_key` and `first_record_confidentiality_key_budget` substitute this into the confidentiality bound for both bits under the same premises, so `collGame` is the only explicit game term left.

### First-record confidentiality: bounding the finish-collision term and the complete statement

The confidentiality chain of `PqxdhFirstRecordConfidentiality` left, for each challenge bit, an explicit game `collGame`: in the selected-key CTX source game of the instrumented confidentiality client, the first-record event holds and some attempted Beacon finish made a selected raw opening, that is, a finish opened its application record with the hidden record key of the attacked chain. Such an opening is only possible if the finish's receive derives its message key on a chain equal to the hidden selected chain, which the adversary does not know. `PqxdhFirstRecordFinishBound.coll_bound` proves that `collGame` is at most `(2 + qSend + 51 (qRaw + qFinish)) / 2^256`, where `qSend`, `qRaw` and `qFinish` are the post budgets for sends, raw receives and attempted finishes. The premise is the same query-budget premise as the nonce-repeat stop bound, and `coll_real` takes it from the resource certificate, so no new assumption is introduced.

The proof treats a hit as a property of the finish request itself instead of recording the finish's derivations in a history. A compiled finish can only make a selected raw opening at the single terminal opening of its application receive, and only when that opening carries the hidden material. The receive path before that opening is deterministic, so whether it happens depends only on the Beacon kernel, the registration candidate and the delivered bytes. The predicate `HitRaw` states exactly this event, and `raw_quiet` and `lower_quiet` show that without it the compiled finish makes no selected raw opening. The finish programs `ownerMarkedHit` and `ownerHit` are the original finish programs with this predicate returned as one extra bit. `hit_dominates` shows that the raw-opening flag of the instrumented compiled run is raised only when that bit is set.

The flag is then carried from the compiled world into the source world. `hitObserved` is the source post of the stop-term analysis with a sticky hit flag that collects the bit of `ownerHit`. The compiled finish and the source finish are two images of one evaluated run of the same finish program, so the two worlds stay coupled with equal replies and matching states, and a raised raw flag always comes with a raised hit flag (`aug_finish`, `aug_run`, `aug_hit`). The source world is in turn coupled with the target-free tagged world that already bounds the stop term, and the coupling is simpler than the stop term's. A hit does not need that coupling's invariant, because a derivation that returns the hidden material on a known chain immediately writes the selected value into the tagged log. Two structural facts make this precise. The first is material provenance: a terminal opening with hidden material is preceded by a derivation that returned hidden material (`terminal_hit`). The second is chain provenance: a receive derives first on the kernel's receiving chain and then on the chains it just derived (`begin_request`, `resume_request`), and the kernel installed by any finish has a known receiving chain (`initial_clean`). Hence every derivation of a finish's tagged receive is on a known chain, and a hit logs the selected value (`stage_hit`, `hit_coupled`, `hit_tagged`). The event therefore reduces to the same target-free tagged run as the stop term. Its final log has at most one builder entry, one entry per send and fifty-one entries per raw receive and per finish. The selected half of the initializer block is drawn independently of the run, which gives `(1 + qSend + 51 (qRaw + qFinish)) / 2^256`. One further `2^-256` pays for the initial half alias when the CTX game is reordered into prepared samples (`client_le_out`). The stop term and `collGame` reduce to the same tagged event, but they arise at different places of the chain, so the final bound keeps one term for each.

`PqxdhFirstRecordConfidentialityComplete.first_record_confidentiality_complete` combines this bound with the key-disclosure bound of `PqxdhFirstRecordKeyBound`. It has exactly the premises of `first_record_confidentiality`; a MetaM comparison checks that all 38 binders agree in name, binder kind and type. The difference between the accepted pending masses of the two challenge bits is at most the sum over both bits of the following terms. The first is the ordinary CTX privacy loss `twinLoss` of the constructed confidentiality client: IND$ advantages of the constructed validation and view reductions, `qHash / 2^128`, twice the INT-CTXT advantages of the constructed attempt-indexed reductions, and `qRaw / 2^512`. The second is the HB-112 first-record target loss of the challenge-fixed post. The third is the completed-branch loss: joint identity, KEM correctness error, one-key IND-CCA, Extract and one HMAC-PRF term. The fourth is the key-recovery loss `recoveryLoss` of the constructed candidate client. The fifth is the finish-collision number `(2 + qSend + 51 (qRaw + qFinish)) / 2^256`, and the sixth is two nonce-repeat stop bounds `(1 + qSend + 51 (qRaw + qFinish)) / 2^256`. Finally, `4 / 2^256` in total covers the initial half aliases. Every loss is the advantage of an explicitly constructed reduction or an explicit number. A check of the elaborated statement confirms that its right side mentions no `collGame`, `keyGame`, `stopGame` and no distribution `𝒟[·]`. `first_record_confidentiality_complete_budget` states the same result with the adversary's own per-kind budget, each challenge counted as one Beacon `b` send, and has exactly the premises of `first_record_confidentiality_budget` (39 binders, checked the same way). Both theorems depend only on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`, and no serialization-library behaviour is used.

## Audit remediation B: the Server-send factor

`PqxdhServerAuthSendFactor` promotes the handed-over Server-send spike into 24 guarded statements. It closes one functional part of B8b: a Server registration build uses the root only through a 108-byte value consisting of the complete 76-byte first sending-chain response and the initial 32-byte receiving chain. `server_send_factor` equates the complete interpreted build with a continuation that takes just that value. The equality preserves the response, Server peers and control, auxiliary state and effects, writer failures, and shared CTX cache. It applies to arbitrary pending registrations and existing Server state; it assumes neither that a peer is installed nor that writing succeeds. It introduces no security assumption, reduction loss or query bound. This module preserves the proofs from the handover; it does not yet factor the authentication experiment's entire adaptive run.

The interpretation lemmas (`native_known`, `settled_native`, `native_embed`, `embed_settled`, `native_settled`, `publish_settled`) give existing peers concrete known chains and show that a kernel with two known chains no longer depends on the interpretation of the hidden chain. `initial_factor` represents the initial Server sending chain by a hidden slot while retaining its receiving chain. `cut_source` and `build_native` carry that representation through the exact preparation gates and generic builder. `send_begin`, `initial_ok` and `send_shape` identify the exhausted-send case and the step that replaces the hidden sending chain with the supplied next chain. `settle_after`, `settle_candidate`, `settle_generic` and `settle_build` then show that every kernel the builder publishes has two known chains; on any rejected branch the original Server state is kept. The root-free `resolve` interpretation is therefore valid for the complete result, not merely for its ciphertext.

`prim_send_source` keeps the same chain interpretation for an arbitrary lawful monad and seal handler whose KDF branch is the real source response.
