## Free-schedule ProVerif registration (fs-registration)

The free-schedule (fs) scenarios are a new ProVerif family in which the attacker, not the model author, chooses the order of the Server and Beacon operations, with one exception in this scenario: a Server object's build or drop directly follows the accept it answers, and the argument that this covers every Rust order is the pending paper obligation L1 (see [Pending paper arguments](#pending-paper-arguments)). `fs-registration` is the first of them and covers registration only; record exchange follows in separate fs scenarios. It addresses three findings of the proof audit for registration: the fixed schedule, the proof-only replay guard and origin tables, and verdicts that hold for reasons unrelated to their reading. Every result below is a symbolic result (Dolev-Yao attacker, free constructors, ideal hash, KDF and AEAD) for a bounded process. None of them is a computational bound, and none may be presented as one. Until the paper arguments L1 and L5 are written and reviewed, each result is a symbolic result for the fs process, which models the Rust interface under these pending abstraction steps, and every Rust reading below is conditional on them and on the reviewed event projection L6. The 35 earlier ProVerif scenarios are unchanged and keep their exact verdicts as regression fixtures. The [fs-registration guide](impl/proverif-free-schedule-registration.md) records the model files, the Rust mapping, the measured run times and memory, and the open items.

### What the fs-registration model contains

The model runs any number of Server objects. All of them hold the one honest Server identity key, and each keeps its own consumed-registration set and key-ID counter, as a Rust `Server` object does. Each object handles up to three attacker-chosen registration bundles in the exact Rust order: decode, identity tag, the three signature checks, `validate_init_kex`, the registration ID, the consumed-set check, the fresh ephemeral and KEM coins, the four DH calls, the root, and only then the insertion into the consumed set. After each accepted bundle the attacker decides whether the application builds the response on the same object (assigning the next key ID and sealing the sequence-one frame) or drops the token. Any number of honest Beacons run alongside: each draws fresh keys, signs and sends exactly one bundle, and finishes registration at most once, aborting for good on any failure. The attacker can build its own identities from public keys and signatures it makes itself, and the same Server code serves them. There is no replay guard, no origin table and no special malicious server: honesty appears only in the queries, as the condition that the attacker does not hold the identity's secret key. Every step carries a file:line citation of the Rust code it mirrors, and the transcript-fidelity test checks that each cited line range still starts with the cited code; a Rust change inside a cited range that leaves its first line in place is not detected by that check.

The primitive theory is the existing `crypto.pvl`: X25519 with role-asymmetric DH and a private shared value, and ML-KEM with explicit rejection. A richer theory with symmetric DH, encoding aliases, low-order points and implicit rejection could not be run at these bounds (every attempt exhausted memory), so audit finding F13 stays partly open: these results say nothing about same-role DH equalities, high-bit or torsion aliases of X25519 keys, or ML-KEM implicit rejection. Under `crypto.pvl` a DH call fails exactly on an input that is not an X25519 public key, and that failure stands in for every Rust DH refusal; the core all-zero check can never reject a value that reached it, so the model does not repeat it.

### What fs-registration proves

| Claim | Class | Bound | Verdict | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A1 | security | K_reg = 3 | TRUE | Registration agreement, in runs where no Server object sends a record after registration (this scenario has none): every honest Beacon that pins the honest Server key and finished registration received a response that one Server object built for exactly that Beacon, with the same Beacon identity, verified key tuple, assigned key ID, root, associated data and payload, and no two Beacon completions are matched to the same build (injective). The Beacon's sequence-one gate is in the model and pinned to the Rust source, but without later records it decides no verdict here; agreement under later Server records, where the gate matters (the HB-95 substitution), is the record-scenario A1 of stage P2 with its control C-NOGATE. |
| A2 | security | K_reg = 3 | TRUE | Bundle origin: whenever a Server object accepts a bundle in the name of an identity whose secret the attacker does not hold, a Beacon with that identity really sent exactly that verified key tuple and registration ID. |
| R1 | security | K_reg = 3 | TRUE | Replay rejection: one Server object never accepts the same registration ID (identity and one-time key) twice. |
| R1' | security | K_reg = 3 | TRUE | One registration per honest Beacon: one Server object accepts an honest Beacon identity at most once, whatever the registration ID, because an honest Beacon outputs at most one signed bundle (so one one-time key) and the consumed set refuses its second use. |
| S3 (Server form) | security | K_reg = 3 | TRUE | The attacker never learns the root of a session that a Server object built for an identity whose secret it does not hold. |
| S3 (Beacon form) | security | K_reg = 3 | TRUE | The attacker never learns the root of a session that an honest Beacon pinning the honest Server key established. |
| R2 | definitional | K_reg = 2 | TRUE | A replay rejection follows an earlier acceptance of the same ID on the same object. This holds by construction, because the rejection reads slots that only acceptance writes, so it is not counted as evidence. |
| R3 | witness | K_reg = 2 | reachable | An honest Beacon's bundle replayed to the object that accepted it is refused, so R1 and R1' are not vacuous. |
| R5 | witness | K_reg = 2 | reachable | A failure after the consumed-set check leaves the set unchanged: the same registration ID is accepted later by the same object. |
| W1 | witness | K_reg = 1 | reachable | An honest Beacon completes registration with the first assigned key ID, so A1 and the Beacon form of S3 are not vacuous. |
| W2 | witness | K_reg = 2 | reachable | An honest Beacon completes with the second key ID of an object, so the key-ID counter is exercised. |
| W3 | witness | K_reg = 1 | reachable | A Server object accepts a bundle for an identity whose secret the attacker holds, so attacker identities really are served and the corruption condition of A2 is not vacuous. The corruption conditions of R1' and of S3's Server form need more than this accept: R1' needs a second accepted bundle of the same attacker identity on the same object, which in the model follows after more attacker inputs, and S3's Server form needs a build, which follows such an accept after one more attacker choice; no separate witness runs either. |
| R4 | limitation | K_reg = 1 | FALSE (expected) | Two Server objects built from the same identity key have separate consumed sets, so both accept the bundle of one honest Beacon. |
| C-NOCHECK | control | K_reg = 2 | FALSE (expected) | With the consumed-set comparison removed, R1 fails: an attacker identity registers twice on one object with the same one-time key. |
| C-UKS | control | K_reg = 1 | FALSE (expected) | If the root input and the associated data did not bind the Beacon identity, A1 would fail: an attacker identity re-signs an honest Beacon's keys, the Server builds the response for the attacker identity, and the honest Beacon completes with it (an unknown-key-share). |

Only the six security results count as evidence. The definitional check holds by construction. The witnesses show that the events the claims talk about really happen in the model, which rules out a TRUE verdict that holds only because nothing happens. The two negative controls are mutants of the model, each loaded from its own small library in place of the real one: each must make its target claim FALSE with a reconstructed attack trace, which shows that the check it removes is what makes the claim hold. The result checker requires the exact expected result line of every query, including both lines of an injective FALSE result, and rejects "cannot be proved", unknown or inconclusive results and unconfirmed traces. A1 and both forms of S3 speak only about runs without record traffic, because fs-registration has none.

### Pending paper arguments

The verdicts above are exact statements about the fs process. Reading them as statements about the Rust API needs three paper arguments of the staged ProVerif plan; two of them are not yet written, so every Rust reading in this section is pending.

- **L1 (Server decomposition and accept/build scheduling)** is not yet written. It must show that every Rust schedule of `get_shared_secret` and `build_registration_response` calls maps to a model run with the same events: (i) accept and build made adjacent; (ii) builds in another order than the accepts, which renames key IDs in build order; (iii) an accept that is never built, which is the model's drop; (iv) a token accepted by one live Server object and built by another live object with the same identity key and `server_kid`, which the core accepts because it checks only these two values (`pqxdh.rs:853-858`), and in which the key ID comes from the building object's counter; (v) failures between the registration ID and the insertion, which leave the state unchanged. Case (iv) is not settled by OD2: the model itself runs many live objects with one identity (R4 relies on this), but it never builds a token on another object than the one that accepted it.
- **L5 (Beacon lifecycle)** is not yet written. It must show that a Rust Beacon outputs at most one signed bundle (a failed bundle call outputs nothing and may be repeated), finishes at most once, and that a failed finish aborts for good and is never retried, which the model's honest Beacon builds in. The injectivity of A1, the single bundle behind R1' and the finish collapsed to sequence one rely on it.
- **L6 (each event as a Rust API outcome)** was written as a paper draft during stage P0 and is now maintained as the [fs event-meaning reference](proverif-fs-event-meaning.md), with its Rust citations re-checked. Its separate review was made at the start of stage P2; it approved the projection with minor findings, which the reference applies. The event meanings below are taken from it.

The Rust readings of all six security results rest on L1, L5 and L6. The obligations L2 to L4 concern the record scenarios and are not used here.

### Bounds and what they do not cover

K_reg is the number of registration bundles one Server object processes, counting bundles that fail to parse, replays and failures. The security results hold for any number of Server objects, any number of honest Beacons and any number of attacker identities, but only for the first three bundles each Server object processes. They say nothing directly about a Server object's fourth or later bundle; the per-object replay rule at any depth is the Lean result `no_reacceptance`, and the bounded results do not discharge global closure item 1 (arbitrary reached states). Witnesses and controls run at the smallest bound that exhibits them; because every Server step waits for an attacker-chosen input, a trace at a smaller bound is also a trace at a larger one, so this is not a weakening. This scenario has no record exchange after registration; the records, the sequence-one gate witness (A3), record secrecy and record replay are the subject of the record scenarios. One full serial pass of the fifteen fs-registration targets takes about 44 minutes of ProVerif time and must run alone on the machine. The 10 GiB cap limits each run's address space (virtual memory), which is always at least its resident memory: the largest run, A1, reached a peak address space of 10130732 KiB (9.66 GiB, 96.6% of the cap) with a peak resident memory of 9866724 KiB (9.41 GiB), so it keeps only about 3.4% (0.34 GiB) of headroom under the cap.

### Replay is per live Server state

Following owner decision OD2, the protocol identity of a Server is its identity key, and the proof Server is an idealisation with perfect key management and no backup or restore. Persistence is out of scope. Replay claims are therefore stated per live Server object: R1 and R1' say that one object never accepts twice. Two Server objects built from the same seed are the same Server for the protocol but keep separate consumed sets, so both accept the same honest bundle; R4 shows exactly this and is an expected consequence of OD2, not a security failure of the model. Deployments must run one live Server object per identity key for the replay claims to apply. OD2 does not settle a token that one live object accepts and another builds: the model never builds on another object, and that run is case (iv) of the pending L1.

### Which Server key a Beacon pins

A Rust Beacon can pin any Server key, and a registration bundle carries no Server field. A2 therefore leaves the pin of the sending Beacon open: it says that a Beacon with that identity sent the bundle, whatever Server key that Beacon pinned. R1' does not mention the pin at all, and the Server form of S3 speaks only of Server events and attacker knowledge. In this scenario the pin enters only the Beacon's finish, which outputs nothing, so every model Beacon may pin the honest key without loss for these three claims. A1 and the Beacon form of S3 are statements about Beacons that pin the honest Server key, which is the deployment described by the [threat model](threat_model.md): the Server public key is compiled into the staged Beacon and the attacker cannot replace it. The restriction is essential for the Beacon form of S3: a Beacon that pins a key the attacker holds runs its key exchange with the attacker, who then knows the root.

### Model steps and event meanings

The model differs from a line-by-line transcription of the Rust code only in the following reviewed steps, each argued in the guide. The bundle parse and the four DH calls are process-level `let` bindings instead of a helper function with internal bindings; ProVerif would expand the helper into a longer chain of failure branches, and the semantics is the same. Accept and build are separate Rust calls, which the model makes adjacent on the same object with the attacker choosing build or drop; the argument that reordering, dropping and building a token on another live object with the same key change nothing observable is the pending obligation L1, and OD2 does not cover the last case. The Beacon finish opens the response frame only at sequence one, because the Rust general receive followed by the sequence-one gate ends every other sequence in the same terminal abort with no output; this relies on the pending Beacon lifecycle argument L5. The Beacon's nonempty-payload check can only reject and is omitted. The registration payload is a fresh value per build, so authentication is shown for fresh application payloads; the default payload of a build without application data, the public byte `REGISTRATION_WITNESS` (0xFF), is not covered. The plan also allows the "na" form for the record scenarios, in which a fresh name is written without session arguments (`new x[]`); this changes only ProVerif's internal abstraction of names, making it coarser, and not the process semantics, so a TRUE verdict stays sound and a FALSE verdict still needs a reconstructed trace. The Server-to-Beacon record scenario does not use it.

Each fs event is defined, by the reviewed L6 projection ([fs event-meaning reference](proverif-fs-event-meaning.md)), as the outcome of one Rust public call: which call on which object, what it returned and which state change it made. The shared vocabulary also fixes the events of the record scenarios: `FsSent` means the allocation of a sequence number for a plaintext, not the successful return of the encrypt call, because the counter stays advanced when sealing fails; `FsReceiveRejected` records a rejected receive with the entry state preserved and, like the other failure-cause events, is used only by witnesses, definitional checks and negative controls, never by a security result. Under `crypto.pvl` the failure-cause event `FsServerAcceptFailed` arises only when the prekey or the one-time key is not an X25519 public key; in the theory the identity conversion and the DH call on the identity cannot fail once the signatures verified. In Rust, libsodium can refuse to convert a Beacon identity key that verified the signatures but lies outside the prime-order subgroup; that failure returns `None` with no state change and emits no event. Some event fields are not values that the call returns: the root on build and record events (inside the opaque registration token at the build, dropped once the chains are derived), the verified key tuple at the build, the registration ID at the Beacon (computed only by the model) and the key ID on Beacon receives (the Beacon's stored assigned ID, which the receive does not return). A claim that mentions such a field quantifies over it as a function of the run, and no Rust caller observes it at that event.

### The fs selection heuristic nx

`fs-common.pvl` contains one `nounif` declaration, `nounif y: bitstring; attacker(x25519_public(y)).`, called nx. It is a selection heuristic: it tells ProVerif not to choose facts of the form "the attacker knows an X25519 public key" as the next fact to resolve during saturation. It is not an axiom, a restriction or an assumption, and it removes no attacker behaviour. ProVerif's soundness holds for any selection, so a TRUE verdict still means that no attack exists in the model, and a FALSE verdict still comes with an attack trace that ProVerif reconstructs and checks against the process. The only possible effect of a selection heuristic is that ProVerif may fail to decide a query, and the result checker rejects such a run. The heuristic is needed because the Server serves attacker identities with arbitrary keys: without it, saturation repeatedly unfolds an attacker-supplied X25519 key into another Server object's ephemeral public key, whose own bundle again needs such a key, and the runs diverge (the P0 spike measured divergence, out-of-memory failures at 10 GiB and time-outs without it, and runs of a few seconds with it at K_reg = 2). This divergence is legitimate attacker behaviour, an attacker identity signing another object's ephemeral key as its prekey, and not an attack.

### ProVerif declaration policy

The transcript-fidelity test scans every `.pv` and `.pvl` file under `beaconcrypt-core/proofs/pro-verif`, including the generated extraction library, after removing comments the way ProVerif 2.05 does: comments nest, and each comment separates the tokens on either side, so `axiom(* c *)event(E) ==> false.` is read as an axiom declaration. It fails on any `axiom`, `restriction`, `elimtrue` or `clauses` declaration, because those add assumptions to a model. It requires every `set`, `param`, `nounif`, `select`, `noselect`, `lemma` and secrecy-assumption (`not`) declaration, and every `[precise]` input, to match an entry of the reviewed [declaration allowlist](../beaconcrypt-core/proofs/pro-verif/declaration-allowlist.tsv), which records its file, its exact text, its number of occurrences and the paragraph below that explains it.

The Python checkers and generators in the same directory also write ProVerif text at run time, which ProVerif then reads from temporary files. The test therefore also reads every string literal of every Python file there, docstrings included, decodes its escape sequences, and replaces each format placeholder (an f-string replacement field or a `%` conversion) by `{}`. It then decodes the result a second time, as Python's `re` module decodes a replacement template: a group reference (a backslash followed by digits, or `\g<...>`) also becomes `{}`, and a backslash followed by a letter, such as `\n`, becomes a space. The second stage is applied to every literal, whether or not the code uses it as a template, because it can only add places where a keyword counts. In that text a declaration keyword counts when it starts a literal or follows a placeholder, a period, a brace or the end of a ProVerif comment, which are the places where run-time text can be joined to it. Forbidden declarations fail, and every other declaration and every `[precise]` must be on the allowlist under the Python file's path. This finds six entries: `set preciseActions = true.` in `check-registration-set.py`, `set preciseActions=false.` and `set maxHyp=2.` in `check-registration-response.py`, and one `[precise]` input in each of `check-general-registration.py`, `generate-general-registration.py` and `generate-kem-controller-auth.py`, all explained in [the precision settings](#proverif-precision-and-approximation-settings). The scan does not cover a keyword that the Python code assembles from smaller pieces at run time, reads from a file other than the scanned ones, or produces by a decoding step other than a literal's own escapes, its format placeholders and a `re` replacement template (the Python files there use no other, such as `string.Template` or `unicode_escape`), and it skips secrecy assumptions (`not`) in Python text, because literals quote expected `RESULT not ...` lines; ProVerif verifies every secrecy assumption itself and stops with an error when it cannot (checked with ProVerif 2.05), so such an assumption can stop a run but cannot change a verdict. A new heuristic, precision setting or lemma, in a model file or in a Python template, therefore needs a reviewed allowlist entry and a documentation paragraph before any gate accepts it. No `lemma` and no secrecy assumption is used anywhere.

### ProVerif precision and approximation settings

`set preciseActions = true` and the `[precise]` annotation on an input ask ProVerif to remember that one execution of an input receives one value, which makes its Horn-clause abstraction more precise; `set preciseLetExpand` selects how process-level `let` bindings are expanded. Neither restricts the process traces or adds an axiom, so a verdict means the same with or without them, and setting them to `false` keeps ProVerif's less precise abstraction. `set maxHyp` drops hypotheses of large Horn clauses, which can only add derivations: it is a sound over-approximation that may cost precision but never turns a false property into a TRUE verdict. It does not bound sessions, counters or the attacker. The fs Server and Beacon processes mark every attacker input `[precise]`. The same settings and `[precise]` inputs also appear in the ProVerif text that the legacy Python checkers and generators write at run time, with the same meaning.

### ProVerif output-only settings

`set traceDisplay`, `set explainDerivation`, `set verboseClauses`, `set verboseRules` and `set verboseGoalReachable` change only what ProVerif prints. They do not affect the analysis or any verdict.

## Free-schedule ProVerif records, Server to Beacon (fs-records-s2b)

`fs-records-s2b` is the second free-schedule scenario. After registration, the Server sends records (taskings) to the Beacon it registered, and the attacker chooses when every registration step, every tasking and every Beacon receive happens and which frame each receive gets. The scenario addresses the remaining parts of audit findings F2 and F11 for the Server-to-Beacon direction: the fixed record schedule of the earlier model, record replay shown only for a fixed delivery order, and controls that held by construction. Every result below is a symbolic result (Dolev-Yao attacker, free constructors, ideal hash, KDF and AEAD) for a bounded process. None of them is a computational bound, and none may be presented as one. Each Rust reading is conditional on the reviewed event projection L6 and on the pending paper arguments L1 to L5 and the two model steps written in the guide (see below). The [fs-records-s2b guide](impl/proverif-free-schedule-records.md) records the model files, the Rust mapping, the measured times and memory, the deviations and the open items, and the [fs event-meaning reference](proverif-fs-event-meaning.md#server-to-beacon-records-fs-records-s2b-stage-p2) says what each claim means for Rust calls.

### What the fs-records-s2b model contains

Any number of Server objects run, all with the one honest Server identity key. Each object accepts one registration bundle in the Rust order, except that the Server's ephemeral key and KEM coins are drawn before the bundle is read (see below), builds the response when the attacker schedules it, and then sends two taskings, at sequences 2 and 3, to the Beacon identity it installed. Any number of honest Beacons run alongside: each sends one bundle, finishes registration at most once, aborting for good on any failure, and then makes up to three receive attempts. A receive attempt follows the Rust ratchet: it accepts a later sequence and caches the keys it skips, accepts a cached sequence once and then removes its key, refuses an old sequence that is not cached without opening anything, and keeps its exact state when an open fails. Sequences up to three are modelled exactly. A frame claiming a higher sequence goes to a "far" branch, which admits every higher sequence, more than Rust admits, but opens it only with model-only key material derived from the secret chain of the session, not with Rust's material at that sequence, and which stops the receive worker if it ever accepts. Within these bounds no honest frame lies above sequence three, and one result (C4) shows that the branch never accepts; because the far material is model-only, the branch would refuse a genuine frame above sequence three, so C4 means something only as long as no honest sender goes beyond the highest modelled sequence. The attacker can register its own identities, and the same Server code serves them. As in fs-registration there is no replay guard, origin table or special malicious process, and honesty appears only in the queries. Every step cites the Rust code it mirrors, and the transcript-fidelity test checks every citation.

The Beacon's registration finish opens the response frame with the general receive, as Rust does, so a later genuine tasking can be opened there; the sequence-one gate (`beacon.rs:468-470`) then aborts the Beacon. This is the gate that closed the HB-95 later-record substitution, and the scenario both witnesses that it is reached and shows, with a control, that it is what keeps registration agreement true.

Taskings come in two forms. In the first, the application's plaintext is an 8-byte prefix that the adversary chooses (it may look like a key-ID binding) followed by fresh bytes. In the second, the adversary may also choose a whole plaintext for each tasking, which covers applications that send adversary-known or adversary-chosen data. The authentication results run in the second form; the secrecy result runs in the first, because a plaintext the adversary chose is not secret. The witnesses and the controls also run in the first form: every trace of the first form is a trace of the second, so a witness or a failed control found in the first form also exists in the second. Neither form changes the registration response, whose payload stays a fresh value (see below).

### What fs-records-s2b proves

| Claim | Class | K_r | Verdict | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A1 (record form) | security | 3 | TRUE | Registration agreement still holds when the Server sends later taskings, with plaintexts the adversary chooses, before or after the Beacon finishes: every honest Beacon that pins the honest Server key and finished registration received a response that one Server object built for exactly that Beacon, with the same identities, key tuple, key ID, root, associated data and payload, and no two finishes are matched to one build. A later genuine tasking spliced into the response never completes a registration. |
| A2 (re-proved) | security | 3 | TRUE | Bundle origin, as in fs-registration, in the record process. |
| C1 | security | 3 | TRUE | Record agreement: every record that such a Beacon accepts, at sequence t with plaintext m, was sent by a Server object to the peer installed for that Beacon, at sequence t with plaintext m, in the same session (same identities, key ID and root), and no send is matched to two acceptances. This holds when the attacker delivers frames in any order, replays, forges and interleaves rejected frames, and when the application's taskings are adversary-chosen. |
| C3 | security | 3 | TRUE | Record replay rejection: such a Beacon never accepts the same sequence twice in one session, the registration response included. |
| C4 | security | 3 | TRUE | No such Beacon ever accepts a frame above sequence three, so the far-branch over-approximation never fires here. |
| S1 | security | 3 | TRUE | Record secrecy: the attacker never learns the registration payload or the fresh bytes of a tasking that a Server object sent to a peer whose identity secret the attacker does not hold. |
| A3 | witness | 1 | reachable | A later genuine tasking spliced into the response is opened by the finish before the sequence-one gate aborts it, so the gate is really reached. |
| C5a | witness | 2 | FALSE (reachable) | Out-of-order and cached acceptance: sequence 3 is accepted, which caches 2, and then 2 is accepted from the cache. |
| C5b | witness | 2 | FALSE (reachable) | A forged frame at sequence 3 is rejected and the genuine frame at 3 is accepted afterwards: a failure leaves the sequence acceptable. |
| C5c | witness | 1 | FALSE (reachable) | A frame that the Beacon accepted, the sequence-one frame of the registration response, is delivered to it again and refused: a replay is refused (the replay-rejected witness; see below). |
| S4 (Server-to-Beacon half) | witness | 1 | reachable | An identity the attacker registered reads the tasking the Server sends it at sequence 2: attacker peers are really served. |
| C-RETAIN on C1 and on C3 | control | 3 | FALSE (expected) | If the Beacon kept a cached key after using it, the attacker could replay the cached record and both C1 and C3 would fail. |
| C-NOGATE | control | 1 | FALSE (expected) | Without the sequence-one gate, A1 fails through the HB-95 later-record substitution, which is the behaviour of the branch `vcvio`. |
| C-STALE | control | 3 | FALSE (expected) | If a failed open restored the receive state from before the previous success, an accepted record could be accepted again and C3 would fail. |
| C-FAILMUT | control | 2 | TRUE (expected) | If a failed open consumed its sequence, the C5b witness would become unreachable: keeping the exact state after a failure is what lets the genuine frame through after a forgery. |

Only the six security results count as evidence. The witnesses show that the events the claims speak about really happen: a later genuine tasking reaches the gate, records are accepted out of order and from the cache, a rejected forgery leaves the sequence acceptable, a replayed frame that the Beacon accepted earlier is refused, and an attacker-registered peer reads its own taskings. Each negative control loads one mutant library in place of the real one, runs like the witnesses in the first tasking form, and must change a verdict with a confirmed trace (or, for C-FAILMUT, must make a witness unreachable), which shows that the Rust behaviour it removes is what decides the claim. The checker requires the exact expected result lines and rejects "cannot be proved", unknown and inconclusive results and unconfirmed traces.

The replay-rejected witness C5c ties the refused frame to an accepted one: the receive events record the frame itself, and the query asks for a frame that the Beacon accepted and later refused. The trace that ProVerif reconstructs is the attacker delivering the registration response frame, which the finish accepted, to the Beacon's first receive attempt, which refuses it without opening it. An earlier form of C5c, whose events did not record the frame, could be satisfied by a frame the attacker built itself, so it showed only that some frame at an already accepted sequence was refused; the P2 review found this, and the witness was changed. C3 shows, in addition, that within the bounds no Beacon session accepts any sequence twice.

### Bounds and what they do not cover

Each Server object processes one bundle and sends two taskings (K_s = 2), each Beacon makes three receive attempts after its finish (K_r = 3), and sequences up to three are modelled exactly (T_max = 3), with the far branch above. The security results hold for any number of Server objects, honest Beacons and attacker identities within these bounds; a third tasking, a fourth receive attempt and anything after a far acceptance are not covered, and these bounded results do not discharge global closure item 1 (arbitrary reached states), which stays with the Lean side. Witnesses and controls run at the smallest number of receive attempts that exhibits them (one, two or three); since every receive waits for an attacker input, a trace with fewer attempts is also a trace with more. In the serial verification pass, run on the tree that applies the fixes of the P2 review, all sixteen record targets gave their exact expected results in 3521.2 s of ProVerif time (about 59 minutes). The largest, C1, took 1087 s and at most 6.7 GiB of address space, about 60% of the time cap and two thirds of the memory cap. The whole fs group, registration included, took 1 hour 43 minutes of wall time, within the budget of about three hours that the owner set for it, which leaves about 77 minutes for the Beacon-to-Server record scenario. In the same pass the registration A1 again came within 3.3% of its address-space cap. The guide records the time and memory of every target.

### Model steps and pending arguments

The model departs from a line-by-line transcription of the Rust code in the following steps, each argued in the guide. Each Server object takes one bundle; a Rust Server with several peers corresponds to several model objects with the same key, and the argument that this, together with letting the attacker route frames to any receive, covers every Rust run is the pending obligation L2. The Server's ephemeral key and KEM coins are drawn when the object starts rather than after the bundle is checked; with one bundle per object, nobody can observe the difference, because neither value is used before the point where Rust draws it or output before the response is sent, and a failed check discards them either way (written in the guide, not yet separately reviewed). The scenario has only the Server-to-Beacon direction: the Beacon's own sends use the other half of the root's key derivation, carry another sender ID and touch other parts of the ratchet state, so leaving them out removes nothing that these claims depend on (also written in the guide). Failures keep the exact receive state (L3), a send counts from the moment its sequence is allocated (L4), and a Beacon finishes at most once (L5). The `FsReceiveRejected` event is recorded, with the refused frame, for every parsed frame from the pinned Server ID that a receive attempt refuses at sequences up to three, but not for a refused far frame, which no witness needs. A "fail-stop" variant, in which a failed open ends the receive worker, was measured but is not used for any result.

As in fs-registration, all results are for Beacons that pin the honest Server key and for Server objects with the modelled identity key; A2 and the Server-side results S1 and S4 do not depend on the Beacons' pins, because in this scenario a Beacon outputs nothing after its bundle. The registration response payload is a fresh value in every target, so registration agreement (A1) and the agreement and secrecy of the sequence-one record (C1 and S1 at sequence one) are shown only for fresh registration payloads: an adversary-known or adversary-chosen payload, and the public default payload of a build without application data, are not covered.

## Free-schedule ProVerif records, Beacon to Server (fs-records-b2s)

`fs-records-b2s` is the third free-schedule scenario and covers the other record direction. After registration, each Beacon sends records to the Server object that registered it, and the attacker chooses when every registration step, every Beacon record and every Server receive happens and which frame each receive gets. The scenario addresses the remaining parts of audit findings F2 and F11 for the Beacon-to-Server direction, and the isolation of peers inside one Server: the Server serves every identity with the same code, including identities the attacker registered, and nothing but cryptography keeps one peer's records from being accepted as another's. Every result below is a symbolic result (Dolev-Yao attacker, free constructors, ideal hash, KDF and AEAD) for a bounded process. None of them is a computational bound, and none may be presented as one. Each Rust reading is conditional on the reviewed event projection L6, on the pending paper arguments L1 to L5, and on the model steps written in the guide. The local E21 trace argument is separately reviewed; direction splitting, pin independence and source lifting remain pending (see below). The [fs-records-b2s guide](impl/proverif-free-schedule-records-b2s.md) records the model files, the Rust mapping, the measured times and memory, the deviations and the open items, and the [fs event-meaning reference](proverif-fs-event-meaning.md#beacon-to-server-records-fs-records-b2s-stage-p3) says what each claim means for Rust calls.

### What the fs-records-b2s model contains

Any number of Server objects run, all with the one honest Server identity key. Each object accepts one registration bundle, builds the response when the attacker schedules it, and then makes up to three receive attempts for the peer it installed. Any number of honest Beacons run alongside: each sends one bundle, finishes registration at most once, aborting for good on any failure, and then sends two records, at sequences 1 and 2. A Server receive attempt follows the Rust code: it reads the sender ID that the frame claims, looks up the peer installed under that ID, and opens the frame with that peer's ratchet and with associated data built from the two identities. Every peer in the model has the same key ID, so the attacker decides which Server object's peer receives each frame, and a frame meant for one peer reaches every other peer; only the authenticated encryption and its key commitment, which bind the session keys, the sender ID and both identities, can reject it. The ratchet accepts a later sequence and caches the key it skips, accepts a cached sequence once and then removes its key, refuses an old sequence that is not cached without opening anything, and keeps its exact state when an open fails. Sequences 1 and 2 are modelled exactly; a frame claiming a higher sequence goes to the same kind of "far" branch as in the Server-to-Beacon scenario, which opens only with model-only key material and stops the receive worker if it ever accepts. No honest Beacon sends above sequence 2 here, so the branch can only accept a frame built by someone who knows the session's keys. The attacker can register its own identities, and the same Server code serves them. As in the other fs scenarios there is no replay guard, origin table or special malicious process, and honesty appears only in the queries. Every step cites the Rust code it mirrors, and the transcript-fidelity test checks every citation.

Records come in two forms, as the taskings of the Server-to-Beacon scenario do. In the first, each record is fresh bytes; in the second, the adversary may also choose a whole record for each send, which covers applications that send adversary-known or adversary-chosen data. Registration agreement, bundle origin and replay rejection run in the second form. Record secrecy and record identity agreement run in the first, because a record the adversary chose is not secret and could be re-sent by the adversary on a peer it registered itself, which would make those statements fail for a reason that says nothing about the protocol. Record agreement (C2) runs in both: in the first form with the receive behaviour described above, and in the second with a "fail-stop" receive worker that ends at its first failed open, because the second form did not fit the memory and time limits otherwise. The far-branch claim (C4) runs in the second form with the fail-stop worker only. The [reviewed E21 argument](impl/proverif-failstop-trace-simulation.md) transfers these exact C2/C4 formulas by deleting only failed receive opens and reindexing at most three retained attempts per worker. It preserves all ten worker parameters, honest outputs, attacker knowledge and non-rejection event order and multiplicity. Its projection omits receive-input consumption and call labels; no optional-reply observation or computational probability bound follows.

Rust Beacons may pin any Server key and ID. The scenario has two main processes: one in which every Beacon pins the honest Server key and ID, and one in which the attacker chooses the pin of every Beacon, so that Beacons pinning the honest Server run next to Beacons pinning a key the attacker controls. Registration agreement, bundle origin, record secrecy, record identity agreement (UKSr) and C4 run in the second process, so they hold whatever the Beacons pin. The other two record claims, C2 and C3, run only in the first. Seven claims were timed in both processes in development runs: the second process took about 1.8 to 2.9 times as long for five of them (A1, A2, S2, UKSr and C3) and about 10.8 times, or more than 7.5 times, for the two runs with adversary-chosen records and the fail-stop worker (C4, and C2, which did not finish within the per-target time limit). C3 gave its expected result in the second process in a development run, which is not part of the verification record, but making it a target next to UKSr would take the fs group past its time budget of about three hours, and UKSr was preferred because Beacons with other pins bear directly on its statement. C2 with fresh records was not run in the second process; at the measured factors it would take about 30 minutes to 2 h 58 min (1780 s to 10660 s, from the 986.91 s honest-pin C2 of the pass on `974eedf`), which does not fit the budget even at the lowest; that is an extrapolation, not a measurement. For C2 and C3 the guide gives an argument, not yet reviewed, that Beacons with other pins cannot change the results: a Beacon that pins another key either never finishes registration or finishes only on keys the attacker computed itself, so everything it sends afterwards is something the attacker could have made on its own. Until that argument is reviewed, C2 and C3 are statements about runs in which every Beacon pins the honest Server key.

### What fs-records-b2s proves

| Claim | Class | K_r | Verdict | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A1 (re-proved) | security | 3 | TRUE | Registration agreement still holds when Beacons send records, with plaintexts the adversary chooses, and whatever key the other Beacons pin: every Beacon that pins the honest Server key and finished registration received a response that one Server object built for exactly that Beacon, and no two finishes are matched to one build. |
| A2 (re-proved) | security | 3 | TRUE | Bundle origin, as in fs-registration, in the record process and whatever key each Beacon pins. |
| C2 | security | 3 | TRUE | Record agreement at the Server: every record that a Server object accepts from the peer installed for an identity whose secret the attacker does not hold, at sequence t with plaintext m, was sent by the Beacon with that identity, at sequence t with plaintext m, in the same session, and no send is matched to two acceptances. This holds when the attacker delivers frames in any order, to any Server object, replays, forges and interleaves rejected frames. With adversary-chosen records it is shown with the fail-stop worker and carried over by the deletion argument. Shown with every Beacon pinning the honest Server key; other pins rest on the pending argument above. |
| C3 | security | 3 | TRUE | Record replay rejection: no Server peer accepts the same sequence twice in one session, whoever registered it and whatever the records. The query covers Server receives only. Shown with every Beacon pinning the honest Server key; other pins rest on the pending argument above. |
| C4 | security | 3 | TRUE | A Server peer accepts a frame above sequence 2 only if the attacker holds that peer's identity secret, so the far-branch over-approximation never fires for an honest Beacon's session. It is shown with adversary-chosen records and any Beacon pins, with the fail-stop worker. |
| S2 | security | 3 | TRUE | Record secrecy: the attacker never learns a fresh record that a Beacon pinning the honest Server key sent, whatever the other Beacons pin. |
| UKSr | security | 3 | TRUE | Record identity agreement: when a Server peer accepts a fresh record that a Beacon sent, the peer is installed for that Beacon's identity; the Server never attributes an honest Beacon's record to another identity, such as one the attacker registered. It is shown in the process with attacker-chosen pins, so it holds whatever key the other Beacons pin, including Beacons whose fresh records the attacker reads because they pin its key. |
| C3-finish | definitional | 1 | TRUE | A Beacon's registration finish accepts sequence one only once. In this scenario that holds by construction, because each Beacon finishes at most once with a fresh identity and has no later receive, so it is not evidence; it is kept as a check of the model's structure. |
| C5a | witness | 2 | FALSE (reachable) | Out-of-order and cached acceptance: a Beacon's record 2 is accepted, which caches 1, and then its record 1. |
| C5b | witness | 2 | FALSE (reachable) | A forged frame at sequence 2 is rejected and the genuine record 2 is accepted afterwards: a failure leaves the sequence acceptable. |
| C5c | witness | 2 | FALSE (reachable) | A frame of a Beacon's record that the Server accepted is delivered again and refused: a replay is refused. |
| S4 (Beacon-to-Server half) | witness | 1 | reachable | A record of an identity the attacker registered is accepted by the same Server code: attacker peers are really served. |
| FAR | witness | 1 | reachable | The far branch accepts a frame of an attacker peer, so C4's condition on the identity secret is needed. |
| PINREAD | witness | 1 | reachable | In the process with attacker-chosen pins, a Beacon that pins an attacker key finishes and sends a record the attacker reads, so that process really contains such Beacons. |
| C-UKS | control | 1 | FALSE (expected) | If neither the root nor the associated data named the Beacon identity, an attacker identity that signed an honest Beacon's keys would have that Beacon's records accepted as its own, and UKSr would fail by an unknown-key-share. |
| C-RETAIN | control | 3 | FALSE (expected) | If a Server peer kept a cached key after using it, a cached record could be accepted twice and C3 would fail. |
| C-STALE | control | 3 | FALSE (expected) | If a failed open restored the receive state from before the previous success, an accepted record could be accepted again and C3 would fail. |

The eight security targets state seven claims, and only these seven claims count as evidence: C2 runs in two forms with one query and counts once, and the checker's summary counts security targets and distinct claims the same way. The definitional check C3-finish holds by construction and is not counted. Until the P3 review, C3 was one query with the direction left free, so its verdict also covered the Beacon's finish, which holds by construction here; the security target now covers Server receives only. The witnesses show that the events the claims speak about really happen: records are accepted out of order and from the cache, a rejected forgery leaves the sequence acceptable, a replayed frame that the Server accepted earlier is refused, attacker peers are served, the far branch fires for them, and Beacons with other pins finish and send. Each negative control loads one mutant library in place of the real one and must change a verdict with a confirmed trace, which shows that the Rust behaviour it removes is what decides the claim. Record agreement C2 cannot serve as the target of the identity control, because its condition on the identity secret excuses exactly the records that an unknown-key-share misattributes; UKSr, which compares the identity of the accepting peer with the identity of the sending Beacon, is the record-form target instead (stage P0). The checker requires the exact expected result lines and rejects "cannot be proved", unknown and inconclusive results and unconfirmed traces.

### Bounds and what they do not cover

Each Server object processes one bundle and makes three receive attempts (K_r = 3), each Beacon sends two records (K_s = 2), and sequences up to two are modelled exactly (T_max = 2), with the far branch above. The security results hold for any number of Server objects, honest Beacons and attacker identities within these bounds; a third record, a fourth receive attempt and anything after a far acceptance are not covered, and these bounded results do not discharge global closure item 1 (arbitrary reached states), which stays with the Lean side. The definitional check, the witnesses and the controls run at the smallest number of receive attempts that exhibits them. In the serial verification pass of the whole fs group, run again on the tree that moves UKSr to the process with attacker-chosen pins, all eighteen targets gave their exact expected results in 4212 s of ProVerif time (about 70 minutes). The longest, C4 in the process with attacker-chosen pins, took 1069 s, about 59% of the time cap, and UKSr in that process took 873 s, about 2.8 times its time with honest pins in the previous pass; the largest in memory, C2 with fresh records, took 987 s and at most 6.6 GiB of address space, about two thirds of the memory cap. The whole fs group, registration and both record directions, took 2 hours 54 minutes of wall time, 96.5% of the budget of about three hours that the owner set for it, which leaves about 6 minutes, and the registration A1 again came within 3.3% of its address-space cap, so further fs targets need a budget decision or a separate group. The guide records the time and memory of every target.

### Model steps and pending arguments

As in the Server-to-Beacon scenario, each Server object takes one bundle (pending L2, which now also covers routing a received frame by the sender ID it claims), the Server's ephemeral key and KEM coins are drawn when the object starts (argued in the s2b guide), failures keep the exact receive state (L3), a send counts from the moment its sequence is allocated (L4), and a Beacon finishes at most once (L5). The registration response payload is a fresh value, so registration agreement is shown only for fresh registration payloads. Two model arguments remain pending in the guide: the scenario has only the Beacon-to-Server direction, because the Server's own records use the other half of the root's key derivation, carry the Server's own ID, which the Server never installs as a peer, and touch other parts of the ratchet state; and Beacons with other pins do not change the results of C2 and C3, which run only with honest pins. The `FsReceiveRejected` event is recorded, with the refused frame, for every frame routed to a peer that the peer refuses at sequences up to two, but not for a refused far frame, which no witness needs.

## Joint registration source schedule and complete sampling bill

The eight new `PqxdhRegistrationSchedule` modules contain 81 statements connecting complete native Server accept/build operations with dynamically addressed native Beacon creation, bundle and finish calls, sharing both primitive caches. The actual raw surface runs initialization and then the 32-byte pin parse before source-ordered generation; like `Beacon::try_new`, it does not check that the pin is a valid Ed25519 point. Every active InitSent attempt ends established or aborted, while a pre-bundle finish retains its original Fresh state. Supported adaptive continuations preserve complete terminal owners and allocated moved tokens; future numeric handles remain ordinary requests. Actual consumed-pair admission stays duplicate-free, every accept attempt allocates its index, and successful outer response publication alone advances the same public counter. Literal supplied/generated Server construction supplies the empty initial state and actual public adversary input; its intermediate runtime is retained separately from final runtime.

Pin parsing was aligned with the Rust code on 2026-10-03. Before that, `PqxdhRegistrationSchedule.parsePin` refused to create a Beacon unless the 32-byte pin also passed the abstract point predicate `checks.identityPoint`. Rust does not do this: `Beacon::try_new` calls libsodium-rs `crypto_sign::PublicKey::from_bytes`, which only checks the length, and then generates the identity, prekey and ML-KEM keys. Rust notices a pin that the Ed25519-to-X25519 conversion rejects only during `finish_registration`, which converts the identity carried in the response and later requires it to equal the pin byte for byte. Such a Beacon can publish bundles and be registered by the Server; a finish call before its bundle leaves it unchanged, and its first finish attempt after the bundle aborts it, so it never becomes established. `parsePin` is now exactly the width check (`parsePin_eq_toWord32`), so the model creates these Beacons too, with the same three draws. By construction, the unchanged finish model refuses them at the same two places as Rust, the conversion of the response identity and the identity comparison inside the extracted `beacon_prepare_finish`; this is not proved as a separate theorem. No proof relied on the old point check. Every statement about the raw surface, its costs, its executions or its experiments keeps its wording but now also covers these Beacons. In particular, "the pin parsed" in `rawCreate_cases` and `rawCreate_continuation` now only means "the input was 32 bytes long", and `surface_relation` and `surface_count` label and count every 32-byte creation request, while the accept and build counts used by the execution theorems are unchanged. This corrects what the model describes; it does not weaken any guarantee about the Rust code.

The complete interpreted uniform bill is `qCoin + (I+64+G)qCreate + 32qBundle + (96+E)qAccept + 64qBuild + 69max(64,D)qFinish + 64qHmac + 64qHash`, plus initial Server initialization `I` and a 32-byte draw only when no seed is supplied. Every cap quantifies arbitrary reply continuations and counts rejected attempts. `G`, `E` and `D` include the declared primitive uniform and interpreted base costs for all applicable inputs. Full source cache/history, signing/DH/real KDF/AEAD, optional writer and deterministic local work remain present; zero uniform queries is not zero runtime. The 69-callback finish allowance is conservative and is not a logical-decapsulation count.

[The joint source guide](impl/registration-joint-schedule.md) explains every theorem group and the exact narrower capability scope. Logical primitive-oracle instrumentation, dynamic imported Beacon identities, wider disclosures/records, exact joint symbolic transition/trace relation and cryptographic event consumers remain substantive obligations. Signing or sealing does not imply successful writer publication, and no origin table gates source admission. This operational milestone proves no complete registration authentication, applied-pi soundness or global security result. It makes no snapshot or persistence claim and leaves primitive/codec/compiler implementations external.

## Raw singleton R1 common authentication and its source ledger

The registration R1 lane now connects the actual raw singleton constructor and adaptive suffix to the existing complete session and decoded-record authentication theorem. Six modules add 28 statements: `PqxdhRegistrationR1RootAudit`, `PqxdhRegistrationR1RootJournal`, `PqxdhRegistrationR1RootSurface`, `PqxdhRegistrationR1RootProbability`, `PqxdhRegistrationR1Authentication` and `PqxdhRegistrationR1Resources`. The [lane guide](impl/registration-r1-restriction.md) explains every new statement, the complete bounds, retained contracts and unclosed global scope.

The key change is a same-run connection. The source-ordered Beacon seed, prekey, KEM and one-time draws feed one private `RootExecution.execution`. Its complete context, generation coordinate, private callback and root receipts, both native state components and actual caller return value are retained. The actual Phase 1 result supplies the native invariant, including failed publication. `recorded_surface` adds the actual create and bundle replies and the public projection of that same private callback log while retaining the entire common-event outcome. `surface_audit` and `surface_journal` then connect both initialization calls, every source refusal, the complete adaptive continuation and the final runtime to the actual raw scheduler. No marginal-state equality, reconstructed witness or independent second run substitutes for that joint execution.

For a generated Server seed, `generated_failure_le` drops both initialization gates by probability monotonicity. A constructor refusal has a false target event; a refused Beacon construction still executes its actual missing-owner tail, without drawing Beacon material. The seed is never assumed uniform conditional on successful construction, and the full production order is checked by `generated_order`. `generated_authentication` therefore applies the existing `common_authentication_with_resources` theorem with exactly its previous contracts and constructed reductions. The target failure is the actual Beacon acceptance without an index having the existing eleven-field common session and chronological publication of the exact accepted decoded record. The inherited bound remains Gap-DH plus `choose(Q, 2) * 64 / 2^256`, the sum over `Fin(Q + 1)` of the same record and five-schedule losses, and one joint Ed25519/X25519 weak-EUF advantage. The exact same `ReductionBills` is returned, including three signing requests, `qFinish` converted-DH requests and the full interpreted KEM/base uniform costs. The constructor transport adds no selection or probability factor. Supplied seeds retain exact operational equations and receive no such generated-key security conclusion.

The source ledger is separate from the reduction ledger. Each routed suffix request stays in its original class, and the actual prefix contributes one raw create and one bundle. With initialization cap `I`, evaluated KEM costs `G`, `E` and `D`, and the seven suffix caps, the generated source uniform bound is `2*I + 128 + G + qCoin + (96 + E)*qAccept + 64*qBuild + (69*max(64,D))*qFinish + 64*qHmac + 64*qHash`. The four 32-byte source draws and both initialization calls are explicit, and every KEM cost includes `baseUniform * baseQueries`. Zero uniform cost for deterministic local work or current-kernel reads is not zero runtime. The same supported source run has duplicate-free consumed registrations, at most `qAccept` consumed registrations and allocated sessions, and counter growth at most `qBuild` over all attempted builds. No claimed/assigned-ID agreement follows from that counter bound.

The proof still concerns one constructed Server and one attempted pinned Beacon owner with the original seven-capability R1 suffix. It is not arbitrary multi-owner or replicated-session closure, KCI resistance, later assigned-ID agreement, or the final computational/ProVerif bridge. Correct primitive implementations remain trusted; the existing restricted Extract ROM and shared classical CTX/BLAKE2b ROM contracts, source correctness, X25519 class/spread, joint verification adapter and abstract codec contracts remain unchanged. Snapshot/persistence behavior and serialization implementations are outside this lane. The 109 absent published authentication dependencies are a byte-exact port from `adabe9a`, with source/artifact evidence; central already contains them. The new statements are checked with exact standard-axiom guards, and the topic remains pending independent review and semantic central integration with regenerated root/checker/inventory metadata.

## Free-schedule ProVerif records, Beacon to Server (fs-records-b2s)

`fs-records-b2s` is the third free-schedule scenario and covers the other record direction. After registration, each Beacon sends records to the Server object that registered it, and the attacker chooses when every registration step, every Beacon record and every Server receive happens and which frame each receive gets. The scenario addresses the remaining parts of audit findings F2 and F11 for the Beacon-to-Server direction, and the isolation of peers inside one Server: the Server serves every identity with the same code, including identities the attacker registered, and nothing but cryptography keeps one peer's records from being accepted as another's. Every result below is a symbolic result (Dolev-Yao attacker, free constructors, ideal hash, KDF and AEAD) for a bounded process. None of them is a computational bound, and none may be presented as one. Each Rust reading is conditional on the reviewed event projection L6, on the pending paper arguments L1 to L5, and on the model steps written in the guide. The local E21 trace argument is separately reviewed; direction splitting, pin independence and source lifting remain pending (see below). The [fs-records-b2s guide](impl/proverif-free-schedule-records-b2s.md) records the model files, the Rust mapping, the measured times and memory, the deviations and the open items, and the [fs event-meaning reference](proverif-fs-event-meaning.md#beacon-to-server-records-fs-records-b2s-stage-p3) says what each claim means for Rust calls.

### What the fs-records-b2s model contains

Any number of Server objects run, all with the one honest Server identity key. Each object accepts one registration bundle, builds the response when the attacker schedules it, and then makes up to three receive attempts for the peer it installed. Any number of honest Beacons run alongside: each sends one bundle, finishes registration at most once, aborting for good on any failure, and then sends two records, at sequences 1 and 2. A Server receive attempt follows the Rust code: it reads the sender ID that the frame claims, looks up the peer installed under that ID, and opens the frame with that peer's ratchet and with associated data built from the two identities. Every peer in the model has the same key ID, so the attacker decides which Server object's peer receives each frame, and a frame meant for one peer reaches every other peer; only the authenticated encryption and its key commitment, which bind the session keys, the sender ID and both identities, can reject it. The ratchet accepts a later sequence and caches the key it skips, accepts a cached sequence once and then removes its key, refuses an old sequence that is not cached without opening anything, and keeps its exact state when an open fails. Sequences 1 and 2 are modelled exactly; a frame claiming a higher sequence goes to the same kind of "far" branch as in the Server-to-Beacon scenario, which opens only with model-only key material and stops the receive worker if it ever accepts. No honest Beacon sends above sequence 2 here, so the branch can only accept a frame built by someone who knows the session's keys. The attacker can register its own identities, and the same Server code serves them. As in the other fs scenarios there is no replay guard, origin table or special malicious process, and honesty appears only in the queries. Every step cites the Rust code it mirrors, and the transcript-fidelity test checks every citation.

Records come in two forms, as the taskings of the Server-to-Beacon scenario do. In the first, each record is fresh bytes; in the second, the adversary may also choose a whole record for each send, which covers applications that send adversary-known or adversary-chosen data. Registration agreement, bundle origin and replay rejection run in the second form. Record secrecy and record identity agreement run in the first, because a record the adversary chose is not secret and could be re-sent by the adversary on a peer it registered itself, which would make those statements fail for a reason that says nothing about the protocol. Record agreement (C2) runs in both: in the first form with the receive behaviour described above, and in the second with a "fail-stop" receive worker that ends at its first failed open, because the second form did not fit the memory and time limits otherwise. The far-branch claim (C4) runs in the second form with the fail-stop worker only. The [reviewed E21 argument](impl/proverif-failstop-trace-simulation.md) transfers these exact C2/C4 formulas by deleting only failed receive opens and reindexing at most three retained attempts per worker. It preserves all ten worker parameters, honest outputs, attacker knowledge and non-rejection event order and multiplicity. Its projection omits receive-input consumption and call labels; no optional-reply observation or computational probability bound follows.

Rust Beacons may pin any Server key and ID. The scenario has two main processes: one in which every Beacon pins the honest Server key and ID, and one in which the attacker chooses the pin of every Beacon, so that Beacons pinning the honest Server run next to Beacons pinning a key the attacker controls. Registration agreement, bundle origin, record secrecy, record identity agreement (UKSr) and C4 run in the second process, so they hold whatever the Beacons pin. The other two record claims, C2 and C3, run only in the first. Seven claims were timed in both processes in development runs: the second process took about 1.8 to 2.9 times as long for five of them (A1, A2, S2, UKSr and C3) and about 10.8 times, or more than 7.5 times, for the two runs with adversary-chosen records and the fail-stop worker (C4, and C2, which did not finish within the per-target time limit). C3 gave its expected result in the second process in a development run, which is not part of the verification record, but making it a target next to UKSr would take the fs group past its time budget of about three hours, and UKSr was preferred because Beacons with other pins bear directly on its statement. C2 with fresh records was not run in the second process; at the measured factors it would take about 30 minutes to 2 h 58 min (1780 s to 10660 s, from the 986.91 s honest-pin C2 of the pass on `974eedf`), which does not fit the budget even at the lowest; that is an extrapolation, not a measurement. For C2 and C3 the guide gives an argument, not yet reviewed, that Beacons with other pins cannot change the results: a Beacon that pins another key either never finishes registration or finishes only on keys the attacker computed itself, so everything it sends afterwards is something the attacker could have made on its own. Until that argument is reviewed, C2 and C3 are statements about runs in which every Beacon pins the honest Server key.

### What fs-records-b2s proves

| Claim | Class | K_r | Verdict | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A1 (re-proved) | security | 3 | TRUE | Registration agreement still holds when Beacons send records, with plaintexts the adversary chooses, and whatever key the other Beacons pin: every Beacon that pins the honest Server key and finished registration received a response that one Server object built for exactly that Beacon, and no two finishes are matched to one build. |
| A2 (re-proved) | security | 3 | TRUE | Bundle origin, as in fs-registration, in the record process and whatever key each Beacon pins. |
| C2 | security | 3 | TRUE | Record agreement at the Server: every record that a Server object accepts from the peer installed for an identity whose secret the attacker does not hold, at sequence t with plaintext m, was sent by the Beacon with that identity, at sequence t with plaintext m, in the same session, and no send is matched to two acceptances. This holds when the attacker delivers frames in any order, to any Server object, replays, forges and interleaves rejected frames. With adversary-chosen records it is shown with the fail-stop worker and carried over by the deletion argument. Shown with every Beacon pinning the honest Server key; other pins rest on the pending argument above. |
| C3 | security | 3 | TRUE | Record replay rejection: no Server peer accepts the same sequence twice in one session, whoever registered it and whatever the records. The query covers Server receives only. Shown with every Beacon pinning the honest Server key; other pins rest on the pending argument above. |
| C4 | security | 3 | TRUE | A Server peer accepts a frame above sequence 2 only if the attacker holds that peer's identity secret, so the far-branch over-approximation never fires for an honest Beacon's session. It is shown with adversary-chosen records and any Beacon pins, with the fail-stop worker. |
| S2 | security | 3 | TRUE | Record secrecy: the attacker never learns a fresh record that a Beacon pinning the honest Server key sent, whatever the other Beacons pin. |
| UKSr | security | 3 | TRUE | Record identity agreement: when a Server peer accepts a fresh record that a Beacon sent, the peer is installed for that Beacon's identity; the Server never attributes an honest Beacon's record to another identity, such as one the attacker registered. It is shown in the process with attacker-chosen pins, so it holds whatever key the other Beacons pin, including Beacons whose fresh records the attacker reads because they pin its key. |
| C3-finish | definitional | 1 | TRUE | A Beacon's registration finish accepts sequence one only once. In this scenario that holds by construction, because each Beacon finishes at most once with a fresh identity and has no later receive, so it is not evidence; it is kept as a check of the model's structure. |
| C5a | witness | 2 | FALSE (reachable) | Out-of-order and cached acceptance: a Beacon's record 2 is accepted, which caches 1, and then its record 1. |
| C5b | witness | 2 | FALSE (reachable) | A forged frame at sequence 2 is rejected and the genuine record 2 is accepted afterwards: a failure leaves the sequence acceptable. |
| C5c | witness | 2 | FALSE (reachable) | A frame of a Beacon's record that the Server accepted is delivered again and refused: a replay is refused. |
| S4 (Beacon-to-Server half) | witness | 1 | reachable | A record of an identity the attacker registered is accepted by the same Server code: attacker peers are really served. |
| FAR | witness | 1 | reachable | The far branch accepts a frame of an attacker peer, so C4's condition on the identity secret is needed. |
| PINREAD | witness | 1 | reachable | In the process with attacker-chosen pins, a Beacon that pins an attacker key finishes and sends a record the attacker reads, so that process really contains such Beacons. |
| C-UKS | control | 1 | FALSE (expected) | If neither the root nor the associated data named the Beacon identity, an attacker identity that signed an honest Beacon's keys would have that Beacon's records accepted as its own, and UKSr would fail by an unknown-key-share. |
| C-RETAIN | control | 3 | FALSE (expected) | If a Server peer kept a cached key after using it, a cached record could be accepted twice and C3 would fail. |
| C-STALE | control | 3 | FALSE (expected) | If a failed open restored the receive state from before the previous success, an accepted record could be accepted again and C3 would fail. |

The eight security targets state seven claims, and only these seven claims count as evidence: C2 runs in two forms with one query and counts once, and the checker's summary counts security targets and distinct claims the same way. The definitional check C3-finish holds by construction and is not counted. Until the P3 review, C3 was one query with the direction left free, so its verdict also covered the Beacon's finish, which holds by construction here; the security target now covers Server receives only. The witnesses show that the events the claims speak about really happen: records are accepted out of order and from the cache, a rejected forgery leaves the sequence acceptable, a replayed frame that the Server accepted earlier is refused, attacker peers are served, the far branch fires for them, and Beacons with other pins finish and send. Each negative control loads one mutant library in place of the real one and must change a verdict with a confirmed trace, which shows that the Rust behaviour it removes is what decides the claim. Record agreement C2 cannot serve as the target of the identity control, because its condition on the identity secret excuses exactly the records that an unknown-key-share misattributes; UKSr, which compares the identity of the accepting peer with the identity of the sending Beacon, is the record-form target instead (stage P0). The checker requires the exact expected result lines and rejects "cannot be proved", unknown and inconclusive results and unconfirmed traces.

### Bounds and what they do not cover

Each Server object processes one bundle and makes three receive attempts (K_r = 3), each Beacon sends two records (K_s = 2), and sequences up to two are modelled exactly (T_max = 2), with the far branch above. The security results hold for any number of Server objects, honest Beacons and attacker identities within these bounds; a third record, a fourth receive attempt and anything after a far acceptance are not covered, and these bounded results do not discharge global closure item 1 (arbitrary reached states), which stays with the Lean side. The definitional check, the witnesses and the controls run at the smallest number of receive attempts that exhibits them. In the serial verification pass of the whole fs group, run again on the tree that moves UKSr to the process with attacker-chosen pins, all eighteen targets gave their exact expected results in 4212 s of ProVerif time (about 70 minutes). The longest, C4 in the process with attacker-chosen pins, took 1069 s, about 59% of the time cap, and UKSr in that process took 873 s, about 2.8 times its time with honest pins in the previous pass; the largest in memory, C2 with fresh records, took 987 s and at most 6.6 GiB of address space, about two thirds of the memory cap. The whole fs group, registration and both record directions, took 2 hours 54 minutes of wall time, 96.5% of the budget of about three hours that the owner set for it, which leaves about 6 minutes, and the registration A1 again came within 3.3% of its address-space cap, so further fs targets need a budget decision or a separate group. The guide records the time and memory of every target.

### Model steps and pending arguments

As in the Server-to-Beacon scenario, each Server object takes one bundle (pending L2, which now also covers routing a received frame by the sender ID it claims), the Server's ephemeral key and KEM coins are drawn when the object starts (argued in the s2b guide), failures keep the exact receive state (L3), a send counts from the moment its sequence is allocated (L4), and a Beacon finishes at most once (L5). The registration response payload is a fresh value, so registration agreement is shown only for fresh registration payloads. Two model arguments remain pending in the guide: the scenario has only the Beacon-to-Server direction, because the Server's own records use the other half of the root's key derivation, carry the Server's own ID, which the Server never installs as a peer, and touch other parts of the ratchet state; and Beacons with other pins do not change the results of C2 and C3, which run only with honest pins. The `FsReceiveRejected` event is recorded, with the refused frame, for every frame routed to a peer that the peer refuses at sequences up to two, but not for a refused far frame, which no witness needs.
