## Raw-accept source cut and native KEM origin (not yet joined)

Four checked modules prepare the authentication part of the authenticated root theorem without completing it. `PqxdhRegistrationJointAcceptCut` suspends the adversary's adaptive source14 program immediately before a chosen raw accept request. It counts every raw accept, including requests that are later rejected, and resuming the suspended request gives back exactly the original program, so every interpreter, native state, private history and query cap stays the same. `PqxdhRegistrationJointAcceptCutSource` states the same split on the actual command compiler with only its encapsulation step exposed: the pending step is the real accept on the original bytes, followed by the original continuation with the real optional reply. `PqxdhRegistrationJointCutVerification` shows that the signature and tuple check at the start of that accept makes no oracle call and leaves the consumed-registration list unchanged. It is the ordinary public verification of the original bytes, before any encapsulation or KEM-challenge interpreter is chosen, and it uses the source's attached verifier, which takes each signed field as one byte string with its signature attached. `PqxdhRegistrationJointNativeKemOrigin` shows that, in every reachable run of the initialized report compiler, a candidate that the detached typed verifier accepts under the identity key of a fresh generated owner it addresses falls into one of two cases. Either its tuple occurs in that owner's real signing history and the owner's native KEM slot holds the candidate's PQ public key, or the existing native tuple-origin failure event holds. The integrated `NativeOriginEvent.transport` bounds that event with coefficient one by the ordinary final-report detector, and the existing `NativeOriginBound.native_origin_bound`, under its creation-capacity condition, then charges the detector to an explicit sum, over the generated targets, of ordinary joint-use weak-EUF reduction advantages. No premise assumes an honest candidate. The nine statements are guarded so that they depend only on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`. They add no primitive game, contract or assumption.

These results do not yet compose. The cut has not been instantiated as the adversary program of the initialized report compiler. The verification in `CutVerification` and the verification in `NativeKemOrigin` are different interfaces, attached and detached, and the next obligation is to connect them with the existing `RawSignatures.verified_detached` step, which carries the existing `shortRejects` attached-format premise, and then to show that the candidate's identity is the addressed owner's key. Neither step is proved here. No theorem relates the raw-accept position to the encapsulation position of the existing KEM cut, and rejection before encapsulation makes the two differ. Nothing here proves that the selected accept reaches encapsulation with the challenge key, and no selection, freshness or probability loss is derived. The authenticated root theorem still has to join the actual accept/report execution to the retained Phase-1 EUF reduction and the selected one-key ML-KEM challenge. Its final event must cover honest unchanged, honest changed, attacker-owned and rejected candidates without an honest-target premise, and the candidate/KEM value must stay out of the KDF distinguisher's public context. The remaining production/source joins for acceptance, root, records, rollback/replay, publication and associated data are also untouched. Compiler correctness, storage, physical erasure, codec internals and primitive internals remain external, and persistence, snapshots and running-code access remain excluded. The [raw-accept cut guide](impl/registration-joint-accept-cut.md) lists the exact statements, the open join and the evidence.

## Raw-accept cut joined to the report compiler and the Phase-1 EUF bound (stage A)

Four new checked modules join the raw-accept cut to the initialized report compiler and to the ordinary joint Ed25519/X25519 weak-EUF family. This is the authentication half of the authenticated root join; the KEM half is not yet done. `PqxdhRegistrationJointAcceptCutTag` turns the adversary's program into a tagged program that issues exactly the same requests and gets exactly the same replies, and that also returns the raw bytes of the selected raw accept and the public reply it received. It also proves that a selected raw accept that is actually reached has a position below the adversary's raw-accept budget `qAccept`; rejected accepts count, so this position is not the position among encapsulations. `PqxdhRegistrationJointAcceptCutReports` proves that the report run of a program is the report run of its prefix up to the selected accept, followed by a continuation that restarts from everything the run reached at that point: Server, owners, native state, local KEM and runtime state, identity registry, report monitor and report snapshot. It builds from this a coupling of the state reached at the cut with the final result of the tagged program. The final half of the coupling is exactly the report run of the tagged program, and the cut half has exactly the distribution of the report run of the prefix. It also proves that the report run of `AcceptCut.selected`, which returns the suspended raw bytes as the final candidate, is the report run of the prefix with only the program result relabelled. `PqxdhRegistrationJointAcceptCutEuf` applies the existing native-origin chain to that selected program: under the existing creation-capacity condition, the probability of the address-free final-report failure is at most an explicit sum, over the `count + 1` generated identity positions, of ordinary joint-use weak-EUF advantages, with coefficient one. It also restates the five existing query bills (signing, converted DH, public reports, client uniform work, and uniform work per reduction and per endpoint game) for this program.

`PqxdhRegistrationJointAcceptOrigin` fixes what a protected target is. The target is named by two public numbers: the position of the raw accept among all raw accepts, and a KEM creation index. A candidate is protected when the Server's ordinary attached signature check accepts the raw bytes, and the identity key it was checked under is the public identity key of some generated owner in the public owner list whose public KEM index is the chosen one, and that owner's identity has not been revealed at the moment of the accept. Only public values are compared, and no secret key is compared. The module first proves the step from the attached check to the detached signature interface used by the EUF reduction. This step uses only the existing premise that the verifier rejects inputs shorter than a signature, together with the existing `setup.wiring` contract. It then proves a classification: every reached cut is a completed or failed run, a raw registration that fails the Server's attached verification (parsing, identity-key or signature checks), a verified candidate that is not protected (attacker-owned, imported, revealed, missing, for another identity or KEM index, or a generated owner outside the report range, which the creation-capacity condition rules out), a protected candidate whose tuple the owner actually signed and whose PQ key is the native KEM key at the chosen index, or a protected candidate that is the final-report failure. The cases can overlap. Finally it proves that the probability of a protected candidate whose PQ key is not that native KEM key is at most the same weak-EUF sum, with coefficient one and no owner, field or position factor. No honest-target premise appears. Attacker-owned candidates are classified and excluded by the definition of protection; nothing is claimed about them. Freshness of the identity is read at the cut. The owner chose this reading on 2026-10-06; it is kept in an isolated definition so that a whole-run or publicly observable reading can be added later without changing these statements. The 33 statements are guarded so that they depend only on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`, and they add no primitive game, contract or assumption.

Left open by stage A: the classification does not separate a registration that the Server rejects after a successful attached verification, for example because it was already consumed, because a key fails to parse, or because encapsulation, a DH step, the Server's accept step or the root derivation fails. Such a cut lands in one of the last three cases; a replayed honest registration, for example, falls in the honest case although the Server rejects it as already consumed. These candidates are excluded later, through the proof that a selected accept that returns a session reached encapsulation (`accepted_reached`, stage B) and the final classification built on it (`classify_final`, stage C). The KEM side (the KEM cut at the selected accept, the raw-indexed KEM challenge with the ML-KEM correctness-error term and the KEM bills) is stage B, and the bridge from the actual source run to the KEM real game and the main theorem that combines the cut-time authentication bound with the whole-run KEM freshness through the coupling are stage C; both are described below. Still open after stage C are the opaque KEM-ideal continuation and every later item: the Extract/HKDF hybrid at the actual joint sampler, keeping the candidate out of the KDF distinguisher's context, the common experiment, the CTX/AEAD lift, the evolving chain, the production joins and the final validation matrix. Persistence, snapshots, running-code access and codec internals remain excluded. The [stage A guide](impl/registration-accept-kem-join.md) lists the exact statements, the deviations from the plan and the evidence.

Any successful resumed suffix retains the exact ordinary ciphertext/candidate pair, and its actual successful core acceptance supplies `FF32 || DH1 || DH2 || DH3 || DH4 || candidate` to the 192-byte root input. No public-key injectivity, coordinate independence or honest-target premise is introduced.

The [source-suffix guide](impl/registration-encapsulation-source-suffix.md) explains every statement and its relation to the complete source compiler. The real production HKDF wrapper satisfies its existing functional typed-root equation at those exact bytes. This does not replace the inherited restricted Extract-ROM analysis backend or discharge the actual joint input/public-context secrecy obligation. The source-level stopping event, generated-owner/KEM selection, real Extract/HMAC games and global hybrid assembly remain separate. Existing query caps and primitive/deployment scope are unchanged; no new primitive assumption or implementation proof is added.

The three modules were ported unchanged from the reviewed lane commit `1881878f` to the composition topic, where they are checked against the current composition artifacts and imported by the root module; the [port receipt](impl/proof-receipts/registration-encapsulation-source-suffix-port.json) records the source commit, the file hashes and the checks. Stage B of the accept/KEM join builds on `KemSourceSuffix.accept_ordered`, `suffix_cut` and `handler` at the selected raw accept.

## KEM step at the raw-accept ordinal with the correctness error (stage B)

Five new checked modules carry the accept/KEM join from the raw-accept cut to the ordinary one-key ML-KEM challenge. The source command program is changed so that only one encapsulation is visible to the KEM challenger: the encapsulation of the raw accept at the chosen raw-accept position. Every other encapsulation is still carried out by the real encapsulator at its original place, so the program does exactly what the real Server does. Interpreting the visible encapsulation with the real source encapsulator gives back exactly the real source program (`exposeAt_actual`); replacing it by the challenger's encapsulation is part of the source-to-KEM bridge, which stage C proves (next section). Stopping this program at its first visible encapsulation gives the KEM cut. `rawCut_shape` shows that when the cut is reached, the Server's attached signature check on the raw bytes of the selected accept succeeded, the requested key is the PQ key that this check returned, and the saved rest of the run is the literal remaining source code. `accepted_reached` shows that when the cut is not reached, the selected accept did not return a session. This covers the cases where the adversary finished before the selected accept, where the signature check failed, and where the Server rejected the registration before encapsulating, for example because the registration was already consumed or a key failed to parse.

The ordinary KEM games at this position are the existing ones with the new prephase. The new games use no perfect-correctness assumption for ML-KEM, which deployed ML-KEM-768 does not satisfy. Instead, the real game with the true shared secret is compared with the mathematical real-source game through the ordinary ML-KEM correctness-error experiment: one key pair, one encapsulation and one decapsulation, which the adversary wins if decapsulation fails or returns a different secret. When decapsulation recovers the encapsulated secret, the two games agree exactly. Every other case is charged in full, and the one error event covers every repeated use of the challenge ciphertext. The resulting bound is that the real game and the game with a uniform replacement secret differ by at most one ordinary IND-CCA advantage plus one correctness error, each with coefficient one (`KemRawCertified.advantage`). The same bound is also stated one-sidedly, as the main theorem will use it: the real game wins with at most the probability of the replacement game plus these two terms (`KemRawCertified.real_le_ideal`). Both statements name the same constructed adversary whose query bills are proved; the analogous statements in `KemRawGame` are for a plain adversary without proved bills. The correctness-error term is the same number as the correctness-error term `kemError` that existing results already charge (`correctnessError_eq_kemError`). The only inherited contract is the existing `FunctionalDecapsulation`, which the owner allowed in the top-level statement; no assumption or symbolic injectivity is added. Stage B forms no KDF game and no `SecretInputKdf.Context`; keeping the candidate out of the KDF distinguisher's context remains open (handoff item 2).

The constructed adversary has exactly the query bills of the existing encapsulation-position adversary. The encapsulations that the new program carries out in place are charged to its uniform budget, which already includes one encapsulation per raw accept. The saved continuation after the challenge has no further visible encapsulation. The [stage B section of the accept/KEM join guide](impl/registration-accept-kem-join.md) lists every statement and its accounting. Stage C (next section) proves the bridge from the actual source run to the real KEM game, the main theorem that combines the cut-time authentication bound with this KEM step, and the final classification; the opaque KEM-ideal continuation and every later item of the handoff remain open.

## Main theorem of the accept/KEM join (stage C)

Four new checked modules finish the join of the raw-accept cut, the Phase-1 authentication bound and the selected ML-KEM challenge, up to the KEM-ideal game. The target is still named by two public numbers: the position of the raw accept among all raw accepts, and a KEM creation index. The main theorem (`authenticated_selected_kem`) bounds the probability that four things happen together: the selected raw accept returns a session, the adversary's decision on its own result is true, the KEM key with the chosen creation index is never revealed during the whole run, and, at the moment of the accept, the registration is protected in the sense of stage A, that is, it verifies under the public identity key of a generated owner with that KEM index whose identity is unrevealed at that moment. Here "returns a session" means that the selected `get_shared_secret` attempt returned its pending registration output, identified by its session index; failures of the later `build_registration_response` are not excluded from the event. The bound is the probability that the KEM-ideal game returns true, in which the selected encapsulation's shared secret is replaced by a uniform value held by the KEM challenger, plus one ordinary IND-CCA advantage of the stage B adversary, plus one ordinary ML-KEM correctness error, plus a sum over all generated identity positions of the ordinary joint-use weak-EUF advantage, each with coefficient one. No honest-target assumption appears, and no new assumption is added: the only inherited contracts are the attached-format premise `shortRejects` with `setup.wiring`, and `FunctionalDecapsulation`, which the owner allowed in the top-level statement. No perfect-correctness assumption for ML-KEM and no symbolic injectivity is used.

Because protection is read at the accept and KEM freshness over the whole run, the event combines two moments of one execution. It is therefore stated on the coupling of stage A, which runs the report-instrumented execution once and records both the state at the selected accept and the final result. The final half of that coupling is exactly the report run of the tagged program, whose source part is the unmodified actual initialized execution, and the half at the accept has exactly the distribution of the run stopped at the accept. `PqxdhRegistrationJointAcceptCutMonotone` supplies the two facts that link the halves: the private list of KEM keys only grows after the accept, because creation appends a key and no other step removes or changes one, and the final record of the selected accept holds exactly the raw bytes that were pending at the accept. Hence, if the verified PQ key of the pending registration is the native KEM key with the chosen index at the accept, it is still that key at the end.

`PqxdhRegistrationJointKemRawNatural` connects the program that the real run executes, which returns the adversary's result together with the record of the selected accept, to the yes/no program that the KEM games execute, which returns only the decision. Every layer, from the command compiler through the exposure of the selected encapsulation to the KEM cut, treats the two programs alike, so the KEM games stop the yes/no program at exactly the same encapsulation with exactly the same request, and their saved continuation is the saved continuation of the real program with its result mapped to the decision. The module also proves two facts about the KEM-game router that stops before a forbidden reveal: local random coins are drawn exactly as in the real run and do not change the router state, so finishing the stopped encapsulation is one ordinary encapsulation to the requested key followed by the saved rest of the run; and the router's run of a sequential program is the run of the first part followed by the run of the second part.

`PqxdhRegistrationJointKemRawBridge` proves the bridge from the real run to the real KEM game (`actual_le_real`). It starts from the existing theorem that the actual execution has the same distribution as the game that draws the chosen KEM key first. Every later step is a probability inequality or an unconditional program identity inside the chosen-key-first (selected-first) game and the KEM real game; no program is rewritten across the distributional equality. In the chosen-key-first game the final pool consists of the first created reserved keys, so the event says that the verified PQ key of the recorded registration is the chosen key. The existing disclosure monitor turns "the chosen key was never revealed" into a run of the router that stops at a forbidden reveal, with the same complete state. That run is split at the encapsulation of the selected accept. A stop before that encapsulation (the router stops at a forbidden reveal of the chosen key, or at its creation cap) leaves no outcome, and a run that ends before that encapsulation has a selected accept that returned no session; in both cases the event fails. If the encapsulation targets a different key, the event fails too, because the recorded raw bytes are the bytes of the stopped encapsulation, so their verified key is the requested key, which the event equates with the chosen key. In the remaining case the encapsulation targets the chosen key, and finishing it is exactly the challenger's encapsulation followed by the saved rest of the run, which is the real KEM game; the extra uniform draw of that game has no effect. The event implies the game's decision, because the decision of the yes/no program is the adversary's decision combined with "the selected accept returned a session".

`PqxdhRegistrationJointAuthenticatedSelectedKem` assembles the main theorem. An execution either has the final event with a final key match, or it is protected at the accept without a key match there. The first part is bounded by the bridge and the stage B KEM bound; the second part is the stage A authentication bound, which needs no KEM term. A companion theorem (`authenticated_selected_kem_bills`) collects, for the same parameters, the query bills of the KEM adversary, which are exactly the bills of the existing encapsulation-position adversary, and the signing, DH, report and uniform bills of the authentication reductions. The final classification (`classify_final`) separates every execution in which the selected accept returned no session, including every rejection by the Server after a successful signature check, for example a replayed registration that is already consumed or a key that fails to parse. Every other execution had a pending, successfully verified registration at the accept and is attacker-owned or otherwise unprotected, honest with a key match, or the authentication failure of stage A. The 45 statements are guarded so that they depend only on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`. Still open after stage C: the opaque form of the KEM-ideal continuation, which stage D supplies (see the stage D section below), the Extract/HKDF hybrid at the actual joint sampler, including keeping the replaced secret out of the KDF distinguisher's context, which this theorem does not address, global target selection and the common experiment that reconciles the two freshness moments, forward secrecy against a KEM key revealed after the session, and every later item of the handoff. Persistence, snapshots, running-code access and codec internals remain excluded. The [stage C section of the accept/KEM join guide](impl/registration-accept-kem-join.md) lists every statement, the deviations from the plan and the evidence.

## Actual Server continuation with an opaque KEM value

The thirty-one statements in `PqxdhRegistrationJointKemOpaqueSuffix`, `KemOpaqueCore`, `KemOpaqueClient`, `KemOpaqueReal`, `KemOpaqueTail`, `KemOpaqueResume` and `KemOpaqueCosts` remove the selected KEM bytes from the executable saved Server suffix and actual root/erasure/publication continuation. The full source collector is independent of its retained KEM word until final input assembly; literal extracted admission tests the four DH values, and every cleared pending-token field is independent of that word. A private challenge/known marker therefore preserves all optional failures, actual DH order, complete consumed state, allocation on failure, root/consume effects and successful pending publication. Interpreting the marker recovers the exact native client and tail computations, including their cache and instrumentation. The join of the saved suffix and the tail is proved for every outer monad into which the native game maps by a monad morphism, with any prefix interpreter in that monad. It is then instantiated at the exposed encapsulation-cut client, under the real encapsulator, at the stateful private services of the actual accept state, at the ordinary challenge reply of the saved suffix continuation, and under the interpreter chain of the KEM reduction's post-challenge step. These are equalities of programs; they charge no advantage. A separate interpretation recovers the existing real fixed-HKDF source consumer with every auxiliary callback and full private state retained.

This is source correspondence, not an Extract security premise. The current initialized restricted-ROM backend is unchanged; the real and ROM equations are distinct. The client has at most one private root request and four total internal requests, the allocation/publication tail at most six, and the current interpreted root retains its existing 64-byte uniform allowance. Earlier native, primitive and uniform work stays in the program rather than being declared free, but the existing prefix uniform charges are not carried over to the resumed program here. Showing that the scan of the complete source program reaches the accept-form continuation used by the reply and reduction instantiations is the separate raw-accept cut join. The actual dynamic Beacon finish routing, publicly permitted Extract context, hidden-state simulation, repeated related root requests, same-run freshness/selection and real-HKDF hybrid remain open. In particular, saved native closures and private derivation histories cannot be handed to the Extract distinguisher; the known-KEM correlated DH endpoint is not automatically a hidden-KEM contract. See [the opaque-source guide](impl/registration-opaque-kem-source.md) for every statement, exact scope and remaining joins.

The seven modules were ported unchanged from the reviewed lane commits `97cb784e` (modules) and `158e11ae` (guide) to the composition topic, where they are checked against the current composition artifacts and imported by the root module; the two paragraphs above are the lane section verbatim, with its heading raised one level because it now follows the stage C section instead of the source-suffix section. Their import closure outside the seven modules is byte-identical to the lane, so no other lane module is needed. The [port receipt](impl/proof-receipts/registration-opaque-kem-source-port.json) records the source commits, the file hashes and the checks. It also records that the earlier frozen twenty-two-statement manifest of this cohort is superseded: five module files, the guide and this section changed after it, the twenty-two original statements are unchanged in text, and nine statements were added. Stage D of the accept/KEM join applies `KemOpaqueResume.resume_reply` and `resume_post` at the raw-accept KEM cut.

## Opaque KEM-ideal continuation of the accept/KEM join (stage D)

One new checked module, `PqxdhRegistrationJointKemRawOpaque`, rewrites the KEM-ideal game of the main theorem of stage C into an equal game in which the replacement secret, the candidate, is an argument only of the private Server root interpreter and of the KEM router, which hands it to the source's own Beacon-finish code only on a decapsulation of the exact challenge ciphertext under the selected key; routing those finishes into root requests is part of the next step (handoff item 2). In the KEM-ideal game the shared secret of the selected encapsulation is replaced by a uniform value held by the KEM challenger, and the game continues the actual Server code from the moment of that encapsulation. The rewrite has three steps. First, the point where the game stops the Server, just before the encapsulation of the selected raw accept, is described by plain data instead of the Server's saved continuation: the raw registration bytes, the record returned by the Server's signature check, the Server's ephemeral value, the consumed-registration set, the Server's native state, the owner list and the adversary's remaining program. All of these are fixed before the selected encapsulation. The module proves that stopping the actual source there is exactly the same program as computing this data and rebuilding the Server's saved continuation from it. Second, using the opaque-source results ported in the previous section, that continuation, given the challenge ciphertext and secret, is exactly the Server's remaining code run with a marker in place of the secret, where the secret is handed only to the interpreter that answers the Server's private root request. Third, putting these together, the KEM-ideal game is exactly, as a program and not only in distribution, a game in which the uniform secret is passed only to that root interpreter and to the KEM router, which hands it to the source's own Beacon-finish code only when the exact challenge ciphertext is decapsulated under the selected key (theorem T6, `branchRaw_opaque`). The main theorem is restated with this opaque game in place of the KEM-ideal game (`authenticated_selected_opaque`); the event, the assumptions and the loss terms are unchanged.

These are equalities between programs. They charge no advantage and add no assumption, contract or premise; the restated main theorem carries exactly the inherited contracts of stage C. They are not an Extract or HKDF security step, and they say nothing about whether the replacement secret stays out of what a KDF distinguisher may see: the saved data, which includes the Server's private native state and histories, and the other KEM key pairs remain private values of the reduction. The root interpreter is the restricted Extract random-oracle root that the actual initialized source uses, because the opaque game must equal the game built from that source; the choice of the KDF backend for the next step remains open, and the existing fixed-HKDF reading of the same Server code is a separate equality that is not used here. Every decapsulation of the challenge ciphertext under the selected key receives the same single secret, so repeated uses stay tied to one draw. The existing uniform charges of the Server's earlier steps are not carried over to the resumed program. The nine statements are guarded so that they depend only on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`. Still open: the Extract/HKDF hybrid at the actual joint sampler, starting from this opaque game, including keeping the secret out of the distinguisher's context and routing later Beacon finishes into root requests under one joint sampler; the transport of the earlier uniform charges; global target selection and the common experiment; and every later item of the handoff. Persistence, snapshots, running-code access and codec internals remain excluded. The [stage D section of the accept/KEM join guide](impl/registration-accept-kem-join.md) lists every statement and the deviations from the plan.

## Common deployment experiment and its compile lemma (CE-3 trial)

Twelve new modules (`PqxdhDeployment*`) define a first version of the common deployment experiment and prove that it compiles into an ordinary program of the existing registration schedule. In the experiment the adversary talks to one Server, built from a freshly generated seed, and to any number of Beacons it creates with pins of its choice. It can ask for bundles, raw accepts, builds and finishes, use the public HMAC and BLAKE2b oracles, and send and receive raw records on every installed Server peer and every Beacon. Registration runs the existing scheduler code unchanged. Records run the existing Server and Beacon record handlers on the live Server and the live Beacons, with real HKDF and AEAD, the codec's frame reader and writer, and the shared BLAKE2b cache. A Beacon `create` first checks that the pin has 32 bytes and does not re-run runtime initialization (deviation D1 of the plan). There is no reveal command, no public getter, no snapshot API and no test or fresh-message command in this version, and the adversary receives no input at the start.

The compiled program forwards every registration, HMAC and BLAKE2b command unchanged and keeps a log of the successful public replies. It runs every record command itself, on a local copy of the addressed Server peer or Beacon. It builds that copy from public data and one internal read of the registration schedule: the Server's installed kernel for a peer, or the Beacon's established kernel field for a Beacon. It keeps a kernel it has read, so an installed peer or established Beacon is read only once; an empty answer is not kept, so the read is repeated for a key ID that is not installed or a Beacon that is not established. The public data are the pin and key ID given to `create`, the Beacon's bundle bytes, its finish input, the raw accept bytes of each session and the build response of each assigned key ID. The theorem `compile_game` states that the experiment and the initialized execution of the compiled program have exactly the same joint distribution of the Server's public data, the adversary's output and the whole experiment state, once the compiled program's local copies are merged back into the final schedule state. `compile_source` transfers this to the annotated initialized execution that the KEM, root and report theorems are stated for. The proof shows four things. The registration commands never read a Server peer's kernel or an established Beacon's kernel: they read the peer map only to test whether a key ID is taken, and build adds a new peer only at a free key ID. Each record command reads exactly one peer or one Beacon, and the copy agrees with the real one on every field the command reads. Every BLAKE2b query of a local record command goes to the same shared cache, and HKDF, AEAD and the frame writer are computed locally with the real functions. Finally, every copy can be rebuilt from the log: a peer's Beacon identity is the identity key read from the accept bytes of its session, the Server identity is the one read from the build response, and a Beacon's key ID, binding and 153-byte associated data come from its `create`, its bundle and its finish input.

The proof uses two codec laws, both approved as contracts of the common experiment: `Phase1ReadBack` gives the Beacon's identity key from its bundle bytes, and `Phase2ReadBack` gives the Server's identity from a build response. It uses no other premise, charges no advantage and adds no assumption. `FrameReadBack` and the router law `DecoderAgreement` are not needed, because the experiment and the compiled program use the same frame reader, frame writer and router. Two further results check the plan's second risk. In the annotated execution, the compiled program's two internal reads return the current kernel and leave the whole state unchanged, including the private identity pool, the KEM pool and both of their histories. The raw-accept report wrapper also emits nothing for them. So they count as no disclosure for the existing freshness and report predicates. The reads are proof devices: the experiment never gives a kernel to its adversary. `compile_bound` transports query budgets. If the adversary makes at most a given number of commands of each of the twelve classes, the compiled program stays within explicit caps for each of the fourteen query kinds of the registration schedule: one query per coin, registration, HMAC or BLAKE2b command; at most one kernel read and one BLAKE2b query per record command; nothing for a create with a wrong-width pin; and no identity, KEM, prekey or one-time read at all. Local HKDF and AEAD are real work, but they are not counted as queries. All 130 statements are guarded so that they depend only on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`: 126 depend on all three, three on a subset and one on none. Not covered: the test and fresh-message commands and the hidden-bit sampling swap; the record logs the plan uses for origin claims; the success-bit observation mode, which is defined only as a wrapper; the comparison of the transported caps with the budget ledgers of the KEM and root theorems; several Server objects; and a start input for the adversary. The registration theorems are stated for programs with no input, so the compiled program cannot pass on a Server public key given at the start. In this version the adversary can learn the Server's key only from build responses. The owner accepted this on 2026-10-06 as deviation D5: the adversary takes no input and learns the Server identity key through the protocol, which is not an exact reduction from an adversary given the key in advance. Persistence, snapshots, running-code access and codec internals remain excluded.

An independent review of the trial approved it with one major and four minor findings, all fixed in documentation; none needed a Lean change. The two codec laws used, and the approved but unused `FrameReadBack` and one-codec rule with `DecoderAgreement`, are listed in both assumption lists: the functional contracts in [Assumptions made by the proofs](#assumptions-made-by-the-proofs) and the [composition assumptions](composition-assumptions.md#primitive-guarantees-additional-assumptions-and-idealizations). They are abstract message-model laws, not facts about Cap'n Proto. The transported caps for the two internal reads are looser than the plan's, because of the repeated reads described above. Server reveals are bounded by the number of Server record commands, not by the number of builds, and established-kernel reads by the number of Beacon record commands, not by the smaller of the numbers of creates and finishes. This does not affect soundness: the budget premise of the KEM theorem T4 is met with these caps, and its creation-count premise uses only the create cap. It is recorded as a plan change, so any later bill that counts reveals or kernel reads uses the record-command budgets. The plan's caps would need the reads gated on the public log and an amortized count over the whole run in place of the present per-command bound, which is more than a small change. The interface also stays open to the post-run "later quantum" reveal mode that the owner chose on 2026-10-06: after the run ends, every honest X25519 secret, every DH output and every honest Ed25519 identity secret is revealed, and only confidentiality of the run's records and keys is claimed. Because `compile_game` equates the whole final deployment state, not only a projection, such a mode can be added as a phase after the run that is a function of that final state, without changing the command set or the per-command compile cases. The open point is the compiled side. There the secrets can be reached only through the registration schedule's identity, prekey and one-time field reads. `compile_bound` currently caps these at zero, they interact with the freshness predicates `revealedAt` for identity disclosures and `GoodKem` for KEM keys, and prekey and one-time fields follow the native erasure. The Server's identity seed, the erased ephemeral and prekey scalars and the DH outputs have no read at all. How the reductions obtain or simulate that phase is still to be designed. The [common deployment experiment guide](impl/common-deployment-experiment.md) lists the statements, the contracts, the open adversary-input gap and the evidence-based re-estimate.

## Common deployment experiment, unit A: complete interface, selection and publicity

Unit A of the common deployment experiment completes the experiment that the CE-3 trial began, proves that it still compiles into an ordinary program of the registration schedule, adds exact identities for choosing a target, and proves that the public functions used to name targets mean what the hidden state says. It adds nine modules and modifies seven of the twelve trial modules; four of those gain statements, 11 in all, and two others only start from a state with one more, empty, component. With the trial, 250 statements are guarded so that they depend only on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`, and none uses `sorry` or an axiom declaration. An independent review approved the unit with minor findings and nits; all of them are addressed by the fix pass described here and in the guide.

The experiment now has its secrecy commands, its transcript and both observation modes. `test` sends one of two equal-length messages chosen by a hidden bit. The bit is drawn with one coin at the first accepted test, which also fixes the test session; a later test is accepted only on the same record handle or on a handle that the public designation assigns to the same session. `fresh` sends a uniformly random message of a length the adversary picks within fixed bounds; the experiment draws it with one coin per byte when the command is issued and keeps it secret. In the success-bit mode the adversary sees each raw-receive reply only as success or failure, and a lemma shows that this is exactly the projection of the full reply. Secrecy is claimed only in the success-bit mode: in the full-reply mode, forwarding a test or fresh ciphertext to the partner's raw receive would return the hidden message, so there the secrecy commands are ordinary sends. Every query is recorded in a transcript with its full reply, and a log of produced records lists every record that a send sealed and handed to the frame writer, including records whose writer then failed; a lemma shows that keeping this log changes nothing else. Each produced record is tagged only with the record handle of its command, never with its plaintext, so the hidden test and fresh messages do not enter the log. Both logs are analysis logs rather than the adversary's view: the transcript keeps the full replies even in the success-bit mode, and the produced log contains records that were never published. These commands are built as a layer on top of the trial's experiment, so the experiment with the layer is the trial's experiment run on an adversary that carries out the layer itself.

Because of that layering, the trial's compile lemma carries over. For an adversary in either mode, the experiment has exactly the distribution of the registration schedule running the compiled program, jointly over the Server's public data, the adversary's output, the transcript, the hidden bit and fresh messages, the produced-record log and the whole deployment state. The compiled program draws the bit and the fresh messages at the same moment as the experiment, so no lemma about reordering independent draws is needed. The proof again uses only the two approved codec laws `Phase1ReadBack` and `Phase2ReadBack`. Query budgets are transported to the registration schedule in closed form: coins grow by one per test and by the fresh-message byte budget, BLAKE2b queries by one per record command (tests and fresh messages count twice), Server kernel reveals and established-kernel reads by the record commands of their side, and there is no identity, KEM, prekey or one-time read. These caps meet both premises of the KEM theorem T4 that concern budgets. The per-test coin and the doubled count for tests and fresh messages are looser than the plan's figures but sound; they are listed in the guide as a plan change for the owner to confirm, next to the looser read caps already accepted.

The selection identities are generic and exact. If a run ends in an outcome and a public function of the outcome names at most one target from a finite set, then the probability of an event on outcomes that name a target is the sum over targets of the probability of the event together with that target being named. Equivalently, it is the number of targets times the probability that a target guessed uniformly before the run is the one named. For a left-or-right guess, the same sum holds for the advantage weighted by eligibility. A separate identity turns a sum of per-target differences into the number of targets times the difference for a uniformly guessed target, which gives the owner's `N · Adv(B_guess)` wording when every step of a later proof has such signed differences. No assumption is involved. The guessing forms need a nonempty target set; the guide records how a later proof supplies it.

Publicity is proved as an invariant of every run of the experiment, in either mode. The transcript summary always counts exactly the Beacons that exist, the public phase of every Beacon is the class of its real lifecycle phase, each Beacon's created binding is the Server identity and key ID it is pinned to, every published bundle is the writer's output on the tuple that Beacon signed with its own identity key and its own KEM public key, and every build response is the writer's output on fields carrying the Server's identity, which never changes. Hence the public phase, the public owner numbering and the public flag for a rejected bundle in the Fresh phase mean exactly what the hidden state says. These functions, and the designation below, read only queries and the replies of registration commands, never a raw-receive reply, and lemmas prove that two transcripts that look the same in the success-bit mode give the same values. So they are public in that mode too, although the transcript stores full replies. In the annotated execution used by the KEM theorems, the Beacon created k-th holds KEM key number k, for every program.

The designation compares keys, not signed bytes. A Server peer built by session i is designated with Beacon k when the key that the attached-signature check extracts from session i's accept bytes is the PQ key read from Beacon k's published bundle, and the accept carries Beacon k's identity; a Beacon is designated with session i when it is established and pinned to the protected Server, session i's response carries the ciphertext the Beacon received, and session i's accept bytes verify to the Beacon's published key. So an accept that carries an honest Beacon's identity and published key under a different valid signature still counts, and the later corollary that recovers the broader Server-side symbolic eligibility needs only the existing weak-unforgeability bound, not strong unforgeability or unique signatures; the Beacon-side corollary keeps its planned A1 term. Two lemmas show that the designation is made whenever its conditions hold. The designation lemmas read it back into protocol facts. If a Server peer is designated with session i and Beacon k, then whatever key the Server verified from the accept bytes of session i is the KEM public key that Beacon k signed in its published bundle, and the verified identity key is Beacon k's own; this uses `Phase1ReadBack` and no property of the signature scheme. If a Beacon is designated with session i, it is Established and pinned to the protected key ID and to the Server's own identity, the ciphertext it decapsulated is the one the Server wrote in session i's response, and the key verified at accept i is the one it published; this also uses `Phase2ReadBack`. These facts tie Beacon k's published key to its KEM key pair only while Beacon k has not finished registration, because finishing erases the pair from the hidden state. Turning them into the key match of the KEM theorem, which compares with the KEM pool of the annotated execution, therefore needs a new invariant: every bundle of Beacon k in the compiled program's transcript carries pool key k, which holds when the bundle is made and persists because the pool only grows. That step is part of the per-target KEM transfer, CE-9, whose estimate the guide raises accordingly. Finally, in exactly the execution that T4 is stated for, the compiled program discloses no KEM key and no identity seed during the whole run, because its only internal reads are kernel reads and Server kernel reveals, and every other step records only creations, signatures, DH requests and decapsulations. This proves the plan's `approved_goodkem` and `kernel_reads_unrevealed` for the complete interface, both with a budget, as T4 uses them, and for every adversary without one, as the plan states them.

Not covered by unit A: replay, provenance, the A1 embedding, the per-target KEM transfer and everything after it in the plan, including the step to the KEM theorem's key match described above; a lemma that budget-respecting runs designate inside the budget's target set; a concrete run in which an honest relay is designated; the post-run reveal mode, which was then still to be designed (its first two stages are described in the later-quantum section below); several Server objects; and an input for the adversary, which the owner left out as deviation D5. The deviations D1-D5 from production Rust are listed in the guide with their Rust locations and owner decisions. The router that reads a record's claimed sender stays a free parameter, and the approved law `DecoderAgreement` is not used yet. Persistence, snapshots, running-code access and codec internals remain excluded. The [common deployment experiment guide](impl/common-deployment-experiment.md) lists the statements, the decisions taken where the plan left a choice, the names a later proof should use, the review fix pass and the re-estimate.

## Common deployment experiment, unit 3: replay and provenance

Unit 3 proves the replay and Phase 1 provenance claims of the common deployment experiment, the single experiment in which an adversary drives one live Server and any number of Beacons through registration, records and the secrecy commands. It adds seven modules with 148 statements, all guarded so that they depend only on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`; none uses `sorry` or an axiom declaration, and no existing module changed. An independent review approved the first pass (129 statements) with minor findings and nits; the fix pass adds the resource bills of the reductions, the proof that the reveal condition of the provenance claim always holds, and per-Beacon forms of the published-tuple claims, all described below, and is not yet reviewed itself.

Registration replay (CE-R1). The live Server object keeps the list of registration IDs it has consumed. A new lemma about the native accept code shows that a successful accept appends the registration ID of its raw bytes, which was not in the list, and that a rejected accept leaves the list alone; every other command leaves it alone too. The registration ID is read from the public accept bytes: the identity key and the one-time key that the attached-signature check extracts. So on every run, in either observation mode and for every adversary, the consumed list is exactly the list of registration IDs of the successful accepts in the transcript, and no registration ID is carried by two successful accepts. Nothing is assumed and no probability is involved.

Record replay (CE-C3). No Server peer and no Beacon accepts the same record sequence number twice. For a peer this means the successful Server raw receives whose decrypted record names that peer's key ID; for a Beacon it means its successful raw receives and, for sequence one, its successful finish, which accepts the registration record. The proof follows every ratchet kernel from its creation. A Server build installs a peer only at a key ID that was free, and its kernel is the fresh kernel of the registration root after the first send, which consumes no receive position; a Beacon finish installs the fresh kernel of its root after the receive that accepted sequence one. From then on the existing consumption relation of the receive code applies: a successful receive consumes the position of its sequence number, which was neither consumed before nor in the skipped-key cache, a rejected receive restores the kernel, and a send touches only the send chain. Every other command leaves the kernels alone. This is again a deterministic statement about one live object; replay across copies, restorations or persistent state is outside the experiment.

Provenance at the accept (CE-A2). The question is how likely it is that a successful accept carries a Phase 1 key tuple, under a generated Beacon's identity key, that this Beacon never signed. The proof runs the deployment adversary inside the existing report-instrumented execution, which keeps the private signing log of every generated identity and reports every successful accept to a monitor at every identity position; a lemma shows, using the approved codec laws `Phase1ReadBack` and `Phase2ReadBack`, that this instrumentation does not change what the adversary sees, its output or the transcript. The bound itself needs neither law; the two laws are what makes it a statement about the deployment experiment. The new idea is to stop the run right after the accept in question: the monitor's last report then is the one made for that accept, and the existing origin argument shows that an unsigned tuple under an unrevealed generated identity makes that report detect a failure. The monitor's flag stays raised to the end of the run. Since the accept position is a parameter of the event and not a guess, the probability of a violating accept anywhere in the run is at most the sum, over the generated identities (the Beacons plus the Server's generated seed), of the ordinary weak-unforgeability advantage of one reduction each, with coefficient one: no factor for guessing the accept, the owner or the field and no collision term. The event counts every final outcome that some run through a violating accept can reach, so the bound covers the event that the actual run passes through one and may only be larger than it. The origin argument asks that the identity is unrevealed at the accept, but in this experiment that condition always holds: the compiled program never asks for an identity secret, even when stopped right after an accept, so the private log records no reveal, and the bound holds equally for the event without the condition. The owner's post-run reveal mode discloses identity secrets only after the run, so it does not touch this event, which is about accepts during the run. The resources of each reduction are stated in the same form as for the earlier accept and KEM join: at most three signing requests per bundle command and one converted Diffie-Hellman request per finish or accept command of the adversary's budget, a uniform-randomness bill made of the compiled program's own randomness plus 32 uniform queries for each of the other reserved identity seeds, and the same plus the challenger's own seed for the complete weak-unforgeability game. These are all the query classes of that game.

Signing history of a Beacon without a failed bundle call. A Beacon whose bundle call in the Fresh phase fails may have signed a key tuple it never published. For every Beacon whose bundle call never failed in the Fresh phase, a new invariant shows that its whole signing history is either empty, when it published nothing, or exactly the three messages of the tuple of its published bundle, and that the published bytes are the writer's output on the candidate the Beacon signed; other Beacons may have failed. The invariant follows the compiled program, the secrecy layer and the Server schedule together, query by query.

Published-tuple provenance and published-tuple replay (CE-A2pub, CE-R1'). For a Beacon without a failed bundle call in the Fresh phase, an accept that carries its identity key with a key tuple other than the one in its published bundle, or when it published nothing, therefore carries a tuple the Beacon never signed. The statements are per Beacon: only the Beacon whose identity the accept carries must have had no failed bundle call, and failures of other Beacons do not matter. The planned forms, which require that no Beacon had a failed bundle call, follow as corollaries. With a generated Server seed every identity of the instrumented execution is a generated one, so the same reductions apply and the probability has the same bound as CE-A2. The comparison is between key tuples read from public bytes, never between signatures, so strong unforgeability or unique signatures are not needed. Two successful accepts under the identity of such a Beacon cannot both carry its published tuple, because they would carry the same registration ID, which the Server consumes once; so one of them is a published-tuple forgery, and the probability of two such accepts has the same bound again. These two statements use the approved codec laws `Phase1ReadBack` and `Phase2ReadBack` to identify the instrumented execution with the deployment experiment. That identification produces the experiment with the Server's identity index 0, so they are proved for that index; the index enters the experiment only as a label in the Server's metadata, but no lemma shows that the probabilities are the same for other indices.

Not covered by unit 3: Beacons with a failed bundle call in the Fresh phase for the published-tuple statements, where a second accepted tuple need not be forged; other Server identity indices for the published-tuple statements; a count of the public reports that the reductions process, which are not queries of the weak-unforgeability game; replay across Server objects; a concrete run showing that the events can occur; and all later stages of the plan, from the A1 embedding on. The [common deployment experiment guide](impl/common-deployment-experiment.md) gives the exact statements, the decisions and the checks.

## Common deployment experiment, later-quantum mode: post-run reveal and its compile lemma

The later-quantum mode models a classical adversary that takes part in the run and, after the run ends, receives the X25519 secrets and the Ed25519 identity secrets of the honest Beacons, from which it can derive every Diffie-Hellman output those Beacons computed, while ML-KEM secret keys and shared secrets and every Server secret are never revealed (deviation D6); it is not a QPT or QROM model and transfers no soundness from the passive-quantum ProVerif lines. It is motivated by an attacker who records a run today and later breaks X25519 and Ed25519 but not ML-KEM; in this profile such an attacker receives only the Beacon-side elliptic-curve secrets. After the disclosure the adversary may keep computing, but it cannot talk to the protocol any more. Only confidentiality of what was sent during the run is meant to be claimed in this mode, not authentication. Two new modules build the first two stages, LQ-1 and LQ-2 of the design, with 58 statements; no existing module changed, and every statement is guarded so that it depends only on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`. These stages define the game and prove that it compiles into an ordinary program of the registration schedule; they make no security claim yet.

The game has two adversaries. The first runs the common deployment experiment exactly as before, with one bookkeeping change that the adversary cannot see: just before a Beacon's finish, the experiment copies the Beacon's prekey and one-time secret scalars into a private snapshot, because finish and abort erase them. A lemma shows that the run phase of the new game, with the snapshot forgotten, is exactly the classical experiment, jointly over the Server's public data, the first adversary's output, the ledger, the deployment state and the runtime state. Another shows that every event of the Server's public data, the ledger and the final deployment state that does not change when only the Extract family, the BLAKE2b cache and the ghost touch list (the record of HMAC inputs by sessions, Beacons and the adversary) change has the same probability at the end of the new game as at the end of the classical experiment with the same first adversary; the adversaries' outputs and the runtime state are not part of such an event. So results about the run that are stated on these values carry over unchanged. When the first adversary stops, the experiment computes the reveal: for every Beacon it created, in creation order, the Beacon's Ed25519 identity seed and its X25519 prekey scalar and one-time scalar, taken from the live state if still present and from the snapshot otherwise. The second adversary receives the first adversary's output and this reveal. It may draw coins and query the public HMAC oracle and the BLAKE2b oracle, the same oracles with the same tables as during the run, but nothing else, and a lemma shows that its queries change only those tables and a log of adversary queries.

What is revealed is precisely the Beacon side. The Beacon's X25519 identity secret follows from its seed by the production conversion, and every Diffie-Hellman value a Beacon computed follows from revealed scalars and public keys, so neither is listed separately. Deviation D6 records what is not revealed: the Server's identity seed and the Server's per-registration ephemeral scalars. Diffie-Hellman values that only the Server could compute, against keys whose secret the attacker does not know, therefore stay hidden; the owner's full profile would reveal them too, and two extensions (LQ-S for the Server seed, LQ-F for everything) are still to be decided. The scalars of bundle attempts that failed are not revealed, because neither Rust nor the model keeps them and their public keys were never sent. ML-KEM secret keys and shared secrets are never revealed, as in the owner's profile, which lists X25519 secrets, Diffie-Hellman outputs and Ed25519 identity secrets only: the mode assumes ML-KEM stays secure, and revealing a Beacon's ML-KEM key would let the attacker decrypt its key exchange and recompute its keys. Nothing that depends on the ML-KEM output, such as the random-oracle tables for the root, the analysis logs, roots, chains or record keys, can enter the reveal, whose type holds only seeds and scalars.

The compile lemma has the same form as for the classical game. The compiled program runs the classical compiled program of the first adversary, but before every finish it reads the Beacon's prekey and one-time fields from the registration schedule and keeps them, which matches the experiment's snapshot. After the run it reads the identity, prekey and one-time fields of every Beacon its own log counts and builds the reveal. Then it runs the second adversary and passes its coin, HMAC and BLAKE2b queries to the schedule. The key fact is that merging the compiled program's local record state back into the schedule state changes no identity, ML-KEM, prekey or one-time field, so the reads see exactly what the experiment reveals. The theorem states that the later game has exactly the distribution of the schedule running the compiled program, jointly over the Server's public data, the second adversary's output, the ledger, the snapshot and the whole final state, and a second form transfers this to the annotated execution that the ML-KEM and root theorems use. It uses only the two approved codec laws `Phase1ReadBack` and `Phase2ReadBack`. The finish read is added as a wrapper around the existing compiler, so the existing compile modules did not change; they were re-checked and produced identical artifacts.

Query budgets carry over: the compiled program's queries are bounded by the classical bounds plus two reads per finish, three reads per created Beacon and the second adversary's own coin, HMAC and BLAKE2b budgets. The field-read caps need only the first adversary's budget and hold for every second adversary: at most as many identity reads as creates, at most finishes plus creates prekey reads and one-time reads, and no ML-KEM read, which holds for every pair of adversaries even without a budget. The terminal identity reads are disclosure requests to the identity pool, so the lemma that no identity is revealed during the whole run, which the classical compiled program satisfies because it reads no identity, is not available for this program. They come after every accept, because the terminal reads and the second adversary's queries contain no accept, so they change no freshness reading made at an accept: the authentication input T5 reads its protection just before the selected accept, and it can even be instantiated on this program with the transported budgets. The provenance result A2 and T5 are nevertheless never to be cited on this program, for a reason of scope. Authentication is not claimed in this mode, and authentication is a property of the run: the run phase of the new game is exactly the classical experiment, so the run-phase authentication terms that later stages keep are classical terms of the first adversary, and the event lemma above carries the events they bound to the new game when those events are stated on the Server's public data, the ledger and the final deployment state. A2 is planned for the classical compiled program, and T5 on this program would bound events whose reductions are built from the whole program, including the reveal and the second adversary. The remaining stages (the ML-KEM transfer, the random-oracle and key-schedule steps with the post-run budgets, the ideal world and the headline confidentiality theorems) and the amendment of the reveal text in the [composition assumptions](composition-assumptions.md) are listed in the [common deployment experiment guide](impl/common-deployment-experiment.md). The second adversary's coin, HMAC and BLAKE2b queries are classical queries; no quantum access to the random oracles is modeled.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-9: per-target KEM transfer

CE-9 connects the common deployment experiment to the ML-KEM step of the accept and KEM join, one target at a time. A target is a pair of public numbers: the session handle of a raw accept, which is also its position among all accept attempts, and the creation index of a Beacon, which is also the index of its ML-KEM key. A claim about a run names a record handle, and the experiment's public designation, computed only from the transcript, turns that handle into at most one target. Three new modules add 70 statements, all guarded so that they depend only on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`; no existing module changed. An independent review approved the first 65 statements with nits, and the fix pass that answers it, which adds the other 5, is not yet reviewed.

The first step is an equality. Take any event that reads the adversary's output, the secrecy ledger (including the hidden bit and the fresh messages) and the produced record frames, and a target made of session i and Beacon k. The probability that the experiment ends with the event and with the claim designating that target equals the probability of the event that the earlier ML-KEM theorem T4 starts from, in exactly the execution T4 is stated for: the compiled program tagged at its i-th accept attempt. That event says that the i-th accept attempt returned a session and the event and designation hold, that Beacon k's ML-KEM secret key was never disclosed, and that the bytes of that accept verify to the public key that the private key pool holds at index k at the end of the run. The second part was proved for the compiled program before. The other two parts needed a new argument, because the designation is read from the transcript and the key match from the private key pool, and nothing proved so far connected the two after a Beacon finished registration, when the Beacon forgets its ML-KEM key pair.

The connection is made by tracing. Any program of the registration schedule can be run with a log of the replies to its accept and bundle requests, without changing anything it does. For the compiled program this log is exactly the accept and bundle part of the experiment's transcript, and T4's tag at position i is the i-th logged accept; both facts hold for every possible reply. On the private side of the execution, three facts hold at every step and therefore at the end of the run. The Server's session counter equals the number of logged accepts, so an accept that returned session i was the i-th attempt. The bytes of every successful accept pass the Server's verification. Every published bundle of Beacon k carries the public key that the pool holds at index k: when the bundle is made, the Beacon signs its own ML-KEM public key, which sits at its creation index in the pool, and later steps only append to the pool. The designation says, on both the Server side and the Beacon side, that the PQ key verified from session i's accept bytes is the key read from Beacon k's published bundle. Together with the approved codec law `Phase1ReadBack`, which reads the published key back from the bundle bytes, this gives the key match.

The remaining steps chain existing theorems. T4 bounds the event by the real ML-KEM game at the same position, with the compiled program's query budgets transported from the adversary's budget. The certified ML-KEM step bounds that by the game with the encapsulated secret replaced by a uniform one, plus one ordinary IND-CCA advantage of an explicit adversary and one ML-KEM correctness error, each with coefficient one. The opaque form of that game is equal to it. So, for one target, the probability that the experiment ends with the event and the target is at most the probability that the opaque ideal game accepts, plus one IND-CCA advantage and one correctness error. The IND-CCA adversary's query counts are stated explicitly in terms of the adversary's budget. Unlike the earlier authenticated forms of the join, this per-target chain charges no signature-forgery term: the key comparison in the designation replaces the authentication step, so the per-target cost is only the ML-KEM terms.

Summing over targets is exact. The probability that the experiment ends with the event and a designated claim equals the sum, over all pairs of an accept position below the accept budget and a Beacon index below the create budget plus one, of the per-target probabilities, so it is at most the sum of the per-target bounds: one IND-CCA advantage and one correctness error per target, with no factor for guessing the target and no forgery term. A further lemma closes a gap left by the earlier unit: when the adversary keeps to its budget, every designation in every run has an accept position below the accept budget and a Beacon index below the create budget, because a session handle is the position of an accept attempt among at most budget-many attempts and a designated Beacon was created by one of at most budget-many create commands. So the sum covers every designated claim, not only the ones inside the range. The range is in fact narrower than the sum by one Beacon index: no claim is ever designated with a Beacon index equal to the create budget, so those targets contribute nothing to the probability, yet each of them still adds an IND-CCA advantage and a correctness error to the bound. A second form of the headline therefore sums only over Beacon indices below the create budget and leaves these terms out; the per-target bound it uses is the same.

What this uses and what remains. The premises are the two approved codec laws `Phase1ReadBack` and `Phase2ReadBack`, the existing `FunctionalDecapsulation` contract of the ML-KEM step, and the adversary's budget, and the explicit query counts of the IND-CCA adversary also use the existing cost premises of the ML-KEM bills; nothing new is assumed. The range lemma uses only the two codec laws and the budget. The bound is one-sided, because T4 is; left-or-right secrecy needs a two-sided form of T4 (stage CE-9b), which can compose with the two-sided ML-KEM step stated here for one target. The ideal side of the bound is still a game about the compiled program, with the key derivation steps after ML-KEM untouched; replacing them by ideal keys (item 2) and moving back to a game about the deployment adversary (CE-11) are later stages, as are the same transfer for the later-quantum mode, the corollaries for the broader symbolic eligibility notions, and a concrete run showing that the event can occur. The experiment is stated with the Server's identity at index 0 of the empty identity pool, which is where T4's execution starts. The [common deployment experiment guide](impl/common-deployment-experiment.md) gives the exact statements, the decisions and the checks.

## Common deployment experiment, later-quantum mode: LQ-F, the owner's exact profile

The owner's later-quantum profile reveals after the run every honest X25519 secret, every Diffie-Hellman output and every honest Ed25519 identity secret; for this mode the owner later fixed it exactly, with two documented exceptions described below. The Beacon-side mode above leaves out the Server's identity seed and the Server's per-registration ephemeral scalars (deviation D6), because no program of the registration schedule can read them: the seed is read by no command, and the ephemeral scalar exists only inside the Server's accept. A time-boxed spike tested the design's way to close this gap: a logged version of the schedule that also records each accept's ephemeral scalar in a private log, and one extra request, issued after the run, that returns the Server's seed and the log. The spike added nine modules on a separate branch, guarded so that they depend only on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`, and changed no existing module. It was reviewed, and a fix pass brought it to 112 statements. The owner then chose this profile, and six more modules with 100 statements built it at the level of the deployment experiment: the later game for the exact profile, its compile lemma and the per-target ML-KEM transfer. The fix pass and the six modules were reviewed in turn, a second fix pass corrected the documentation and strengthened two lemmas, and a confirming review approved it. No headline theorem is claimed yet; what is proved is that the deployment experiment with the exact reveal compiles to the logged schedule and that its ML-KEM step goes through unchanged.

The logged schedule is the registration schedule with two changes. Each accept runs the literal Server accept and, whenever it generated an ephemeral key, also hands back the ephemeral scalar; the schedule appends it to the log, one entry per accept attempt, and an empty entry when the accept stopped before generating one. The new request, which the compiled program issues once after the run, reveals the Server's identity seed by the ordinary disclosure request of the identity pool, together with the log. Forgetting the log gives back the original schedule exactly, for every program that does not use the new request, so nothing proved about the original schedule is disturbed. A lemma shows that this Server request returns the Server's actual seed and changes nothing but the disclosure record, to which it appends one observation, and another that, for every accept whose collection succeeded, the logged scalar is the one the Server used in its three ephemeral Diffie-Hellman steps. An accept that generated its ephemeral and then failed the check of the ML-KEM public key, the only step between generation and encapsulation, also logs its scalar, as the design specifies; the spike first left it out, and the review fix pass added it. The owner stated the profile of this mode as every honest X25519 secret and every honest Ed25519 identity secret, except two kinds of scalar that are never published or used: the one-time scalars of failed Beacon bundle attempts, which a Beacon drops when signing or serializing its bundle fails, and the Server ephemeral of an accept that fails the check of the ML-KEM public key, which the Server drops before encapsulating, before any Diffie-Hellman step and before publishing anything. No value that an attacker who records traffic sees depends on either kind. These two documented exceptions take the place of deviation D6 of the Beacon-side mode, and no further proof work is done for them. Together with the Beacon-side reveal, the reveal covers this profile: it leaves out only the one-time scalars of failed bundle attempts, which are in no state, and it even contains the ephemerals of the second kind, because the log records every generated ephemeral; no result depends on that. Diffie-Hellman outputs are not listed, because each is computed from revealed scalars and public keys; ML-KEM secrets, the random-oracle tables and every key derived from the ML-KEM output stay hidden, as in the Beacon-side mode.

The spike then re-proved, for programs of the logged schedule, every step of the ML-KEM part of the argument: the reservation that draws the selected ML-KEM key pair first, the monitor that tracks whether that key is ever disclosed, the cut of the run at the encapsulation of the selected accept, the bridge from the real run to the ML-KEM game (T4), the ML-KEM hop itself, the rewriting of the ideal game into a form in which the replaced shared secret is used only by the Server's own root derivation and the router (T6), the combination of the three, and the query budgets of the constructed ML-KEM adversary. The key point is the cut: at the selected encapsulation the Server's ephemeral scalar is already fixed, so the saved rest of the run logs it as a known value that does not depend on the ciphertext or on the shared secret, and the existing rewriting of T6 applies with the logged rest. The loss is the same as in the classical chain: one ordinary ML-KEM IND-CCA advantage of the constructed adversary and one ordinary ML-KEM correctness error, each counted once, and the adversary's query budgets are exactly the classical ones, because the Server request is one disclosure request to the identity pool and costs nothing in any counted class. Several existing results needed no change at all: the ML-KEM hop is now stated once for any cut program, and the reservation, the monitor and the rewriting lemmas of T6 were already general.

The later game for the exact profile is the Beacon-side later game with one more ghost change. While the first adversary runs, each Server accept is the native accept with the logged collection, and the experiment keeps the ephemeral log beside its state, one entry per accept attempt; a lemma shows that each step either appends one entry and advances the Server's session counter by one, which is what an accept does, or leaves both alone, so the log grows exactly as the counter does; it follows, although no theorem states it separately, that entry number j belongs to the accept that allocated session j. After the run the second adversary receives the Beacon-side reveal together with the Server's identity seed and the log, and then has only post-run coins, the public HMAC and the BLAKE2b oracle. Forgetting the log gives back the Beacon-side game, and forgetting the snapshot as well gives back the classical experiment, so every event of the run that ignores the caches has the same probability in all three; this is how the classical authentication terms of the first adversary carry over. The post-run queries are classical: the model is a classical adversary that receives a disclosure after the run, not a quantum adversary.

The compile lemma has the same shape as for the Beacon-side mode, and it reuses that mode's step relation. The compiled program now runs on the logged schedule: it is the Beacon-side compiled program with the Server request inserted between the final Beacon reads and the second adversary. The new work is the accept: the logged native accept must commute with the compiled program's local copies of record state, which holds because the Server's core acceptance and root processing never look at the peers that those copies describe. Every other command issues no accept, so on the logged schedule it behaves as in the Beacon-side mode and leaves the log alone.
