The chain lift replaces real chain values by uniform ones one table coordinate at a time, so two neighbouring hybrids differ only at one coordinate, a child whose input is the selected parent's hidden next-chain value. Up to the first lookup of the parent the two hybrids behave identically: `PqxdhRecordLiftPrefixPolicy` (6 statements) shows that before that lookup the execution never reads the child, because reading it requires the stored parent, which is still missing, so the two prefixes are exactly equal, with all state, for every client, for both frozen programs and for the proof-attached samplers. At the parent itself, the published `PqxdhRecordLiftGlobalCut` already bounds, with one Extract advantage and one HMAC-PRF advantage, the difference between the real continuation and a continuation that receives an independent uniform child value. `PqxdhRecordLiftChildPolicy` (19 statements) identifies that second continuation with the next hybrid: running the rest of the execution with one independent uniform child value drawn up front (by `ChildRelay.deferred_source`, equivalently drawn at its first use and reused afterwards) has the same distribution as the actual record program under the policy in which the child coordinate is also uniform, under every later observation of the result, the shared hash cache, the frame logs and the whole private state except its native and uniform analysis counters. The identification assumes that the execution stands at the selected parent, that the parent's position is at least its direction's start position, that the parent is already uniform and the child still real, and that the child's table entry is still missing. These conditions are not yet derived at the sampled cut, and the cost of the child draw is not yet charged; both belong to the next increment, which composes the three parts into one hybrid step, adds the analogue for the initial child of a fresh seed, and sums the steps.

Per-operation bills for the CTX lift. The later CTX lift has to charge every record operation against the query budgets of the CTX component: uniform bytes, hash queries, seal queries and raw verification queries. `PqxdhRecordLiftCtxProgramBounds` (12 statements) proves, for every send and receive, with a hidden or a caller-known key and under every possible reply, that a send costs at most 76 uniform bytes, one hash query, one seal query and no raw query, and that a receive costs at most 51 · 76 uniform bytes, one hash query, no seal query and one raw query. These are counting bounds on what the program can ask, not probabilities. Summing them over a whole run and expressing the totals in the budget fields of the experiment remains to be done.

What remains. None of these statements is a security theorem of the record layer. The chain lift, the CTX lift, their composition, the origin and hiding facts of the ideal record world and the later-quantum forms remain open; this increment supplies components for the first two. Review and integration status are recorded in `doc/impl/proof-receipts/record-lift-increment-a.json`. The guides [no refusal](impl/record-lift-ctx-no-refusal.md), [seed scope](impl/record-lift-seed-scope.md), [child policy](impl/record-lift-child-policy.md), [prefix policy](impl/record-lift-prefix-policy.md) and [per-operation bills](impl/record-lift-ctx-program-bounds.md) give the exact statements, their premises and their provenance.

## Items 4 and 5, stage S1: the record-lift ideal worlds and target statements

The record-layer lift (handoff items 4 and 5) has to show that, in the experiment in which the selected session's root material is already ideal, the session's evolving chains and record encryption can be replaced by ideal versions at an explicit cost. Before any of that is proved, `PqxdhRecordLiftIdeal` writes down exactly what the ideal versions are and what each statement must say, so that the chain work, the record-encryption work and the later headline theorems all aim at the same fixed targets. The module proves none of the targets; its 28 theorems only check that the definitions are well-formed and fit together. No assumption or contract is added. See [the guide](impl/record-lift-ideal.md).

The worlds all run the same compiled adversary-and-environment program and differ only in how the hidden record material is produced. In the real world every chain step calls the real key derivation. In the chain-ideal world `idealChains` every step of a hidden session's chains reads a persistent table of uniformly random outputs instead, which keeps its values when a failed receive is rolled back and the same step is derived again. In the integrity-ideal world `idealAuth` the hidden sessions' record keys come from that table and every hidden record is additionally handled by an idealized encryption: sealing still produces real ciphertexts, but a receive accepts a frame only if it is one of the frames sealed at that position, in which case it returns the sealed message. In the record-ideal world `idealRecords` the same holds and, in the observation mode used for secrecy (mode P, where the adversary sees only whether a receive succeeded), the sealed ciphertexts are random bytes of the right length. Everything else, including registration, known-key records of other sessions, adversary hash queries, rejections, rollback and the transcript, is exactly as in the chain-ideal world; in the idealized encryption modes only the hidden records' commitments move from the shared hash oracle to a private dictionary, as in the existing one-key bounds. The module checks that its real world is the existing record world on the view that the common deployment experiment uses, that its real and replay encryption modes are exactly the two endpoints of the existing one-key integrity bound, and that its random mode agrees with the replay mode except on sealing. That the step from the replay mode to the random mode is exactly the replay-to-random comparison that the existing one-key indistinguishability-from-random result prices was not proved at stage S1; the privacy step had to show it, and the privacy track proves it (`PqxdhRecordLiftCtxRandom.randomTargetView_randomView` and `replay_random_target`; see the section "Items 4 and 5, stage S4: the privacy half of the record-encryption lift").

The targets are stated for every environment and adversary that respect the existing budgets. The chain target says that the real and chain-ideal worlds can be told apart by at most the sum, over every chain position of every hidden session and direction, of one key-derivation advantage per position (extraction from a uniform input plus HMAC as a pseudorandom function), plus explicit terms for aliasing and refusals that are intended to be zero. The record-encryption target is split in two: an integrity half that charges, for each hidden record key, the existing encryption-integrity terms, and a privacy half that charges, for each key, one indistinguishability-from-random advantage; their combination is stated as one target as well. A separate integrity-only record target goes from the real world straight to the integrity-ideal world, so the authentication headlines need no privacy step. The module proves that each combined target follows from its parts. The origin target says that in the ideal worlds a hidden session never accepts a frame that its partner never produced, and accepts a frame its partner did not publish before only with probability at most twice the number of receive attempts times the number of sends divided by 2^512. That bound is purely statistical: in the ideal worlds each hidden record carries a fresh random 64-byte commitment that is kept in a private table and becomes visible only when the record is published, and a receive accepts only the complete record, commitment included; a record whose publication failed shows the adversary at most whether the failure happened. The binding target, needed for unknown-key-share, bounds the probability that a frame returned by one handle is accepted by a different handle that is not its partner, with one of the two handles hidden; frames of different Server peers, or of different Beacons, may carry the same sender field, so this too rests on the private commitments rather than on the sender. Finally, in mode P the secrecy targets say that the record-ideal world does not depend on the content of the hidden sessions' messages: a guess of a fresh message sent on a hidden session is right with probability at most 2 to the minus its minimum length, and, among the runs whose admitted tests all went to hidden sessions and that a public rule marks eligible, a public guess of the test bit is right exactly half of the time.

These targets name the reductions they charge as explicit parameters. A target with arbitrary reductions plugged in says nothing (a reduction with unlimited computing power can make every advantage term close to one), so each target becomes a security result only together with the concrete reductions and query bills of the theorem that will prove it, and those are reviewed with that theorem. Each statement lists the only contracts it may use: the functional key-derivation correspondence for the chains, the frame read-back law and the Server routing law for origin, and the read-back law for binding. An independent design review of the first version found that the unknown-key-share and secrecy headlines could not use the targets as written, and that the origin bound needlessly depended on the privacy step; the targets above are the corrected versions, and the changed origin bound implies the earlier one. The authentication and secrecy headlines of the common deployment experiment will consume these targets; they still need two steps of their own, which the guide lists: their events must compare decoded frames rather than raw bytes, and it must be proved, on the ideal worlds as well as on the real one, that the designated handles hold the hidden session and that no other handle does. A confirming review of the corrections raised only documentation remarks, which are fixed.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-11b increment 1: slot programs, the challenger's draws and a startup draw

CE-11b builds the ideal version of the common deployment experiment for one target, a pair of a Server session (the i-th raw accept) and a Beacon (the k-th KEM key created), in which the key material of the target's hidden root is uniform and is read through item 2's table of hidden slots. The first increment adds three modules with 35 statements, all guarded so that they depend at most on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`; no existing proof module changed, and no assumption or contract is added. An independent review found no error in the statements or proofs; its remarks on the documentation, the plan and three module comments are fixed, and a confirming review found them resolved.

Registration steps as clients of the slot table. Item 2 reads every hidden key-schedule output through a "first-touch allocator": the first time a hidden root's coordinates (its four DH outputs) are asked for, they get the next free slot, later requests for the same coordinates get the same slot, and the slot's 108 bytes come from a slot service, for example a lazily filled table. The first module lets a registration step of the common deployment experiment be written as a program that asks for values at coordinates, and turns such a program into a registration handler of the experiment whose state also holds the allocator and the service. Its main fact is that such a handler never looks at the slot values except through the service: if one service can be mapped onto another so that every service step corresponds in distribution, the whole handler corresponds in distribution. CE-11a needs exactly this to replace the 108-byte table by its split into environment material and a world seed; with this module, that step holds for every handler built this way, so for the ideal registration of CE-11b once it is written as slot programs.

The challenger's draws. In the ideal experiment the challenger draws, before the run, the selected Beacon's KEM key pair, the key pairs of every other KEM creation index allowed by the budget (whether or not a Beacon is ever created at that index), and the ciphertext of an encapsulation to the selected public key. Item 2's ideal world draws the same values but in another order: the selected key pair first, then the Server is constructed and the other key pairs are drawn, the run proceeds up to the selected raw accept, and only then is the challenge encapsulated. The second module proves that the two orders give the same distribution: the other key pairs can be drawn before the Server is constructed (if construction fails they are simply unused), and the encapsulation can be drawn before the run because nothing before the selected accept reads it. As a result, item 2's ideal world, for any number of hidden slots and so for the two slots that item 2 hands over, is, in distribution, the challenger's draw followed by the same world with the drawn values fixed. This lets the second compile lemma of CE-11b compare the two experiments for fixed draws.

A draw at startup. The record-lift hand-off needs the ideal experiment as an environment of the record world, and the challenger's draws must belong to that environment's own startup randomness, so that every reduction that uses the environment draws them itself. The third module proves the join of CE-11a for such environments: if an environment first draws a parameter, then runs the Server constructor and afterwards behaves like a registration handler that depends on the parameter, then the draw followed by the common deployment experiment with that handler has the same distribution as the record world with the environment. The proof keeps the parameter in the environment's state and follows CE-11a's join; the world only counts the startup draw, and the join already ignores such counts. The CE-11b design had planned a slightly different construction that would have needed a new fact about the world's counters; the chosen one avoids it. Three consequences follow, the first two of them planned work. For the ideal game itself this join is the last step of the connection to the record world: the ideal registration is first replaced, for each drawn value, by its erased and split form (CE-11a's erasure and split), and the join connects that form to the record world. CE-11a's lemmas for the hash cache, for the reveal of session keys and for the later quantum phase assume that the environment's startup is the Server constructor alone, so they need versions for a startup that draws first; the first two follow from the new join directly, the third needs a new lemma. And because every reduction that uses the environment now makes the challenger's draws itself, its startup randomness grows by the cost of one KEM key generation per creation index and one encapsulation.

What this does not show. These are equalities of distributions and of programs; they make no security claim. The ideal registration itself (the creation of the selected Beacon with the challenger's key pair, the selected accept that uses the challenge ciphertext and reads its root from the slot table, the build of that session and the selected Beacon's finish of the challenge ciphertext), its environment, the second compile lemma and the hand-off theorem are not built yet; scratch versions of the three hidden steps exist and are recorded in the guide.

## Items 4 and 5, stage S3: the chain lift (item 5)

The chain target fixed in stage S1 is now proved. `PqxdhRecordLiftChainLift.chain_lift` shows `PqxdhRecordLiftIdeal.ChainLiftTarget` exactly as defined there: in the experiment in which the hidden sessions' root material is already ideal, the real record world and the chain-ideal world `idealChains`, in which every chain step of a hidden session reads a persistent table of uniformly random outputs, can be told apart by any decision on the permitted view and the final shared hash cache with probability at most the sum, over every chain position of every hidden session and direction up to the derivation allowance of the budget (sends plus 51 times receives), of one extraction advantage (HMAC extraction from a uniform 32-byte input) and one pseudorandom-function advantage of HMAC, each counted once. The aliasing and refusal terms of the target are zero. The bound holds for every environment within its resource frame and every adversary within its budget, in both observation modes and for both directions, and the only contract used is the functional correspondence between the source key derivation and HKDF over HMAC (`SourceFullCorrect`). The reductions are written out explicitly, and each of them makes at most twice the program's random-draw allowance plus 44 plus the decision's own draws, a closed expression in the budget and frame fields. No assumption, contract or target definition changed. See [the guide](impl/record-lift-chain-lift.md).

The proof is an ordered hybrid over the chain positions, depth first: position zero of every session and direction, then position one, and so on. Each step replaces one more position by the random table. Replacing a first position uses one half of the session's fresh 64-byte seed as the uniform 32-byte extraction input; replacing a later position uses the uniform chain value that the previous step left in the table, which is always already random because the order goes depth first. The published cuts of the record lift already bound the distance between the real step and a step in which the derived value is replaced by a fresh random one; what was missing, and is proved here, is that this fresh value has exactly the same effect as the next hybrid's table entry. The table entry is drawn when the position is first needed, while the cut draws it beforehand, and later uses must keep seeing the same value even after a failed receive is rolled back; the new seed relay and seed policy show, for the first positions, that drawing once and reusing gives the same law over the whole remaining run, as the earlier child policy did for later positions. Two further facts are needed: the part of the run before the cut is the same in both hybrids, because the position being replaced cannot be used before its slot's seed exists or before its predecessor is computed; and the last hybrid, which randomizes only positions up to the budget's allowance, is the chain-ideal world, because a run within its budget never derives a position beyond that allowance. Both are proved from the run itself: a position that a run uses stays recorded in its table, and every final table respects the depth and slot facts already established for the record world. A run that never reaches a position gives two identical games.

No aliasing or refusal term arises, and the module `PqxdhRecordLiftChainAlias` records why. Each step of the hybrid changes how one labelled position is computed and nothing else; positions are kept apart by their labels, never by comparing derived bytes, so two positions with colliding outputs are still separate. An adversary or environment that evaluates the key derivation on a guessed chain value does so inside the explicit reductions, so this is already covered by the two advantages. Hidden kernels are always constructed without failure, and whether a hidden installation is accepted depends only on the public control state, so the chain worlds never refuse a step.

The query bills are derived from the program, not assumed. Every private operation of the world has a fixed maximum number of random draws (a seed 64 bytes, a randomized chain step one 76-byte output, a hash or an encryption or decryption at most one 64-byte digest), every request of the environment and adversary costs a bounded number of private operations (a send at most one chain step and one sealing, a receive at most 51 chain steps and one opening), and the existing budget results bound how many requests of each kind the program makes. The same per-request bills in the integrity and privacy ledgers are proved along the way and are available to the record-encryption track.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-11b increment 2: the ideal registration

This increment defines the ideal experiment that CE-11b compares with item 2's ideal world, for one target: one raw accept of the Server (counted from the start of the run) and one Beacon creation index. The challenger has drawn, before the run, the selected Beacon's KEM key pair, the key pairs of every other creation index and the ciphertext of an encapsulation to the selected public key (increment 1). The ideal registration answers every registration command of the common deployment experiment; it is the real registration except at four places.

Creation. A new Beacon receives the key pair that the challenger drew for its creation index instead of a freshly generated one; its identity and prekey are still generated by the actual code, in the same order. If more Beacons are created than the challenger drew for (which the adversary's budget excludes), a fresh key pair is generated as in the real code.

The selected accept. When the selected raw accept carries a Phase 1 message whose signatures verify and whose post-quantum key is the selected public key, the Server runs its actual checks up to the encapsulation. If it gets that far, the accept is marked active: instead of encapsulating, the Server uses the challenger's ciphertext, and instead of deriving its root from the shared secret, it reads a hidden value from a table of independent values at the four Diffie-Hellman outputs of the exchange, remembers those coordinates for the session, and keeps a placeholder root that nothing uses. On every other message the selected accept is the real (logged) accept, by construction.

The selected session's build. When the Server builds the response of that session, the key-schedule output that the real Server would derive from its root is replaced by the hidden value at the remembered coordinates; everything else of the build is the actual code.

The selected Beacon's finish. After an active selected accept, when the selected Beacon finishes its registration, a decapsulation of exactly the challenge ciphertext is answered by a marker instead of a key; for that marker the Beacon reads the hidden value at its own four Diffie-Hellman outputs (the same coordinates as the Server's when both sides agree) and continues from it. Any other ciphertext is decapsulated with the Beacon's actual secret key. Every other Beacon, and the selected Beacon before the selected accept, is real.

The hidden values are read through item 2's first-touch allocator, which gives each new coordinate the next of two table slots, as item 2's two-slot ideal world does (a third coordinate would receive a fresh value outside the table). Only the selected accept and the selected Beacon's finish can read a hidden value at a coordinate not read before; the build of the selected session reads the accept's coordinates again, and the selected Beacon's finish reads at most once, since a finish from the waiting phase always ends established or aborted. That at most two coordinates occur in a run is therefore expected, but it is not yet proved: it is part of the run invariant planned for a later unit of CE-11b. The game `CE.idealGame g` draws the challenger's values and runs the common deployment experiment with this registration. A variant with the Beacon's hidden finish replaced by its erased form is also defined; it is the form CE-11a's erasure lemma will produce.

What was checked. Besides the definitions, the module proves that the selected accept without the selected key is exactly the logged accept, that the build with the real services is the native build, that every accept other than the selected one is the real accept, that every build is the real build except the build of the selected session while its token is pending, that every finish is the real finish except the selected Beacon's finish in its waiting phase after an active selected accept, that the challenge marker is returned exactly for the challenge ciphertext and that other ciphertexts are decapsulated as item 2's CCA evaluation does, and that the hidden steps answer as the corresponding steps of item 2's ideal-world skeleton (the Server's hidden root request, the Beacon's hidden finish, and a Beacon finish with a known decapsulation result). For the two hidden steps this is one statement about the joint outcome: the same reply, the same game state apart from the bookkeeping that the analysis adds and does not observe, and the Extract family state of the native side and the table cache of item 2's side both unchanged. For the Server's hidden root request, the native side's session mark is item 2's mark with the coordinates in place of the hidden value read there, and the native state is entirely unchanged. For the Beacon's hidden finish, the remembered coordinates of the native side become the four Diffie-Hellman coordinates (when the Diffie-Hellman outputs are nonzero) and item 2's marks are unchanged. These per-step facts, and scratch proofs of a first layer of the prefix comparison and of the reveal step, are the outcome of the CE-11b design's spike; they support the planned route and reduce its estimate.

Review. An independent review found no error in the statements or proofs. Its fix pass made the two hidden-step agreements state everything listed above (before, they compared only the reply and the game state, which left the unchanged caches and the marks unstated), added the statements that cover every build while a session is marked, and corrected this section's account of which steps read hidden values. A confirming review found every finding resolved; its remarks on the wording of the summaries (how the native marks and remembered coordinates relate to item 2's marks, and how a step that sets a ghost treats its earlier value) are fixed in the module comments and here, without changing any statement.

What this does not show. These are definitions and program equalities; they make no security claim. The comparison of the whole ideal experiment with item 2's ideal world (the second compile lemma), the erasure and split of the hidden finish, the environment form, the provenance facts and the hand-off theorem are later units of CE-11b.

## Items 4 and 5, stage S4: the integrity half of the record-encryption lift

Status: the integrity half of the record-encryption step is proved, as the integrity target of stage S1 with explicit reductions and explicit query budgets (`PqxdhRecordLiftCtxBills.ctxAuthLiftTarget`); the privacy half is proved in the section "Items 4 and 5, stage S4: the privacy half of the record-encryption lift" below. The six modules below were written one after another, and each paragraph describes what its module adds and what it left to the later ones.

The record-encryption step of items 4 and 5 replaces, one hidden record key at a time, real authenticated encryption by an idealized encryption that accepts only frames that were actually sealed. Before that replacement can start, the world in which every hidden record is handled by the separate per-key encryption interface must be shown to be the same as the chain-ideal world, in which the hidden records use the native encryption code directly. `PqxdhRecordLiftCtxHybrid` proves this: with every key in real mode, the per-key world and the chain-ideal world produce the same distribution of everything the analysis may look at, and of the shared hash cache, the effect ledger, the chain table and the produced frames as well. Only the per-key bookkeeping and two counters that exist for the analysis are dropped. See [the guide](impl/record-lift-ctx-hybrid.md).

The comparison is made one operation at a time. A hidden receive is first checked by the same parser as the native code; if it reaches decryption, the per-key interface decrypts with the same key and nonce from the chain table and checks the same commitment in the same shared hash cache, so it returns exactly the native result. A hidden send encrypts with the same key and nonce and stores the same commitment, logs the same frame and gives the same reply, also when the writer fails. One difference had to be ruled out: the per-key interface refuses to reuse a nonce, while the native code does not. The proof shows that the refusal never happens, because an existing fact about the program says that every hidden key is used for at most one send on every possible execution path, and a key that has not been used for a send has never seen a nonce. Every other operation is literally the same in both worlds.

The module also defines the sequence of intermediate worlds that the integrity proof walks through: the hidden keys are ordered by chain depth, then slot, then direction, as for the chain proof, and the k-th world uses idealized encryption for the first k keys and real encryption for the rest. The module proves that the first world is the chain-ideal world, that one step changes exactly one key from real to idealized, and that the last world idealizes exactly the keys whose depth is below the budget's bound on derivations. This module left one fact to a later one: the integrity proof also needs to know that in every intermediate world each record operation uses a key that has already been derived and lies below that depth bound. This is true by the structure of the ratchet, but it had to be proved for worlds whose decryption answers differ from the native ones, because the existing proofs of it covered only the native worlds; the third module below, `PqxdhRecordLiftCtxAvailability`, proves it. The module has no assumption or contract hypothesis; its proof that the two worlds are equal uses one functional fact of the primitive AEAD, that its tags are 16 bytes, and nothing else from the list of allowed contracts.

The second CTX module, `PqxdhRecordLiftCtxLink`, turns one step of that sequence into a game against the existing one-key encryption challenger. It builds a reduction that runs the whole compiled program without ever seeing the key of the step's record position: it samples every table entry itself, including the step position's entry, whose key bytes it never reads, sends the records of the step's position to the challenger, encrypts and decrypts the records of every other hidden position itself, idealized or real according to the step, and routes public coins and hash queries through the challenger so that both share one hash cache. The module proves, operation by operation and for every state, that this reduction run against the challenger is the per-key world in which the step's position has a fresh random key held by the challenger, in the challenger's mode. When the challenger is real, the modes are those of the intermediate world before the step; when it is idealized, those of the world after the step. This module left two facts to later ones: the step that replaces the record key read from the chain table by a fresh key held outside, which the fourth module, `PqxdhRecordLiftKeyCut`, proves, and the fact that every record operation uses an already derived key below the depth bound, which the third module proves. The module uses no assumption or contract.

The third CTX module, `PqxdhRecordLiftCtxAvailability`, closes a gap that the earlier design notes had missed. The per-key worlds read a hidden record's key and nonce from the chain table, and if the table has no entry yet they silently use an all-zero key. If a world could ever encrypt or decrypt with a record position before deriving it, that position would be keyed with a known value, and the key-by-key argument would break; similarly, a position deeper than the budget allows would fall outside the numbered sequence of intermediate worlds. The module proves that neither can happen, for every adversary that stays within its budget and for every way of choosing keys and modes. It first shows a fact about the compiled program alone: on every possible run, every derivation is of a position whose predecessor was derived before, and every encryption or decryption uses a position that was derived before. Counting the derivations (at most one per send and 51 per received frame) then bounds every used position's depth by the budget. The module transfers this to any implementation of the hidden services whose table only grows, as a general simulation principle; as a first use, it proves that two per-key worlds that agree on every derived position within the budget are identical, and therefore that the last intermediate world is exactly the integrity-ideal world `idealAuth`. It uses no assumption or contract.

The fourth CTX module, `PqxdhRecordLiftKeyCut`, connects one step of the sequence to the one-key encryption challenger, which uses a fresh uniform key of its own. In the per-key world the key of a hidden record position is part of the chain table entry that the position's derivation samples. The module proves that, for every choice of idealized and real keys and every adversary within its budget, the adversary's view is distributed exactly as if the key of one chosen position had been sampled separately at the start and supplied from outside. The proof first moves the key's sampling to the start, which is possible because nothing uses the key before the position is derived and its derivation samples it exactly once; then it shows that reading the key from the table and using the supplied key agree, because every encryption at the position happens after its derivation (this is where the third module is used); and finally it shows that the table's copy of the key is never read at all once the key is supplied, so its bytes can be erased without changing anything the adversary sees. It uses no assumption or contract.

The fifth CTX module, `PqxdhRecordLiftCtx`, assembles the integrity half. For each step of the sequence it builds an explicit one-key adversary from the adversary and the protocol, shows that the worlds before and after the step are exactly the challenger's real and idealized games played by that adversary, applies the existing one-key integrity bound, and adds up the steps; the first world is the chain-ideal world and the last the integrity-ideal world. The result is the integrity target with its explicit sum of per-key losses, and in this module it is conditional: it takes as a premise that each constructed one-key adversary stays within explicitly stated query budgets. Those budgets are a property of the construction, not a security assumption; the sixth module, `PqxdhRecordLiftCtxBills`, proves them from the outer adversary budget and so removes the premise.

The sixth CTX module, `PqxdhRecordLiftCtxBills`, removes that condition, so the integrity half of the record-encryption step is now established. It counts, for the constructed one-key adversary of every step, how many random coins, hash queries, idealized-key seals and decryption attempts it can make, and bounds each count by explicit formulas in the outer adversary's budget: every coin, hash, derivation and record operation of the protocol program is charged a fixed price, the program as a whole issues at most a budget-determined number of each (using the existing budget accounting of the protocol), and the step's own coordinate is sealed at most once because the protocol never reuses a record position for sending. With these numbers the existing one-key bound applies to every step, and the sum over the steps is the bound of the integrity target. The final theorems add no assumption or contract hypothesis. From the list of contracts that the brief allows, they use three, through the existing one-key integrity bound and the first module's equality of worlds: functional AEAD correctness (decryption returns what was encrypted, and tags are 16 bytes; both are fields of the primitive record that every statement takes as a parameter), the two standard games for authenticated encryption with modified nonces (IND$ and INT-CTXT), which enter only as the advantage terms of the per-key loss, and the random-oracle model of BLAKE2b, which is the model of every world here and within which the hash-guessing terms of the loss are stated. Apart from these final theorems and the fifth module's theorems that lead to them, only the first module's proof that the all-real world is the chain-ideal world uses a contract, the 16-byte tag length; the hybrid-family, link, availability, key-cut and bill theorems use none. The guide lists the contracts theorem by theorem. The privacy half, which replaces idealized real ciphertexts by random ones, is the subject of the section "Items 4 and 5, stage S4: the privacy half of the record-encryption lift" below.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-11b unit U5: the prefix at the challenger's pool

CE-11b's second compile lemma must show that the ideal experiment of increment 2 and item 2's two-slot ideal world give the decision the same probability, for one target and one draw of the challenger's values. This unit proves the first half of that comparison: everything up to the selected raw accept, and the facts that the second half (unit U6) starts from.

The difficulty. In the ideal experiment the challenger draws the KEM key pairs of all Beacon creations before the run, and the Beacon created at index `j` gets entry `j` of that pool. Item 2's ideal world draws the same pool, but its proofs run the adversary's compiled program through several intermediate descriptions (an annotated source schedule that tracks the private identity and KEM services, an encoded client that talks to those services through an open interface, and a router that answers the KEM requests), and each of those layers was written for keys generated on demand. The unit adapts the layers to the pool: wherever a creation draws a key, it now reads the pool entry at the creation's index, and every other step is the existing one.

What is proved. First, CE-3's compile lemma (the deployment experiment equals the native execution of the compiled program, after merging the compiler's local copies) holds with both sides creating keys from the pool; the proof shows that no compiled command other than a creation issues a creation request, so only the creation step needed a new argument. Second, the annotated source schedule with pool creations erases to that native execution, and its encoding is the encoded client's execution when KEM creations are answered from the pool; again only creations are new, because every other request compiles to a program without a KEM creation, on which answering from the pool and generating on demand coincide. Third, item 2's router, which stops if the selected KEM secret is ever revealed, answers such a program exactly as the pool does, as long as the program reveals no KEM key and creates no more keys than the pool holds. For the compiled program the deployment adversary's budget (CE-9's caps) gives both, so it never triggers the stop; within this unit, that budget is a hypothesis, discharged when the second compile lemma is assembled.

The cut. The ideal experiment and item 2's world are then cut at the selected raw accept (the accept whose position is the target's). On the ideal side the registration is the real one with pool creations until that accept, so the run up to the cut is the native run with pool creations; the bookkeeping that the ideal registration adds for the later-quantum mode (a log and a snapshot) is never read, so it does not matter for the rest of the run. On item 2's side the program is the compiled program, which issues the deployment adversary's raw accepts one for one, so its cut at the same position is the compiled form of the ideal side's cut. The result is that both sides, up to the cut, are two views of one computation: the Server's construction followed by the annotated source execution, with pool creations, of the compiled program stopped at the selected accept. The ideal experiment continues from the merged deployment state at that point; item 2's world continues from the encoded state with its router state. On every outcome of the shared computation, the Server's identity slot, the ownership facts of every Beacon, CE-3's invariant for the merge, and the fact that the created KEM keys are the first entries of the pool all hold. Two more facts hold there, both added after the review. Every Beacon's KEM index is its position in the list of Beacons, so the Beacon created at index `j` holds pool entry `j`. And the rest of the program after the cut creates at most as many keys as the budget allows minus those already created: after the cut, item 2's router answers a creation beyond its reserved keys by stopping, while the ideal experiment would draw a fresh key, so the comparison after the cut needs the keys created before and after the cut together to fit the pool, which this fact gives whenever the budget fits the pool.

What this does not show. These are equalities of programs and facts on their outcomes; they make no security claim and charge nothing. The comparison after the cut (the selected accept with the challenge ciphertext, the hidden build and finish, every later command and the decision) is unit U6. That item 2's scan of the compiled program reads no identity or KEM field and stays within the pool, and (for the fact about the rest of the program) that the whole compiled program stays within the budget, are hypotheses here, to be discharged from the deployment adversary's budget (CE-9's caps) when the second compile lemma is assembled; scratch checks confirm that both follow from that budget. The only codec contracts used are the two approved read-back contracts, through CE-3's compile lemma.

Review. An independent review of the unit found no error in the Lean statements or proofs. It found that the facts at the cut lacked the bound on the creations after the cut that the comparison after the cut needs, and that one description claimed the Beacon positions without a proof; the fix pass proves both as separate theorems (nine in all, with no existing statement changed) and corrects the wording. A confirming review found every finding resolved and raised no new finding.

## Items 4 and 5, stage S5: composing the record lift, and the ideal-world facts

Status: the integrity form of the record lift is proved (`PqxdhRecordLiftComposition.record_auth_lift`); the full record lift is proved under the privacy half of the record-encryption step as an explicit hypothesis of the theorem, because that half is still being proved; of the world-level facts about the ideal record worlds, the hiding fact is proved (`PqxdhRecordLiftHiding.idealRecords_hiding`), and the origin, binding, fresh-message and left-or-right facts are not yet proved. See [the guide](impl/record-lift-world-facts.md). (Later: the full record lift without the hypothesis and the left-or-right and fresh-message facts are proved by the facts track; see the section "Items 4 and 5, stage S5, continued" below.)

The record lift is the statement that the real record layer can be replaced by its ideal version: in the real world every hidden record key comes from the real key schedule and records are sealed with real authenticated encryption, while in the ideal world the keys are uniform table entries, a hidden record key accepts only frames previously sealed under that same key, and in the privacy observation mode its records look like random bytes. (That the frames a hidden handle accepts were sealed by its partner is the separate origin fact, which is still open.) Stage S3 proved the first half of this replacement (the chain lift: real key schedule to uniform keys) and stage S4 the integrity part of the second half (real encryption to the replay-only ideal encryption). `PqxdhRecordLiftComposition` puts the two together. For every environment and adversary within their budgets and every way of deciding from what the analysis may observe, the probability of any decision in the real world differs from that in the integrity-ideal world by at most the sum of the two losses: the chain loss (one Extract and one HMAC-PRF advantage per position of the key schedule) and the integrity loss (per hidden key, the two standard authenticated-encryption advantages, a hash-guessing term and a frame-guessing term). The proof is the triangle inequality through the chain-ideal world, every term with coefficient one, so the composed theorem uses exactly the contracts of its two parts: the key-schedule correctness contract of the chain lift, functional correctness of the authenticated encryption, the standard security games as the terms of the loss, and the random-oracle model of BLAKE2b. The same composition with the privacy half added gives the full record lift, whose ideal world uses random ciphertexts in the privacy mode. Since the privacy half is not yet proved, the module states the full record lift as a theorem that takes the privacy half as an input: whoever proves the privacy half obtains the full record lift by applying this theorem, and until then nothing is claimed about privacy. In the authentication observation mode no privacy step is needed at all, because there the two ideal worlds coincide; for that mode the module proves the record-lift bound outright in its Boolean form, that is, for every decision on what the analysis may observe (the event form and the query budgets of the reductions, which the full statement also contains, are not restated for that mode; the integrity form above already gives them, because in that mode its ideal world is the same).

`PqxdhRecordLiftHiding` proves the hiding fact about the ideal record world in the privacy observation mode, where every hidden record is sealed with random ciphertext bytes. It says that the plaintexts of hidden records do not matter: if every plaintext that a hidden record encrypts is replaced by another of the same length, everything the hiding analysis looks at has exactly the same distribution, namely the adversary's output, what the adversary saw of the transcript (in this mode a received record shows only whether it was accepted), the secret test bit and the fresh messages of the experiment, the environment's state, the produced frames, the attempt counters and which handles hold hidden records. The later secrecy statements (fresh-message secrecy and left-or-right indistinguishability) build on this fact. The proof runs the two worlds side by side with the same random coins and shows, step by step through every layer of the world, that they stay in lockstep: a random-ciphertext seal looks only at the length of its plaintext, so both worlds produce the same record; a hidden receive accepts a frame by comparing it with the recorded seals without looking at their plaintexts, so both worlds accept or reject together and differ only in the decrypted bytes they return; the receiving side updates its ratchet only according to whether the frame was accepted; the environment never sees records; the experiment's bookkeeping decides which tests to admit only from the part of the transcript the adversary sees; and the adversary itself sees only acceptance bits of received records, so it behaves identically in both worlds. The theorem has no assumption or contract, and its proof uses none.

## Items 4 and 5, stage S4: the privacy half of the record-encryption lift

Status: proved, as the privacy target of stage S1 with explicit reductions and explicit query budgets (`PqxdhRecordLiftCtxPrivBills.ctxPrivLiftStatement`); independently reviewed (a semantic and a hygiene review, both approving with minor corrections, which have been made, and a confirming review of those corrections, which approved them with documentation remarks that have also been addressed). Five modules, described below in the order in which they build on each other; the guide `doc/impl/record-lift-ctx-priv.md` gives the theorem names and the contracts theorem by theorem.

What is proved. The integrity half (section "Items 4 and 5, stage S4: the integrity half of the record-encryption lift" above) ends in a world in which every hidden record key is handled by an idealized encryption that still produces real ciphertexts but accepts only frames that were actually sealed. The privacy half compares that world with the world in which every hidden record is sealed as uniformly random bytes of the plaintext's length, with a uniformly random 16-byte tag and a private commitment computed in the same way as in replay mode, which in the secrecy observation mode is the record-ideal world of the targets. For every environment and adversary that respect the existing budgets, and for every decision on the permitted view that ignores the hash cache, the two worlds can be told apart by at most the sum, over the same ordered list of hidden record keys as in the integrity half, of the standard advantage of one explicitly constructed adversary against the indistinguishability-from-random game (IND$) of the modified-nonce authenticated encryption. Each term appears exactly once, and each constructed adversary stays within explicit formulas in the outer budget. Unlike the integrity half, no forgery or hash-guessing term appears: the privacy step starts where the integrity step ended.

The first module, `PqxdhRecordLiftCtxRandom`, settles the one point that the target definitions had left open: that the "random mode" of the targets is really the random side of the standard IND$ game. The existing one-key analysis of the code base compares a replay-mode game with the IND$ random experiment run on an adversary that is wrapped in a public replay guard, a key-free CTX simulator and a log-based decryption simulator. The module proves that this whole stack, run against the IND$ challenger's random encryption oracle, is exactly the targets' random mode on the shared hash cache, as a probabilistic program and not only in distribution. The proof writes the log simulator as a stateful interpreter, composes it with the random challenger and the CTX simulator, shows that the composite keeps the challenger's nonce and seal history in step with the simulator's own history (so it never needs an invariant premise), and shows that the public guard, whose answers come from the list of successful seals, gives exactly the replay dictionary's answers. As a consequence, for every one-key adversary the replay mode and the random mode differ by exactly the IND$ advantage of the existing view reduction, which is the per-key loss in the target. The module's equalities of programs use no assumption; this consequence uses only the 16-byte tag length of the authenticated encryption (counted under functional AEAD correctness), which enters through the existing one-key comparison of the replay mode with the IND$ game.

The second module, `PqxdhRecordLiftCtxPrivModes`, builds the one-key challenger that a privacy step needs. In a privacy step some hidden keys have already been switched to random mode while the others are still in replay mode, so the constructed adversary must itself simulate random-mode records for the keys other than the one under attack; the existing simulation of other keys only offered real and replay mode. The new challenger lets every other key be handled locally in any of the three modes, keeps one shared hash cache, and puts the attacked key in replay or random mode; the module proves that the challenger's game is exactly the constructed one-key adversary played against the attacked key, as in the integrity half. One new difficulty appeared: simulating a random-mode record by drawing one random byte at a time would let the adversary's number of random draws grow with the length of the messages it chooses, and no budget field bounds message lengths. The budgets count random draws, each of which may pick uniformly from a finite range of any size, as every existing budget of the code base does. The constructed adversaries therefore draw each random byte string with a single random draw of a large number, which has the same uniform distribution; the module proves that this change does not alter the probability of any yes-or-no decision. This change and two further steps are equalities of distributions rather than of programs: dropping the attacked key, which a random-mode challenger draws but never uses, and the selected-key result of the integrity half, which the fourth module applies to each step; the other identifications of worlds, games and views are equalities of programs. Together with the first module it gives the per-key step: the attacked key in replay mode and in random mode differ by exactly the IND$ advantage of the constructed adversary.

The third module, `PqxdhRecordLiftCtxPrivLink`, connects one step of the privacy hybrids to that challenger. It is the reduction of the integrity half with one change, that every hidden key other than the attacked one is handled as a local call in its own mode, random mode included. The module proves, with no condition on the modes, that the challenger's game against this reduction is the protocol world in which the attacked key is a fresh uniform key held by the challenger and every other key keeps its table value and its mode.

The fourth module, `PqxdhRecordLiftCtxPriv`, assembles the privacy half. It walks through the same ordered sequence of hidden keys as the integrity half, switching one key at a time from replay mode to random mode; the first world of the sequence is the integrity-ideal world and the last one is the all-random world, because no protocol run ever touches a key outside the budgeted range (the availability result of the integrity half). Using the selected-key result of the integrity half, which holds for every assignment of modes, each step is exactly the challenger's replay game against its random game for one explicitly constructed adversary, so each step costs exactly that adversary's IND$ advantage, and the sum over the steps is the bound of the privacy target. In this module the result is conditional on the constructed adversaries staying within stated query budgets.

The fifth module, `PqxdhRecordLiftCtxPrivBills`, removes that condition. It counts, for every constructed adversary, its random draws, hash queries, attacked-key seals and decryption attempts, and bounds each count by explicit formulas in the outer budget: the program's own draws and the decision's draws, plus at most 66 draws for every hidden record operation on another key (two for a random record's body and tag, and at most 64 for a private commitment), the program's hash queries, at most one seal at the attacked key (the protocol never reuses a record position for sending) and the budgeted number of receives. The bounds are explicit but not tight; the target only requires that they be functions of the budget.

Assumptions. The final theorems have no assumption or contract hypothesis. From the list of contracts that the brief allows they use the 16-byte tag length of the authenticated encryption (a field of the primitive record that every statement takes as a parameter, counted under functional AEAD correctness; it enters through the existing replay-side simulations and bounds), the IND$ game of the modified-nonce authenticated encryption, which appears only as the per-key advantage term, and the random-oracle model of BLAKE2b, which is the model of every world. The privacy half does not use the decryption-correctness property, the forgery game, the key-derivation contracts or the codec contracts. What it does not show: it is the privacy half of the record-encryption step only; composing it with the chain step and the integrity half into the full record lift is the world track's deliverable (later delivered by the facts track: see the section "Items 4 and 5, stage S5, continued" below), the version with the later-quantum post phase is stage S6, and the explicit query budgets are not optimized.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-11b unit U2: erasing and splitting the ideal registration's hidden values

Unit U2 of CE-11b takes the ideal registration of increment 2 and brings it, in four steps that each preserve the distribution of what the experiment shows, to the form that the record world's environment will run. It adds four modules with 186 statements, all guarded so that they depend at most on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`; no existing proof module changed, and no assumption or contract is added. An independent review found no error in the statements or proofs (see the last paragraph).

Erasing the discarded opening. CE-11a showed that when a Beacon's finish receives a frame whose sequence number is not one, it makes one opening whose result it discards, that this only completes one point of the shared, lazily sampled commitment cache, and that such completions can be erased from a whole run. U2 applies this to the ideal registration. The only command that makes such a discarded opening there is the selected Beacon's hidden challenge finish; every other command, including the selected accept (which reads a hidden value and marks its session) and the selected session's build, either never touches the commitment cache or commutes with completing a point of it. So the experiment with the ideal registration and the experiment in which the selected Beacon's hidden finish makes no opening on such frames have the same distribution of the Server's public data, the adversary's output, the ledger and the final state apart from the commitment cache. The proof needed a small calculus for registration steps that read hidden values through item 2's first-touch allocator, so that facts such as "this step does not touch the cache" or "this step is a pointed step followed by a completion" can be proved for the step itself and carried through the allocator and the slot service.

Splitting the hidden values. Item 2's ideal world gives each hidden slot 108 uniformly random bytes from a lazily filled table. In the record world, the two 32-byte chains among these bytes form the slot's seed, which the world holds itself, while the environment holds the 32-byte key and the 12-byte nonce. CE-11a proved that a handler built from slot programs behaves the same with the 108-byte table and with a service that draws the two parts separately; U2 applies this to the erased ideal registration and then moves the seeds from the service into the place where the join with the record world expects them. The resulting first split form has the same distribution as the ideal experiment for everything except the commitment cache and the internal tables.

Where the seed is used. In that form a slot's seed is drawn at the slot's first touch, but it matters at only two places: the selected session's build, which creates the Server's ratchet for the session, and the selected Beacon's challenge finish when it establishes, which creates the Beacon's ratchet. CE-11a showed that each of these ratchets is exactly the kernel that the record world installs for the seed. U2 shows that the split form is exactly, as a program and with no probability argument, a form in which the steps run with a fixed dummy seed and, after the build or the finish, the true seed is looked up and the record world's kernel for it replaces the dummy one. The selected accept also reads the hidden value, but it only records where it read it, so the seed it sees does not matter.

Drawing the seed only when it is needed. The record world draws a slot's seed when it installs a hidden session, not when the slot is first touched. The last step changes the split form so that the seed is drawn exactly then: the material is still drawn at the first touch, but the seed only after the selected build has published a Server peer, or after the selected Beacon has established. Both forms have the same distribution once the table of seeds is forgotten, because a seed that is drawn early and not looked at until the install cannot be told apart from a seed drawn at the install. The proof generalizes CE-11a's engine to steps that complete several points (a step can give out two slots) and to steps whose factorisation holds only from well-formed states (in the early form, every slot already given out has its seed). Composed with the earlier steps, this gives the unit's main statement: the ideal experiment and the experiment with the final split form have the same distribution of the Server's public data, the adversary's output, the ledger and the observable part of the final state (the deployment state with the commitment cache emptied, together with the allocator and the ideal bookkeeping, the later-quantum snapshot and the log; only the commitment cache's contents, the internal table of the hidden values and the table of seeds are left out).

What this does not show. These are equalities of programs and of distributions; they make no security claim. The fact that in the final split form a slot's seed is present exactly when a hidden install happened at that slot is not yet proved; it needs the same facts about runs as the environment's invariant (for example, that the selected Beacon establishes at most once), so it moves to the next unit. The environment form of the final split registration, its join with the record world and everything after it are later units of CE-11b.

Review. An independent review of the unit found no error in the Lean statements or proofs, and checked in scratch that the unit's main statement composes, under the challenger's draws, with the join of the record world in the way the next unit will use it. Its findings concerned wording and records: one sentence of this section and one Lean description could be read as saying that the observable part of the final state also leaves out the allocator and the ideal bookkeeping, which it keeps; two Lean descriptions named parts of the chain as first designed rather than as built; the proof receipt listed the axioms of each theorem under the last part of its name, so that two pairs of theorems shared an entry; and a design re-check and a remark for the next unit (facts about the commitment cache or the table of seeds are about the final split form, because the observable part leaves those out) were not written down. The fix pass corrects all of them; no statement changed. A confirming review found every finding resolved and raised no new finding.

## Items 4 and 5, stage S6: the record lift with the later-quantum post phase

Status: proved, as later-quantum targets defined in this stage, with explicit reductions and explicit query budgets: the later chain lift (`PqxdhRecordLiftLaterChain.later_chain_lift`), the later integrity and privacy halves of the record-encryption lift (`PqxdhRecordLiftLaterCtx.later_ctx_auth_lift`, `PqxdhRecordLiftLaterPriv.later_ctx_priv_lift`), their compositions (`PqxdhRecordLiftLaterLift.later_ctx_lift`, `later_record_auth_lift`, `later_record_lift`) and the later hiding fact (`PqxdhRecordLiftLaterHiding.later_idealRecords_hiding`). These are all the later-quantum targets that this stage defines; the later forms of the fresh-message and left-or-right facts are not defined (see below). Independently reviewed; the review findings concerned the documentation and are fixed, and a confirming review of the fixes approved them. Seven modules; the guide `doc/impl/record-lift-later-lift.md` gives the theorem names and the contracts theorem by theorem.

What the later-quantum mode adds. In the later-quantum mode the experiment does not stop when the adversary's run ends. The environment's final state is first disclosed to the adversary through a reveal function (any function of the environment's state; in the deployment experiment's exact later-quantum profile, LQ-F, it discloses the honest X25519 and Ed25519 secrets), and then a second adversary may keep computing: it can draw random coins, ask the environment for HMAC values and query the shared BLAKE2b hash. This second phase models an adversary who records everything now and later gains the power to recover the secrets that protected the handshake; it is still a classical adversary, not a quantum one. The record lift asks whether the record layer's hidden material, the ratchet chains and the record keys derived from the handshake, still protects the records' confidentiality in this setting. Stages S3 to S5 proved the record lift for the run phase alone; stage S6 proves it for the whole two-phase experiment.

What is proved. For every environment and run-phase adversary within the existing budgets, every reveal function, and every second-phase adversary within a separate budget for its coins, HMAC queries and hash queries, and for every way of deciding from what the analysis may observe after both phases (the second adversary's output, the run's bookkeeping, the environment's final state, the produced frames, the attempt counters and which handles hold hidden records), the probability of any decision changes by at most the same kinds of terms as in the run phase when the real record layer is replaced by its ideal versions: one Extract and one HMAC-PRF advantage per position of the key schedule for the chain step, per hidden key the two standard authenticated-encryption advantages plus a hash-guessing and a frame-guessing term for the integrity step, and per hidden key one indistinguishability-from-random advantage for the privacy step. Each term appears exactly once, the number of positions and keys is the same as in the run phase, and each term belongs to an explicitly constructed adversary that runs the whole two-phase experiment, second phase included. In the privacy observation mode, the plaintexts of hidden records still do not influence anything the hiding analysis looks at, also after the second phase.

Why the second phase cannot touch the hidden material. The record layer's hidden material lives in the world, not in the environment: the environment's state has no field for seeds, chains or keys, and its HMAC handler can only use what it holds. The analysis proves this structurally. Every request that the second phase makes reaches the world only as a seed allocation (when the environment installs a new hidden peer), a coin, a shared-hash query or a bookkeeping charge, never as a chain lookup or a hidden encryption or decryption, whatever the adversary and the environment do. Consequently the second phase behaves identically whichever positions of the key schedule are real and whichever are ideal, and in every ideal record world it leaves the per-key encryption states untouched. The second phase also makes no record request, so it never derives a new hidden key; this is why the bound has the same number of terms as in the run phase.

How the proof works. The run-phase proofs of stages S3 and S4 were built from general facts about arbitrary programs that issue world requests, applied at one specific program, the run-phase experiment. The two-phase experiment is another such program, with the same number of record requests. Stage S6 therefore restates the last, program-specific steps of those proofs for an arbitrary program within the record budget and applies them to the two-phase experiment; no new hybrid argument is needed. Two places needed care. The integrity-step bound contains a term for guessing a hidden key through the shared hash, proportional to the number of hash queries; the second phase adds hash queries, both its own and those that the environment makes while answering its HMAC queries, so the hash budget of every integrity term includes them. And the hiding proof, which runs the two worlds side by side with the same coins, extends to the second phase because the second phase starts from equal outputs and equal environment states in both worlds and makes only requests whose answers are equal in both.

No later authentication claim. The later-quantum mode claims confidentiality only, so no later origin or authentication statement is made. The analysis proves that every event about the Server's public data, the run's bookkeeping, the produced frames and the attempt counters has exactly the same probability in the two-phase real world as in the run-phase real world, so a run-phase origin or authentication result about an event of that kind carries over unchanged. This does not cover the record layer's own origin and binding events (an accepted record whose frame the partner handle had not published before, or never produced at all, or whose frame a handle other than the partner published): they also look at which hidden slot each handle holds at the end, and the second phase can add handles, because the environment may install new peers while answering its HMAC queries. Carrying these events over would need a further argument that the second phase leaves the slots of the existing handles unchanged; it is not proved, and it is not needed, because the later mode claims no origin. The later record lift to the integrity-ideal world is an intermediate step of the confidentiality argument, not an authentication claim.

Assumptions. The final theorems have no assumption or contract hypothesis. From the list of contracts that the brief allows they use: the correctness of the deterministic key derivation (a premise of the chain and record lifts), the decryption-correctness property and the 16-byte tag length of the authenticated encryption (counted under functional AEAD correctness; the privacy and hiding results use at most the tag length), the Extract, HMAC-PRF, IND$ and INT-CTXT games, which appear only as advantage terms of explicitly constructed adversaries, and the random-oracle model of BLAKE2b, which is the model of every world. No codec contract, no Diffie-Hellman-keyed component and no new assumption is used, and the disclosure reads only the environment's state, never the shared hash cache. What it does not show: the later forms of the fresh-message and left-or-right facts are not stated (their run-phase forms are still open), the composition with the deployment experiment's later headlines is later work, and the explicit query budgets are not optimized. (Later: the facts track proved the run-phase forms; see the section "Items 4 and 5, stage S5, continued" below.)

## Items 4 and 5, stage S5, continued: the full record lift, left-or-right secrecy and fresh-message secrecy

Status: the full record lift is proved without the privacy-half hypothesis (`PqxdhRecordLift.record_lift`, with the record-encryption step alone as `PqxdhRecordLift.ctx_lift`; the target keeps its own premise, the key-schedule correctness contract `SourceFullCorrect` of the chain lift), and two of the four remaining world-level facts about the ideal record worlds are proved: left-or-right secrecy (`PqxdhRecordLiftLor.idealRecords_lor`) and fresh-message secrecy (`PqxdhRecordLiftFresh.idealRecords_fresh`). The origin and binding facts are still open. Independently reviewed; the review findings concerned the documentation and are fixed, and a confirming review of the fixes approved them with documentation remarks that have also been addressed. See [the guide](impl/record-lift-facts.md).

The record lift says that the real record layer can be replaced by its ideal version, at the cost of the chain loss, the integrity loss and, in the privacy observation mode, the privacy loss of explicitly constructed reductions. The earlier S5 work proved it with the privacy half of the record-encryption step as an input, and the privacy track then proved that half. `PqxdhRecordLift` plugs the one into the other; there is no new argument, and the contracts are exactly those of the parts: the key-schedule correctness contract of the chain lift, functional correctness of the authenticated encryption, the standard security games as the terms of the loss, and the random-oracle model of BLAKE2b.

Two generic tools come first. `PqxdhRecordLiftSwap` is a way of running two copies of a probabilistic program side by side so that they use the same random coins, except that chosen coins on one side are renamed by a one-to-one map, and so that the two runs may go separate ways after an "escape" in which both have already lost any chance to win. Renaming a fair coin does not change its distribution, so whenever two outcomes agree on all runs that stay in step, they have the same probability. `PqxdhRecordLiftFlat` rewrites the ideal record world, which is built in layers (the secrecy bookkeeping of the experiment, the native commands, the compiled protocol client and the record encryption service), as one program with one combined state, and proves the facts the two secrecy proofs need about it: a native coin is one fair draw; with every hidden plaintext replaced by zero bytes, sending either of two messages of the same length on a handle whose key the adversary does not know is literally the same computation; a key the adversary knows stays known for the rest of the run; and the bookkeeping only ever appends to its records.

Left-or-right secrecy (`LorStatement`) says that in the privacy observation mode of the ideal record world, the adversary's guess of the hidden test bit is right exactly half of the time, among the runs that the analysis counts (those that are eligible and in which every test message went to a handle with hidden keys). The proof first uses the earlier hiding fact to replace every hidden plaintext by zeros, which changes nothing the statement looks at. In that world it runs the program against itself with the coin that chooses the test bit flipped. As long as the test messages go to handles with hidden keys, the two runs do exactly the same thing, because sending the left or the right message of the same length looks identical; if a test message goes to a handle whose key the adversary knows, the run is not counted on either side. So a guess wins on one side exactly when the opposite guess wins on the other side, both wins have the same probability, and they add up to the probability of a counted run.

Fresh-message secrecy (`FreshGuessStatement`) says that the probability that the adversary names one of the experiment's fresh random messages that went to a handle with hidden keys and guesses it exactly is at most 2 to the power of minus the minimal message length. Again the plaintexts are first replaced by zeros. Then, for the message the adversary names and its length, the program is run against itself with the random bytes of that message shifted by a fixed offset (adding the offset to each byte modulo 256 is a renaming of each byte's coin); the runs agree except for that message, because sending a message or its shifted version looks identical on a handle with hidden keys, and a message sent to a handle with a known key never counts. So the adversary hits the message exactly as often as it hits the message shifted by any offset. The 256 to the power of the length shifted hits exclude each other and all require the same claimed index and length, so each has probability at most 256 to the power of minus the length times the probability of that claim. Adding this up over all claims, which exclude each other, gives the bound; a bound per message, without weighting by the claim, would have been too weak by the number of messages.

Assumptions. These theorems have no assumption or contract hypothesis. The two secrecy facts use no contract at all as a proof step; some fields of the primitive record occur in them only inside definitions (the Diffie-Hellman interface, the key-derivation definitions and the real- and replay-mode CTX code (the `.real` and `.replay` branches of `keyImpl`), the last of which the zeroed random-mode world never runs); the record lift uses the contracts of its parts listed above, all of them on the brief's list. What is not shown: the origin fact (a frame accepted by a hidden handle was produced, and with overwhelming probability published earlier, by its partner) and the binding fact (a frame is not accepted across handles that are not partners, except with a small collision probability) remain open; the guide gives the plan for them.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-11b unit U6 (first part): the key match and the branches of the second compile lemma

CE-11b's second compile lemma must show that, for one target and one draw of the challenger's values, the ideal experiment and item 2's two-slot ideal world accept the per-target decision with the same probability. Unit U5 cut both at the selected raw accept and showed that, up to that point, they are two views of one computation. This first part of unit U6 compares what happens after the cut in every case except the main one, and reduces the whole lemma to that main case.

The key match. On the ideal side the decision is "the event happens and the adversary's claim designates the target". A designation is computed publicly from the transcript, so on its own it says nothing about the hidden steps; the comparison needs to know that a designation of the target can only happen when the selected accept went through the challenge path. This is the key match: if the target is designated, then the selected accept's bytes verify to the PQ key that the target Beacon published, that key is the challenger's selected key (the Beacon created at index `k` holds pool entry `k`, and every published bundle carries the key its owner holds), so the selected accept took the challenge path and marked its session. The proof keeps a small invariant along the whole run between the transcript and the ideal state: the session counter counts the raw accepts, a returned session is always the counter before the call, only the selected accept can mark a session, every Beacon still holding a KEM key holds its pool entry, and every published bundle carries the pool key at its index. Every command keeps it, the hidden ones included, and the secrecy commands only send. The design placed this fact in a later unit (U4); it is built here because the decision step needs it and that unit is not done.

The branches. With the key match, the ideal decision is the same as "the event happens, the claim designates the target, and the selected session is marked". Item 2's world counts a run only if the selected accept took the challenge path with the challenger's key and returned a session. In every other case both sides accept nothing: when the Server's construction fails; when the adversary's program finishes before the selected accept; and when the selected accept's bytes do not verify to the challenger's selected key, because then item 2's world never reaches its post-challenge phase and the ideal side's selected accept takes the ordinary path, which marks nothing, and nothing later can mark a session. When the bytes do verify to the selected key, the Server first runs its checks before encapsulation (freshness, reservation, point and key parsing, the ephemeral). These never use the Server's private identity, so item 2's router lets them through unchanged and both sides run the same steps with the same randomness; if they reject, both sides again accept nothing. What is left is the active case: the selected accept reached its encapsulation with the challenger's key, and both sides continue with the challenge ciphertext. The unit states this remaining case precisely and proves that the second compile lemma follows from it, using the deployment adversary's budget for the bounds that item 2's world needs.
