The relation at the cut is also strengthened by two facts proved in unit U5 (each Beacon holds the pool entry at its position, and the program after the cut creates no more keys than remain in the pool).

What this does not show. The active case itself (the rest of the selected accept with the challenge ciphertext, every later command including the hidden build and the challenged finish, and the decision) is not proved; it is the remaining part of unit U6, and the second compile lemma is therefore not yet established. Everything here is an equality of programs, an equality in law or a fact on the outcomes of a run; it makes no security claim and charges nothing. The only codec contracts used are the two approved read-back contracts, and the deployment adversary's budget enters only through the caps that CE-9 already transports.

Review. An independent review of this part found no error in the Lean statements or proofs, and checked against the Rust code that the Server's checks before encapsulation do not use its private identity. Its findings concerned the records. The main one: the companion guide said that the selected session is marked exactly when the selected accept returned a session. Only one direction is proved (a returned session is marked). The other direction (a mark comes with a returned session) is what the remaining comparison of the two decisions needs, because item 2's world asks whether a session was returned while the ideal side asks whether the session is marked; it holds by inspection of the code, which marks the session only on the path that then returns it, but it is not yet proved, and the guide now lists it as a step of the remaining work. The other findings asked for a complete checklist of the commands and failure cases that the remaining comparison must cover, corrected two Lean descriptions, recorded that the shared main line had moved on twice (with changes to none of this unit's files), linked the proof receipt and refreshed the coordination notes. No statement changed. A confirming review found every finding resolved and raised no new finding.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-11b unit U3: the ideal environment

What this shows. The common deployment experiment has two worlds for the registration: the "ideal registration" of earlier units, which holds back the hidden values of one selected session and one selected Beacon, and the record world of the record-lift work, which owns all record keys and lets an environment drive the registration commands through a small set of capabilities (coins, the shared BLAKE2b oracle, and installs of Server peers and Beacons, possibly at a hidden slot whose kernel the World derives from its own seed). This unit builds the ideal environment, an environment of the record world that plays the ideal registration, and proves that the two match. Each command runs as in the real environment, except three: the selected accept reads its hidden value through a slot allocator in front of a lazily filled material cache that only the environment holds; the build of the session that accept marked reads that slot's material back from the cache, without drawing anything new, runs the build at it and asks the World for a hidden Server install at the slot; and the selected Beacon's finish after an active selected accept reads its own slot and asks the World for a hidden Beacon install. The main theorem (`ideal_splits`) says that from every admissible joint state each command, run against the World, has exactly the probability law of the corresponding command of the final split form of unit U2 on the reassembled state, and the result is again admissible. Admissibility (`IdealInv`) says that the World's "used" markers are exactly the slots where the environment recorded an install, the World's seed table holds exactly the seeds of those slots, at most one slot is allocated until the selected Beacon finishes, the marked session lies below the session counter at an allocated slot, every allocated slot's material is in the environment's cache, and a marked session that still has a pending token has no Server install yet. These include the guard under which the World accepts a hidden install (the slot's marker is still unused), which the proof of `ideal_splits` takes from admissibility before each hidden step; `env_admitted` itself states admissibility on every outcome. With the earlier generic join, the draw of the challenger's parameters followed by the final split game has the same law as the record world run with the ideal environment that draws those parameters itself at startup (`c1_split`), and with unit U2's result the ideal game itself and that record world give the same adversary output, ledger and produced frames (`c1_ideal`, `c1_idealGame`). The same final shared cache (`c3_ideal`) and the same reveal for the later-quantum phase (`ideal_reveal`) are proved between that record world and the draw followed by the final split game, not the ideal game itself: unit U2 relates the ideal game to the final split game only through a view that empties the shared cache. On every outcome of that record world, at most one slot per role is installed (`hidden_server_once`, `hidden_beacon_once`) and the seed table holds a slot's seed exactly when the slot carries an install (`seed_at_install`).

Why it matters. The record-lift reductions are stated for an environment of the record world. This unit gives the ideal registration such an environment, with one environment per target that samples the challenger's parameters itself, so the record-lift results apply to the ideal game of the common deployment experiment without changing their form.

What this does not show. The resource frames of the ideal environment (how many coins, BLAKE2b queries and installs each command uses) are proved only for the build command: from every environment state, the build uses no coin, at most one BLAKE2b query and at most one install (`idealStep_build_bound`), within the planned allowance. The BLAKE2b bound that follows from the frames is not proved. The first version of the build read its slot's material lazily, drawing a fresh one when the cache lacked the slot; that never happens in a real run (the selected accept reads the slot first), but a frame must bound every step from every state, and the planned allowance gives the build no coins, so the planned frame did not hold. The review fix pass made the build read the cached material without drawing and added "every allocated slot's material is cached" to admissibility; at a cached slot the two builds are the same program, so every earlier result about the build carries over. The other commands' frames are not proved. The statement that the seed table matches the installs is proved at the reassembled state of the record world, not yet on the final split game's own outcomes. The provenance unit U4 is not started. Everything here is an equality of programs, an equality in law, a fact about the outcomes of a run or a bound on the number of queries; no security claim is made and nothing is charged. No new assumption or contract is used.

Review. An independent review of this unit confirmed that the planned frame failed for the first version of the marked build, as written above, and judged the fix an implementation choice (no new assumption); the fix described above is the review's preferred option. It also found that this section overstated two results as statements about the ideal game (the shared cache and the reveal, now reworded) and raised smaller points about documentation and bookkeeping, all addressed. It found no other error in the statements or proofs. A confirming review of the fix pass found every finding resolved and no new problem in the statements or proofs; among its checks, a separate scratch proof showed that the build now stays within its planned allowance from every state, both for the environment with fixed parameters and for the one that draws them at startup. Its only remaining point was that these records still described the fix pass as not reviewed again.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-11b unit U6 (second part): the middle execution of the post-challenge simulation

The first part of unit U6 reduced CE-11b's second compile lemma to one remaining case, the active branch: the selected accept reached its encapsulation with the challenger's key, and both sides continue with the challenge ciphertext. In that case the ideal experiment runs the rest of the adversary's program with the ideal registration, and item 2's world runs the compiled version of the same program through a stack of seven interpreters (the grouped client, the services skeleton, the actual encapsulator, the post-challenge router, the challenger's decapsulation oracle, a public table and the two-slot table of hidden values). This second part builds the machinery that compares the two and proves the comparison's first half; the comparison itself is not finished.

Why a middle execution. The two sides do not determine each other's state. The compiled program keeps local copies of the peers and owners that its record commands touched, and the ideal experiment's state is the merge of those copies into the registration state, so item 2's world, which still holds the stale versions inside its source state, knows things that the ideal state has overwritten. The ideal side, on the other hand, keeps analysis records (observation logs and the later-quantum snapshot) that item 2's world erases. So instead of one relation between the two states, both sides are shown to be views of a third computation: the compiled program run against a "middle" handler whose state is item 2's own annotated source state together with the ideal registration's bookkeeping (accept counter, mark, the allocator and the table of hidden values). The ideal side is the merge view of this middle run, and item 2's side will be its projection onto item 2's layers. Because the compiled program is the same on both sides, item 2's side needs to be compared only request by request at the level of the source commands, and the record commands, which the compiled program executes locally, need no new work.

The ideal side's steps, proved. Under CE-3's merge invariant, for every deployment command, merging the copies into the middle state after the middle's step gives exactly the ideal experiment's step on the merged state, with the analysis records erased. For the ordinary commands this follows from the earlier pool version of CE-3's compile lemma. For the three hidden commands it needs that they never look at a copied kernel: the selected accept with the challenge ciphertext, the build of the marked session (whose response is computed from the hidden value by the factored Server build) and the selected owner's challenge finish. Each is shown to commute with the replacement of the copied kernels: the accept and the finish never read the peer map or an established owner, and the build reads the peer map only through occupancy and installs its new peer at an unoccupied key, which no copy can name. The whole-program statement holds under any invariant that implies CE-3's merge invariant and is kept by every middle step; proving such an invariant is part of the remaining work.

Item 2's side, prepared. Item 2's stack is regrouped into an upper layer (the grouped client and the skeleton) and a lower service layer (encapsulator, router, decapsulation oracle and tables). A general simulation lemma then compares a program run through these two layers with a middle run, as long as every request of the middle is answered the same way by the two layers; once it is instantiated with the program's creations as the counted requests and the router's remaining reservation as their room, which is part of the remaining work, it will also show that item 2's router never stops. Every purely native step of the skeleton passes through the encapsulator, the router and the decapsulation oracle untouched and is answered by the tables alone, and the skeleton never reads the analysis records of its game state, so they can be erased along with the router's transcripts. Finally, on the ideal side the selected session is marked exactly when the selected accept returned a session (the converse that the first part's review asked for), so the ideal decision reads the same fact as item 2's decision. Item 2's view of the middle state is fixed (the encoded owners, the game state, the mark with its hidden value, the router's creation count, the public table and the two-slot table), and the first requests (coins, the commitment hash and the Server kernel reveal) are shown to be answered by item 2's layers exactly as by the middle handler.

What this does not show. The active branch, and with it the second compile lemma, is still not proved. Remaining: the invariants of the middle run on both sides (including the read-back of the hidden build's response, which needs the approved Phase 2 read-back contract), the request-by-request comparison of item 2's layers with the middle handler for the remaining requests (creation, bundle, accept, build, finish, HMAC and the read of a Beacon owner's kernel field; the compiled program never reads the other fields, for which the transported budget allows no request) and with it the instantiation of the simulation lemma that excludes the router's stop, the selected accept's steps after encapsulation on item 2's side, and the assembly with the decision. Everything here is an equality of programs or a simulation lemma; it makes no security claim, charges nothing, and uses no codec contract or assumption.

Review. An independent review of this part (semantic and hygiene) found no error in the Lean statements or proofs. Its findings concerned the records. Some sentences, here and in the companion guide, stated results without their premises: the per-command statement of the ideal side holds under CE-3's merge invariant, the whole-program statement needs an invariant that is still to be proved, and the router's stop is excluded only once the simulation lemma is instantiated for item 2. The guide named the wrong commit when it recorded where the shared main line had moved, and it described the module checks as run on the commits with a clean tree, while they ran just before each commit on the same sources. Two module lists left out the fifth module. The plan for item 2's side included steps for field reads that the compiled program can never make, and its list of item 2's invariants left out two facts about the selected accept (that it is done and that it was active) which the remaining steps need. And 31 helper lemmas had no description. The fix pass corrects these texts and adds the descriptions; no statement changed, and all five modules were checked again on the fix commit. A confirming review of the fix pass found every finding resolved and no new problem in the statements or proofs. Its two remaining points were records: the shared main line had moved again shortly before the fix pass's records were committed, so they named an older state of it, and the working notes kept an older plan step that the fix pass had dropped.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-11b unit U3 remainder and unit U4 (first part): frames and provenance of the ideal environment

What this shows. Unit U3 built the ideal environment, the environment of the record world that plays the ideal registration of one target. Its remainder proves the resource frames that the record-lift results need: from every environment state, every command of the ideal environment uses at most the coins, BLAKE2b queries and installs that the planned allowance gives its class (`idealStep_bound`), including the rare branch in which the slot allocator is full and a slot read draws a fresh 108-byte value; the environment's startup, which draws the challenger's parameters, uses at most `qInit + 32 + (count + 1) * keygenCost + encapsCost` coins (`frame_idealD`). From the frames follow the BLAKE2b and derivation bounds C4 (`c4_ideal`, `c4_ideal_later`), and the statement that the seed table holds exactly the seeds of installed slots now holds on the final split game's own outcomes for every choice of parameters (`seed_at_install_split`), carried there from the record world because two programs with the same probability law have the same outcomes. Unit U4 then proves provenance facts about the World-level provenance annotation (`PqxdhRecordLiftOrigins`), which records which record handle holds which hidden slot; the planned `run_origins` (unit U7, not yet proved) relates it to the record lift's own handle-to-slot map. One invariant (`Prov`), kept by every adversary query and every registration command, ties together the public transcript, the environment's state, the World and the annotation. On every run it gives that the annotation is exactly the slot map of the environment's install records (`origins_ghost`), that a Server peer holding a hidden slot holds slot 0 and is the peer the selected session built according to the public transcript, that only the selected Beacon owner can hold a hidden Beacon slot, and, when the codec reads Phase 1 messages back faithfully, that every Server peer which the public designation assigns to the target holds slot 0 (`ideal_slots_server`). The same facts about the selected session's peer hold on the final split game's own outcomes (`ideal_trace`). The Lean statements `ideal_trace_world`, `ideal_trace` and `ideal_slots_server` take the read-back premise for the whole statement, although only the facts about designated peers use it; the other facts also hold without it (`ideal_trace_world_peer`, `ideal_trace_peer`, `ideal_slots_restrictions`).

Why it matters. The common deployment experiment's headline per target conjoins the adversary's claim with "the ideal slots are as expected" before lifting it to the record world; these are three of the four parts of that conjunct (C5 restated in the design), proved on the real record world where the lift needs them. The frames are the remaining resource obligations of the ideal environment, so the record-lift reductions apply to it with their planned query bills.

What this does not show. The fourth part of C5, that the selected Beacon owner holds a hidden slot whenever it designates the target unless its finish came before the selected accept (the anomaly), is not proved: it needs facts about how the Server's build writes the challenge ciphertext into its Phase 2 response that no published module provides for the build the ideal environment runs. Hence the full statement `ideal_slots` with the anomaly as its alternative, its prefix-closed form and the bound on the anomaly's probability are open, both by the ciphertext-guessing quantity `ctGuess` and in the form that the later IND-CCA reduction needs (by the guess of an explicit program that runs the game from the public key alone up to the selected Beacon owner's first attempt to finish its registration while it waits for the Server's reply, the only attempt that reads its secret key). `ctGuess` and `ctGuessPk` are only defined; both are suprema over all guess functions, so they are information-theoretic quantities of the KEM that no approved assumption bounds. The statement that the Beacon's install record implies that the owner is established in the public transcript is also not proved. Everything here is a bound on query counts, an equality in law, a fact about the outcomes of a run or a definition; no security claim is made and nothing is charged. The only premise beyond the cost model is the approved codec contract that Phase 1 messages read back faithfully, used for the facts about designated Server peers; no new assumption or contract is used.

Review. An independent review found no wrong statement, but it found that the planned way to bound the anomaly for the later IND-CCA reduction could not work. The reduction guesses the challenge ciphertext before the challenge, asks the decapsulation oracle about the guess and compares the result with the challenge key; for that, the guess must come from a program built from the adversary. `ctGuessPk` instead takes the best guess over all functions of the public key, including ones that no program can compute efficiently, and no assumption bounds that. The fix pass therefore adds `ctGuessBy`, the probability that a given guessing program, run on a fresh public key before the encapsulation to it, outputs the ciphertext of that encapsulation (`PqxdhDeploymentIdealAnomaly`). For every program this probability is at most `ctGuessPk` (`ctGuessBy_le`): replacing each output by the best guess for the public key can only help, and since ciphertexts form a finite type such a best guess exists. Conversely `ctGuessPk` is exactly the largest value over all programs (`ctGuessPk_eq_iSup`). The guessing program runs unchanged inside the pre-challenge phase of the one-key IND-CCA game, because it never asks the decapsulation oracle (`guess_preChallenge`). The planned anomaly bound is now stated with an explicit guessing program, which runs the game from the public key alone up to the selected Beacon owner's first attempt to finish its registration while it waits for the Server's reply, and its estimate grows accordingly. The fix pass also adds the premise-free forms of the peer facts and the slot restrictions named above and corrects the wording about the annotation and about the replaced design invariant; no earlier statement changed. A confirming review of the fix pass found every finding resolved and no new problem in the statements or proofs. It made the stopping point of the planned guessing program precise: a Beacon rejects a finish attempt that arrives while it is not waiting for the Server's reply without touching its secret key, and the first attempt made while it waits either completes or aborts its registration, so that attempt is the only one that reads the secret key and the program stops there. Its other points concerned the records, among them that one more statement relying on the faithful reading of Phase 1 messages, the key match `keyFacts_marked`, was missing from the list of statements that use it.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-11b unit U6 (third part): item 2's steps of the post-challenge simulation

The second part of unit U6 compared the two sides of CE-11b's active branch through a middle execution: the compiled deployment program runs against a middle handler whose state is item 2's annotated source state with the ideal registration's bookkeeping, the ideal side is the merge view of that run, and item 2's side is to be its projection onto item 2's post-challenge layers. For the projection, every request that the compiled program can send must be answered by item 2's layers, from item 2's view of the middle state, exactly as by the middle handler, without the post-challenge router stopping. The second part did this for coins, the commitment hash and the Server kernel reveal. This third part does it for all remaining requests except owner k's challenge finish.

Requests that touch no private key. The public HMAC is a direct read of the shared Extract table on the zero-key 192-byte slice and the real function elsewhere, on both sides. A read of a Beacon owner's prekey, one-time prekey or established kernel is answered from the owner itself, and item 2's encoding of an owner keeps these fields.

The router after the challenge. Item 2's post-challenge router holds a placeholder in place of the challenge's shared secret, and the challenger answers the selected key's decapsulations through its decapsulation oracle, which refuses the challenge ciphertext. Item 2 compared this router with a router that knows every secret key under the premise that the placeholder is the true decapsulation of the challenge. That premise matters only for the decapsulation of the challenge ciphertext under the selected key; for every other request the two routers agree exactly, whatever the placeholder. This part proves that, which lets every request other than owner k's challenge finish use the plain comparison, with no correctness assumption about the KEM.

Creation, bundle, accept and build. A creation draws an identity, a prekey and the KEM key pair that the challenger reserved for the next creation index; the middle state's creation reads the same pool entry because the number of owners equals the number of KEM key pairs created so far. A bundle makes signatures and draws a one-time prekey but creates and decapsulates nothing, so the router behaves exactly as the plain services. A raw accept other than the selected one runs its prefix (the Server's static Diffie-Hellman and the encapsulation to the Beacon's key) through the encapsulator and the router, and its tail (core acceptance, the root read from the shared table, the consumed registration ID, the pending token) on the game state; both match item 2's annotated source accept. A build of a session other than the marked one runs the source's own response code on both sides. Each of these steps needs some fact about the middle state (for example that the owner count equals the number of created KEM pairs, or that the Server's identity slot holds its seed); these facts are stated as premises of the step lemmas and are to be supplied by the invariant of the middle execution, which is part of the remaining work.

A counting difference. The ideal registration's build of the marked session reads the session's hidden value from the two-slot table again, which the table records as one more lookup; item 2's skeleton takes the value from its own records and does not touch the table. The counters are bookkeeping that no program reads, but item 2's view of the middle state, as the second part fixed it, contained them, so the two sides would differ by one lookup after such a build. This part removes the counters from item 2's view, shows that no layer reads them, and carries every step already proved over to the new view. With that, the marked build matches: both sides run the factored Server response at the hidden value stored at the mark's slot.

Beacon finishes. A Beacon's finish runs the second phase of its handshake: it reads the Server's reply, decapsulates the KEM ciphertext with its own key, computes the Diffie-Hellman values, derives the root key and then runs the continuation that establishes the session. Item 2 writes this program with an opaque handle in place of the decapsulated secret and groups the root derivation and the continuation into one request, while the middle handler runs the source's own finish with the secret. The preparation never looks inside the handle, so answering every decapsulation with a handle that just wraps the secret gives the same preparation as using the secret itself, relabelled; this is proved once for any relabelling. With such handles, item 2's existing realization theorem turns the opaque owner into the source's native finish, and item 2's existing compiler theorem turns that into the middle's annotated finish. On item 2's side, an owner that is not waiting for its second phase with the selected KEM key never decapsulates the challenge ciphertext under that key, so the router behaves as the plain services, and the grouped request splits into the root read from the shared table and the continuation, exactly as the Server's accept tail did. This covers every finish except owner k's challenge finish. The step lemma takes as premises item 2's ownership invariant, the prefix property of the KEM pool, and that the addressed owner, if it holds the selected KEM key, is not waiting for its second phase; for a finish that is not owner k's challenge finish the invariant of the middle execution is to supply them (the last one because only owner k holds that key, and after the selected accept a finish of owner k waiting for its second phase is its challenge finish).

What this does not show. The active branch, and with it CE-11b's second compile lemma, is still not proved. Remaining: owner k's challenge finish against the ideal registration's (which needs a relabelling between item 2's encoded owner, which names identities and keys by index, and the native owner, which holds the seed and the key pair, and the challenge marker carried through item 2's table layers), the invariant of the middle execution on both sides (which also supplies the premises of this part's steps), the selected accept's steps after encapsulation on item 2's side, and the assembly with the simulation lemma at the new view and the decision. Everything here is an equality of programs; it makes no security claim, charges nothing, and uses no codec contract or assumption.

Review. An independent review of this part in two parts (semantic and hygiene) found no error in the Lean statements or proofs and approved with nits. The main finding was one of wording: the implementation guide and the header of the finish module stated the finish step's last premise as if it constrained every owner holding the selected KEM key, whereas the Lean premise, like the description above, concerns only the owner that the finish addresses. Read as a condition on every owner it would be false in reachable runs (owner k waiting for its second phase while another owner finishes), so the invariant of the middle execution is planned in the addressed-owner form. The other findings were missing docstrings of seven helper lemmas and stale records. The fix pass changed only docstrings and records; no Lean statement changed. A confirming review of the fix pass found every finding resolved and no new problem in the statements or proofs. Its one remaining point, taken before publication, was that the new description of one helper lemma named only one of the bookkeeping records that the comparison drops (the session's recorded touch) and not the two entries of the key-derivation history; the description now names all three.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-11b unit U4 (remainder): the Beacon converse, C5 restated and the anomaly bound

This part finishes the statement that the record lift needs about which handles of the ideal world hold hidden slots (C5 restated) and bounds the one exception, the Beacon-side anomaly. It works on the record world in which the challenger's parameters are drawn at the start and the ideal registration answers the adversary, with the World-level annotation that records which handle holds which hidden slot. Four new modules hold 77 checked theorems (four of them from the review fix pass); every theorem depends only on Lean's standard axioms, and no new assumption or contract is used.

The Beacon converse. When the selected Beacon owner `k` publicly designates the target session, the designation says that the owner finished its registration with a Phase 2 message whose KEM ciphertext also appears in the build response of the target session, and that the target session's accept carried the owner's published post-quantum key. The proof first shows several facts about the code that runs, each read off the extracted Rust through existing correspondences: the selected accept marks the session only when it actually encapsulated to the selected key, and then it stores a pending registration that carries exactly the challenge ciphertext; the Server's build writes that stored ciphertext into the Phase 2 message it publishes; a Beacon finish made while the owner is not waiting for the Server's reply is rejected before the secret key is read; and a finish of owner `k` on a message carrying the challenge ciphertext, once the selected accept has encapsulated to the selected key, decapsulates it as the challenge, reads the hidden value, and when it succeeds records the owner's hidden install at a slot. A second invariant of the annotated run, kept by every command beside the provenance invariant of the first part, collects these facts. With the faithful reading of Phase 1 and Phase 2 messages it follows that the designating owner holds a hidden slot unless its designating finish happened before the selected accept, which is exactly the anomaly. Together with the Server-side facts of the first part this gives C5 restated on every run: either every handle's slot is as the record lift expects, or the anomaly happened. The same argument works for a designation computed on any earlier part of the transcript, because the transcript entries that a designation reads stay in the transcript, although the designation itself can change as the run goes on.

The anomaly bound. The anomaly means that owner `k` finished before the selected accept with a Phase 2 message whose ciphertext equals the challenge ciphertext that the selected accept sends later. The proof reads off the transcript the ciphertext of owner `k`'s first successful finish before the selected accept, a public value, and shows that the anomaly implies that this value is the challenge ciphertext. It then moves to the equivalent game of the final split form, which keeps the drawn parameters, and shows that the game does not look at the challenge ciphertext before the selected accept: two runs that differ only in the challenge ciphertext take the same steps until the selected accept, which stops both with the same guess, and the guess no longer changes afterwards. A general coupling lemma for runs that agree until a stop and keep an observed value once stopped turns this into an equality of the guess's distribution for every challenge. So the encapsulation that produces the challenge can be drawn after the guess, and the guess hits the encapsulation's ciphertext with probability at most `ctGuessPk`, the best chance of predicting an encapsulation's ciphertext from the public key, hence at most `ctGuess`. The same holds for the anomaly computed on an earlier part of the transcript, the exception in the statement about designations computed on earlier parts: there too the designating finish is owner `k`'s first successful finish, and the build response it is linked to stays in the transcript, so the guess read off the final transcript equals the challenge ciphertext, and the same bound applies.

Limits. `ctGuessPk` takes the best over all functions of the public key, including ones no program computes efficiently, so it is a property of the KEM that no approved assumption bounds. The planned later reduction to IND-CCA needs the bound with an explicit guessing program that does not use the selected secret key; here the guess is computed from runs that use the whole key pair, because owner `k`'s finishes before the selected accept decapsulate with its secret key. Building that program requires stopping at owner `k`'s first finish while it waits for the Server's reply and showing that, before that point, replacing owner `k`'s secret key by another changes nothing; this is not done yet, and neither are the agreement of the owner's install with the public transcript (L2) and the key-first and key-last forms of the ideal game (unit U8). These results are statements about the runs of the ideal world and a bound by a definition; no security claim about the real protocol is made here.

Review. An independent review found no wrong statement, proof or hidden assumption. It recorded that two planned pieces are still missing: the anomaly bound with an explicit guessing program that does not use the selected secret key, which the later IND-CCA reduction needs, and the key-first and key-last forms of the ideal game. Both are now scheduled as steps of their own, in new modules, and this unit is not counted as complete before the first of them is proved. The review also found that the statement about designations computed on an earlier part of the transcript has its own exceptional case, the anomaly on that earlier part, whose probability no theorem bounded. A designation can change as the run goes on, so the anomaly on an earlier part need not be the anomaly at the end. The fix pass proves that this earlier anomaly also forces the ciphertext guess read off the final transcript to equal the challenge ciphertext, and bounds its probability by `ctGuessPk`, hence by `ctGuess`, exactly as for the anomaly at the end. The shared last step, that the guess equals the challenge ciphertext with probability at most `ctGuessPk`, is now a theorem of its own that both bounds use; no earlier statement changed. The other points concerned the records: central had moved before this part's first commit, so the branch needs a merge before integration; two settings switched off deprecation warnings where none arose and are removed; one statement was missing from the list of statements that rely on the faithful reading of Phase 2 messages; the game was said to read the challenge ciphertext only at the selected accept, while what is proved is that it does not read it before that accept (a later finish of owner `k` reads it again); and the reason why owner `k`'s first finish while waiting for the Server's reply is the only one that reads its secret key needs two facts: a finish at any other time is rejected before the key is read, and that first finish either completes or aborts the registration, after which the Beacon no longer holds the key. The route for the key-first and key-last forms now also records that the ideal game's table of hidden values must first be replaced by one without query counters, because those counters would differ after drawing a value early. A confirming review of the fix pass found every finding resolved or correctly recorded and no new problem in the statements or proofs: it recompiled the changed modules and the root independently with identical results and rechecked the guards, the receipt and the cited Rust lines. Its only point concerned the records: the description of where the merge with the current central version would conflict was inexact (one conflict listed in the wrong file, and the count of handwritten Lean files merges without a conflict to a stale value, so it must be recounted), and it is corrected. The two missing pieces stay scheduled: the anomaly bound with an explicit guessing program first, then the key-first and key-last forms.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-11b unit U6 (fourth part): owner k's challenge finish, the middle invariants and the second compile lemma

The second and third parts of unit U6 proved, for every source request that the compiled continuation can issue after the selected accept except owner k's challenge finish, that item 2's post-challenge layers answer it exactly as the middle handler does, each step under some facts about the middle state (the second part for the coin, hash and kernel-reveal requests, the third part for the others). Reads of an owner's identity or KEM key fields are not among these requests: the budget, carried over to the continuation, allows none of them, and this part uses that when it puts the steps together. This fourth part proves the missing step, collects the facts into an invariant that every step keeps, turns the per-request steps into a statement about whole programs, proves the first step of item 2's post-challenge phase (the rest of the Server's selected raw accept), and then puts both sides together: the ideal side's invariant, the active branch, and CE-11b's second compile lemma.

Owner k's challenge finish. After the selected accept sent the challenge ciphertext to owner k's KEM key, owner k's next finish is where the ideal and the real worlds differ: the ideal registration answers the decapsulation of the challenge ciphertext with a marker, reads the hidden value for owner k's root from the two-slot table instead of deriving it, and runs the Beacon's continuation on that value. Item 2's layers do the same in their own way: the post-challenge router holds a placeholder in place of the challenge's shared secret and answers the decapsulation of the challenge ciphertext under the selected key from it without asking the challenger, item 2's preparation turns that reply into the same marker, and item 2's grouped finish request reads the hidden value from the same table through the same allocator. The two programs also name the owner differently: item 2's owner refers to its identity and KEM key by their creation indices, the native owner holds the identity seed and the key pair. The preparation never uses the identity or key beyond converting the owner's own identity and decapsulating with the owner's own key, so it suffices to relate the two interpretations at that one owner, which this part proves once. Item 2's view of the middle state reads the mark's value from the table; the hidden read of the challenge finish may allocate a new slot, but never disturbs a value already stored, so the mark's value is unchanged. With these pieces, owner k's challenge finish matches. The third part's step for the other finishes needed that the addressed owner, if it holds the selected key, is not waiting for its second phase; after an active selected accept this follows from the finish not being owner k's challenge finish, because each owner's KEM index is its position. So every finish now has its step.

The invariant and the simulation. The facts the steps need are: item 2's record of which identity seed and KEM key pair each owner holds, the Server's own identity seed, one KEM key pair per owner, the created key pairs being the first entries of the challenger's pool, each owner's KEM index being its position, the selected accept being done and active, the allocator being well formed, and the mark's value being stored. This part proves that every step of the middle execution keeps these facts (creations take the next pool entry when there is room, finishes and bundles change only the addressed owner's state, the hidden steps touch only the native state and the table), with one unit of room used by each creation. The second part's generic simulation lemma then gives item 2's side for whole programs: on a program that reads no identity or KEM key field and creates at most as many owners as the pool has entries left, item 2's layers run without the router stopping and end exactly in item 2's view of the middle run's final state.

The selected accept. Item 2's post-challenge phase starts by finishing the Server's selected raw accept after its encapsulation: the Server computes its Diffie-Hellman values (its static one through the identity pool), and its tail requests the root of the challenge-marked input, consumes the registration ID and publishes the pending token. The ideal registration runs the same steps natively, reading the hidden value for the root through the allocator and recording its coordinates as the mark, where item 2 records the value itself. This part proves that the two agree: the Diffie-Hellman part through item 2's layers is the Server's native computation with its seed, and the tail splits step by step, with item 2's mark being the ideal mark together with the value stored at its coordinates (stored because the allocator was empty at the cut). Item 2 resumes from the game state with its analysis observers, which the resumption never reads.

One run, two views. The second part's plan was to compare the two sides through a common middle execution instead of relating them directly. This part carries it out. Item 2's post-challenge phase on an active cut is the selected accept followed by item 2's layers on the rest of the program; by the selected-accept step and the simulation, this is the same as running the selected accept natively and then the middle execution, and reading item 2's view of its final state. The ideal side is the same selected accept followed by the compiled program under the ideal registration; by the third part's commutation, this is the same middle execution with the program's local copies merged into its final state, provided an invariant on the ideal side holds at the start and is kept by every step. The two decisions read the same things from the two views (the event, the designation and the frames the program produced, and whether the selected accept returned a session), so they agree. This reduces the active branch to that one invariant.

The ideal side's invariant. The invariant is CE-3's own invariant of the compiled program, which says that the local copies and the public log describe the native state faithfully: the Server's peers and their identities can be read off the logged build responses and accept bytes, each owner's phase can be read off its logged create, bundle and finish bytes, and every pending token belongs to a logged accept; together with the selected accept being behind the accept counter. CE-3 proved that every real command keeps it, an earlier CE-11b step extended that to the challenger's KEM pool, and the middle execution's real commands are commands of item 2's annotated pool source, whose erasure is that pool source, so they keep it too. The two hidden steps needed new work. The marked build runs the Server's response code with the key schedule replaced by the hidden table value; its effect on the Server is the same as the real build's (one new peer for the session's Beacon at an unused key ID, a response written by the Phase 2 writer with the Server's own identity), because none of that depends on the key schedule, and the approved Phase 2 read-back law lets the log recover the Server's identity from the response as before. Owner k's challenge finish runs the Beacon's continuation on the hidden value; it changes only the Beacon's own state and caches, and when it succeeds the established owner's key ID, binding and associated data are the ones its logged finish bytes and bundle determine, exactly as for a real finish. Finally the invariant holds right after the selected accept: it held at the cut (an earlier result), and the selected accept's steps after encapsulation advance the session counter, publish at most the new session's token, and that token carries the identity key that can be read from the logged accept bytes.

The second compile lemma. With the invariant, the active branch holds at every draw of the challenger, and the earlier reduction turns it into CE-11b's second compile lemma: for every adversary within its budget, the probability that the decision is true in item 2's slot game with the compiled program equals the probability that the event happens with the designated handle in the ideal game of CE-11b, assuming only the approved Phase 1 and Phase 2 read-back laws of the message codec. Unit U7 combines it with C1 for the ideal game (the ideal game and the record world with the ideal environment give the same law of the adversary's output, the ledger and the produced frames, which is all that the decision reads) into the hand-off to CE-12, `ideal_world`.

What this does not show. The second compile lemma is an equality of probabilities between two games; it makes no security claim by itself, charges nothing, and uses no assumption beyond the approved read-back laws (which earlier steps of the same chain already used) and the adversary's budget. Everything else here is an equality of programs or a fact about the support of a run. Central moved during this part (the integration of unit U4's remainder), and the integration into central merges that move first.

Review. An independent review of this part in two parts (semantic and hygiene) rechecked every module, found no error in the Lean statements or proofs and approved with nits. Its findings concerned descriptions and records only. The implementation guide sent the next unit to a lemma that was only planned in the design and never written (an earlier decision replaced it); it now names the existing C1 statement for the ideal game, whose projection is exactly what the second compile lemma's decision reads. This section had called the second compile lemma the statement handed to CE-12, whereas the next unit derives that hand-off from it together with C1, and had credited the third part alone with the per-request steps, some of which the second part proved; both sentences are corrected above. The other findings were an intermediate theorem missing from the list of uses of the read-back laws (it passes them on unchanged) and stale coordination records. No Lean statement, proof or guard changed. A confirming review of the fix pass found every finding resolved and no new problem in the statements or proofs; its two optional points concerned wording only (how this paragraph described that lemma, and which tree one of the fix pass's inventory checks ran on) and are taken.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-11b unit U4 (follow-up) and unit U8: the anomaly guesser with decapsulation access and the key-first forms

What this part adds. The previous part bounded the Beacon-side anomaly (owner `k` designates the target through a finish made before the selected accept) by the best chance of predicting an encapsulation's ciphertext from the public key, a property of the KEM that no approved assumption bounds. The later security argument needs the bound in a form it can turn into an IND-CCA advantage: the chance that a concrete program, which knows only the selected public key and may ask for decapsulations under the selected secret key, predicts the ciphertext of a later encapsulation to that key. This part proves the anomaly bound in that form, `anomaly_le_pk`, with the same bound for the anomaly computed on an earlier part of the transcript. It also proves the key-first and key-last forms of the ideal game, in which the 32-byte message key of the first hidden slot is drawn as a separate value before (or after) the rest of that slot's output.

The guessing program. The program draws everything that the ideal game draws except the selected key pair and the challenge: a key pair of its own, the other Beacons' key pairs and the Server's construction. It then runs the whole ideal game against the adversary at the selected public key, with its own secret key in the place where owner `k` keeps the selected one, and outputs the ciphertext guess read off the transcript (owner `k`'s first successful finish before the selected accept). Wherever owner `k`'s Phase 2 finish would decapsulate a ciphertext, the program asks its decapsulation oracle instead, so it never needs the selected secret key. The proof shows that, until the selected accept, this run takes exactly the steps of the real ideal game: every step other than owner `k`'s finish ignores owner `k`'s secret key (creating, bundling and recording steps only carry it along or never touch it, and the Server's steps and other owners' steps are unaffected), and owner `k`'s finish, answered by the oracle under the selected key, behaves like the real finish. At the selected accept the guess is fixed, so the guess has the same distribution in both runs, and the earlier part's argument then gives the bound. The program asks at most one decapsulation per finish request of the adversary.

The key-first forms. The ideal game draws the hidden output of the first slot the moment the game first reads it. Because every step of the game treats a not-yet-read entry of this lazily sampled table independently of when it is drawn, the entry can be drawn before the game starts without changing what any observer sees, apart from the table itself. Before this argument applies, the table of the ideal game, which counts its lookups and draws, is replaced by one without counters, since drawing early would change the counts. Then the 108-byte output splits into a uniform 32-byte message key and a uniform 76-byte rest, drawn in either order. The same holds for the final split form, whose table keeps only the key and nonce part of each slot, the rest being drawn when it is installed in the World.

Limits. These results are equalities of distributions and bounds by defined quantities; no security claim about the real protocol is made here, and no assumption is added. The predicting program is explicit, but turning its success chance into an IND-CCA advantage is the later reduction's step. That step must also state the reduction's query budget, as the existing KEM step of the chain does: at most one decapsulation per finish request of the adversary plus one for the guess, no query to the KEM's base oracle (the program answers the KEM's internal base queries with its own random draws), and a number of random draws made up of its key generations, the Server's construction and the steps of the game. Only the decapsulation count is a theorem here; the other two counts follow from the cost bounds that the proof already uses (the KEM operations' costs, the bound on the runtime initializer and the adversary's budget), so they need no new assumption. The key-first statements describe everything that the game's outcome shows except the hidden-slot table itself, and no later headline uses them: they are the CE analogue of a step of the item 2 chain, kept because the plan keeps it.

Review. An independent review found no wrong statement, proof or hidden assumption. Its one minor finding was that this section and the guide described the remaining query counts of the guessing program as needed only if the final statement lists the IND-CCA adversary's query budget, while the existing KEM step of the chain already lists such a budget, so a later statement built the same way needs them. They are now recorded as a definite obligation of the later reduction, with the existing cost bounds they are built from, so they cannot be mistaken for a new assumption. The other points concerned the records: the key-first forms were described as the form that a later key-indistinguishability argument expects, although no later statement uses them; a cited plan section is not yet in the plan copy committed on this branch (central's copy has it, and the copy is refreshed before the integration); one sentence said that the new modules import only modules published before this part, although one of them imports another new one; and the full inventory check at the last commit was run by the review, not by this part. No Lean statement or proof changed. A confirming review found all five points resolved. It noted that the existing per-step bound on random draws, which the recorded obligation cited for the program's per-step counts, is stated for the ideal environment's step, while the program runs a different form of that step that agrees with it only in distribution. The per-step bound for the program's step is therefore itself a lemma of the later reduction, proved from the same cost bounds of the individual commands, and the existing bound supplies only the per-step amounts; no Lean change is needed for this, and no assumption is added.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-11b unit U7: the hand-off to CE-12

This unit connects CE-11b's second compile lemma with the record lift, in the forms the next stage (CE-12) composes. One new module holds 23 checked theorems; every theorem depends only on Lean's standard axioms, and no new assumption or contract is used.

The ideal world. The second compile lemma compares two games on one decision, "the event happens and the claim designates the target": item 2's two-slot ideal world, run on the program compiled from the CE adversary, and CE's ideal game for the target. An earlier unit proved that CE's ideal game and the record world, whose environment draws the challenger's parameters at its start and then answers registrations as the ideal registration does, produce the same joint distribution of the adversary's output, the secrecy ledger and the produced record frames. This unit shows that the decision reads nothing else, so the two equalities chain: item 2's two-slot world and the record world with the target's ideal environment give the decision the same probability. The design had planned a separate lemma for drawing the parameters before the environment starts; since the environment itself draws them at its start, that lemma is not needed.

The record lift's slot map. The record lift states its results on its own view of a run, which includes a public map from each Server peer and each Beacon owner to the hidden key-schedule slot it holds, if any. The earlier statement of which handles hold hidden slots (C5 restated) was proved on a different object: the plain record world with an annotation that records, at each successful hidden installation, which handle received which slot. This unit proves that the two agree. Running the record lift's compiler with real key derivations at every coordinate and then keeping only the World state and the slots computed from its stored records gives exactly the annotated world, command by command; per command this combines two results of the record-lift track, that the compiler's commands erase to the World's commands and that the slots it computes after a command are the annotation of that command's reply. Hence the record lift's whole view of its real world (the adversary's output, the ledger, the environment's state, the produced frames, the raw-attempt counters and the slot map) has the same distribution as the corresponding view of the annotated world, and C5 restated holds on every run of the record lift's real world for its own slot map: only the target's Server peer (in slot 0) and owner k hold hidden slots, and a peer or owner that designates the target holds one, unless the Beacon-side anomaly occurred.

The forms for CE-12. Put together, the probability of the decision in item 2's two-slot world is at most the probability, in the record lift's real world with the target's ideal environment, that the decision holds and the view's slot map satisfies C5 restated, plus the probability of the anomaly. Following the recorded decision on the anomaly, CE-12 bounds its probability with the bound through a guessing program with decapsulation access, which the concurrent track of unit U4 proved and which was integrated into the central branch just before this unit: the anomaly term here is exactly the event that bound is about, so the two combine directly, and CE-12 turns the guessing program into a predict-then-compare attack on the IND-CCA security of the KEM, an assumption already in use. With that bound, CE-11b's main line is complete. The bound by `ctGuess` (an earlier unit) is also stated here, but only as a corollary: `ctGuess` is a defined guessing quantity of the KEM that no approved assumption bounds, so it does not appear in CE-12's final bound. CE-12 applies the record lifts to the event "the decision holds and C5 restated holds" and then the facts about the final ideal worlds.

What this does not show. These are equalities of distributions, a fact about the possible outcomes of a run and a bound by the probability of a public event; there is no security claim here. The premises are the approved read-back laws of the message codec, which the second compile lemma and C5 restated already used, and the adversary's budget. The unit is not yet integrated.

Review. An independent review in two parts (semantic and hygiene) rechecked the module, found no error in the Lean statements or proofs and approved with nits. Its findings concerned descriptions and records only. This section and the implementation guide had placed the anomaly bound through the guessing program outside CE-11b's main line and had offered the bound by `ctGuess` as a route for CE-12, whereas the recorded decision is that CE-12 bounds the anomaly through an IND-CCA reduction built from the guessing program and that `ctGuess` does not appear in the final bound; the sentences above are corrected, and the `ctGuess` forms are described as corollaries. The other findings were the description of a few lemmas as having no premise although they take an internal hypothesis (the record compiler's invariant on the start state, which holds initially, or a logical implication), neither of which is a contract or an assumption; a clean-tree run of the inventory check recorded only in scratch notes; and stale status records. No Lean statement, proof or guard changed. A confirming review found all five points resolved, with statements, guards and records intact; its remaining remarks (a punctuation slip, a reference to the wrong section of the working plan, two further inventory checks recorded only in scratch notes, and how to merge the committed copy of the working plan) are taken. Since then the concurrent track of unit U4 has been integrated into the central branch, which this unit's integration merges, and the descriptions above say so.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-11b: what is proved and what CE-12 consumes

CE-11b builds, for one target (the selected Server accept and the selected Beacon KEM key), the ideal registration of the common deployment experiment and connects it to item 2's ideal KEM world on one side and to the record lift's real world on the other. In its ideal game the challenger draws the selected KEM key pair, the other owners' KEM keys and the challenge ciphertext; the selected accept, the build of the marked session and owner k's finish on the challenge are replaced by steps that read the hidden values from a two-slot table. CE-11b proves: that the hidden values can be erased from the parts of the run that do not read them and split between the environment and the World, with the World's seeds drawn only when installed; the ideal environment of the record lift, whose runs have the distribution of the ideal game on what events read (C1) and of the ideal game's split form on the final cache and the revealed values, with its query bounds (C2a, C4) and the admissibility of its hidden installations; which handles hold hidden slots (C5 restated), except on the Beacon-side anomaly, whose probability is at most a defined guessing quantity of the KEM and, by the concurrent track of unit U4 (integrated into the central branch just before this unit), at most the success probability of an explicit guessing program with decapsulation access; the second compile lemma, equating item 2's two-slot world of the compiled program with the ideal game on the designation decision; and the hand-off of the previous section. Everything rests on the approved read-back laws of the message codec and the adversary's budget, and on no new assumption or contract.

CE-12 uses, for each target, the hand-off bound on the record lift's view together with the anomaly bound through the guessing program, which it turns into an IND-CCA reduction (with that bound CE-11b's main line is complete; the bound by the defined guessing quantity is only a corollary), the query bounds of the ideal environment as premises of the record lifts, and C5 restated on the record lift's real world to place the final events inside the facts proved about the ideal record worlds. It adds the steps before item 2's two-slot world (the per-target KEM transfer and item 2's theorem relating its KEM worlds) and after the record lift (the final-world facts and the sum over targets). Outside CE-11b's main line: the later-quantum mode's pieces (deferred, since the results they would build on do not exist yet), the key-first and key-last forms of the ideal game (a concurrent track, also integrated), and whether the defined guessing quantity is small for ML-KEM, which no approved assumption covers and which CE-12's route does not need.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-12 P1: the classical headline theorems

This stage states and proves the five classical headline theorems of the common deployment experiment, the single game in which one adversary drives the whole deployment: a generated Server, any number of Beacon registrations, record traffic in both directions, raw (adversary-built) records, test and fresh secrecy queries, and direct access to the hash and HMAC primitives. Nine new modules hold 116 checked theorems; every theorem depends only on Lean's standard axioms, and no new assumption or contract is used. An independent review checked the statements against the design, re-derived every bound step by step and checked the guards and the inventory; its findings concerned the precision of this explanation, one premise that CE-OR carried without using it (now removed) and the use of deprecated library names, and are fixed. A confirming review of the fixes found every finding resolved; its one remaining remark, that this explanation called the coordinates of CE-KT's key table Diffie-Hellman inputs although they are the Diffie-Hellman outputs that feed the key schedule, is taken. The stage was not yet integrated when this explanation was written.

How the claims are measured. The events are computed only from the experiment's own records and the adversary's output: the transcript of all queries with their answers (including replies that the adversary does not see in the private-reply mode), the test session, the fresh messages and the frames produced by record seals (including frames of failed writes that were never published). They never read roots, keys, which handles are partners, or the registration bookkeeping that the experiment keeps for the proof only. The reductions behind the loss terms run the experiment and evaluate the event and the claim (for CE-LOR also the filter `F` and the adversary's guess), so the advantage terms are small under the contracts only when these functions are efficiently computable. Each claim names a record handle (a Server peer or a Beacon owner), and the public designation reads off the transcript which Server session and which Beacon KEM key, if any, that handle belongs to; that pair is the target `g`. Every headline bound is a sum over all targets `g` of a per-target loss, each counted once (coefficient one), with no factor for guessing the target: the event is split exactly by the target its claim designates. The per-target loss always contains two terms from the earlier stages: the KEM term (one IND-CCA advantage against ML-KEM of an explicit adversary built from the experiment, plus the ML-KEM correctness error) and the key-schedule term (item 2's bound for replacing the target's two hidden registration values by values of a lazily sampled uniform table: a statistical random-oracle term and HMAC-PRF and Extract-on-uniform advantages). Most headlines then add a record-layer term (the losses of the explicit reductions of the record lift against the AEAD and the key chains) and a small final term. Claims that may name a Beacon owner add the anomaly term `β_g`, explained below; claims restricted to Server peers do not.

The anomaly term. The proof places every designated handle on one of the target's two hidden key slots, except in one situation on the Beacon side: owner k's registration finished before the selected Server accept, yet owner k ends up designating the target (the anomaly). An earlier stage bounded the anomaly by the probability that an explicit program, given only the selected KEM public key and a decapsulation oracle, predicts the ciphertext of a later encapsulation to that key. This stage turns that prediction into an attack on ML-KEM's IND-CCA security: the attacker runs the predictor before the challenge, asks the decapsulation oracle for the key of the predicted ciphertext, and after the challenge says "real" exactly when the prediction equals the challenge ciphertext and its key equals the offered key. In the real case this wins whenever the prediction is right, except when decapsulation of the honest ciphertext does not return the encapsulated key (the correctness error); in the random case the offered key is fresh and uniform, so it matches with probability 2^-256. Hence `β_g` is one IND-CCA advantage plus the correctness error plus 2^-256, with coefficient one, and the attacker asks at most one decapsulation more than the predictor (at most the budget's number of finishes plus one) and nothing after the challenge.

CE-KT (key transfer). For any event and any claim, the probability that the deployment experiment ends with the event and the claim designating target `g` differs from the probability of the same in CE's ideal game for `g` by at most the KEM term plus the key-schedule term; summed over the targets, the probability of the event with a designated claim differs from the sum of the ideal-game probabilities by at most the sum of these terms. In CE's ideal game the target's two hidden registration values (the Server session's 108 bytes of key material and owner k's challenge finish) are uniform values from a lazily sampled two-entry table keyed by the 128 bytes of Diffie-Hellman outputs that feed the key schedule: one shared value when owner k's finish reads the same Diffie-Hellman outputs as the target session (the honest pairing), and independent values otherwise. This is a transfer statement: the deployment cannot tell the real registration keys of a designated target from random ones better than these terms, and the ideal probability stays on the right; it is not a statement that an attacker cannot output the root key. Premises: functional decapsulation of the KEM, the approved read-back laws of the Phase 1 and Phase 2 codecs, the full source correctness of the key schedule and the adversary's budget. The same holds with the record world of the target's ideal environment in place of the ideal game.

CE-OR (origin, both directions). An origin failure is an accepted raw record (one the adversary hands to a receive query) on a handle designated `g`, whose decoded frame the handle's partner had not sent before: for a record the Server accepted (b2s) the partner is owner k, and for a record a Beacon accepted (s2b) the partner is the Server peer built by the target's session. The probability of a b2s origin failure is at most the sum over targets of the KEM term, the key-schedule term, the integrity record-lift term and 2·R·S/2^512 (R raw receives and S sends in the budget; the chance of guessing a 64-byte record commitment that was never published); for s2b, `β_g` is added. Which records are covered: for b2s every record the Server accepts through a raw receive, from position 1 of a session on; for s2b every record a Beacon accepts through a raw receive, that is positions from 2. Position 1 of s2b, the sequence-one record inside the Server's Phase 2 response, is decrypted inside the Beacon's registration finish, not by a raw receive; its origin is the subject of the registration-authentication claim CE-A1 (ProVerif row S2b-initial), not of CE-OR. Premises: those of CE-KT, the KEM cost bound and the runtime initializer's query bound (they give the record lift its resource frame), and the read-back law of the frame codec. (The record-lift statement this bound comes from also names the agreement of the Server's header decoder with the frame codec, but its proof does not use it, so CE-OR does not assume it.) Frames are compared after decoding; a raw re-encoding of a published frame is outside the claim.

CE-UKS (no unknown-key share). The b2s form: the probability that the Server accepts, on a peer designated `g`, the decoded frame of a record that some handle sent anywhere in the run, where the two handles are not the designated partners of `g` (owner k and the target's Server peer), is at most the sum over targets of the KEM term, the key-schedule term, the integrity record-lift term and (R + S + H)·S/2^512, where H counts the shared hash outputs. The sender form (an owner designated `g` sent a record that some non-partner handle accepted) adds `β_g`. Premises: those of CE-OR.

CE-APP (fresh-message secrecy, private-reply mode). In the mode where raw receives reveal only their success, the probability that the adversary names an experiment-chosen fresh message sent on a designated handle and guesses it exactly is at most the sum over targets of the KEM term, the key-schedule term, `β_g`, the full record-lift term (integrity and privacy) and 2^-min, where min is the shortest admitted fresh-message length in bytes (the record lift's fresh-guess statement charges one bit per byte, a loose but valid term); a fresh message on a Server peer needs no `β_g`. The final term is paid once per target. Premises: those of CE-KT, the KEM cost bound and the runtime initializer's query bound.

CE-LOR (left-or-right secrecy of the test session, private-reply mode). A run is eligible when a test session exists, a condition `F` holds, where `F` is any function of the transcript view the adversary has in the private-reply mode (the plain claim takes `F` always true; like the events, `F` must be efficiently computable for the advantage terms to be small), and every admitted test query was sent on a handle that designates the same target as the first admitted test. The adversary wins when it is eligible and its output bit equals the hidden test bit. The advantage, the probability of winning minus half the probability of being eligible, is in absolute value at most the sum over targets of the KEM, key-schedule and full record-lift terms for the winning event, half of the same terms for the eligibility event, and half of `β_g`. The proof carries both events through the chain separately and uses, in the final record world, the fact that a test bit used only on hidden handles is independent of everything public, so that the winning probability there is exactly half the eligible probability. With every admitted test on a Server peer, `β_g` is dropped. Premises: those of CE-APP.

What is not claimed. These are the computational headlines with the public designation as the eligibility. The forms phrased with the ProVerif-shaped eligibility (a Server or Beacon whose accepted keys are the expected ones), with their gap and collision terms, are the next unit; so are the explicit query bills of the new reductions beyond the decapsulation count above. The later-quantum unit will cover only key transfer, fresh-message secrecy and left-or-right secrecy (CE-KT, CE-APP and CE-LOR): the later mode claims confidentiality only, with no later origin, unknown-key-share or authentication headline. Claims about a Beacon owner apply only to Beacons pinned to the experiment's Server identity and key ID: an owner is designated only when its pin is that pair, so Beacons pinned elsewhere are never targets. CE-LOR concerns the experiment's single test session. CE-KT is not root secrecy. No plaintext-linked unknown-key-share claim, no agreement on the publisher's pin or the mode-O plaintext of a b2s record, no claim on the registration payload `INITIAL_SECRET`, and no claim about raw-byte record re-encodings is made. The LOR advantage only counts eligible runs: runs whose tests are spread over several targets, or whose first test is not designated, are in neither event. All losses are explicit advantages of explicit reductions or explicit statistical terms; that they are small rests on the stated contracts (ML-KEM IND-CCA, HMAC-PRF, Extract-on-uniform, the random-oracle models of R1 and BLAKE2b, and the modified-nonce AEAD's IND$ and INT-CTXT security), as recorded in the trusted boundary.

## Common deployment experiment, LQ-F upstream unit D: the frozen targets of the later-quantum composition

In the exact later-quantum profile (LQ-F), after the run the adversary learns every honest Beacon secret of the profile, the Server's identity seed and every Server ephemeral, and may keep querying the public HMAC and hash functions. The classical chain of the common deployment experiment (the per-target KEM transfer, item 2's theorem relating its KEM worlds, CE-11b's ideal registration and the record lifts) has to be carried to that mode. Three upstream pieces are missing: item 2 for the program the LQ-F game compiles to, whose source records the Server ephemerals and can read the Server seed (U-L1); the later form of CE-11b's second compile lemma (U-L2); and CE-11b's later pieces. Unit D proves none of them. It fixes, before their proofs exist, the definitions and the statements they will be proved with, so that the pieces can be built in parallel against fixed names; it adds two modules and 20 small theorems, and no assumption or contract.

For item 2 (module `PqxdhDeploymentLaterServerItemTargets`), each new definition is the corresponding classical one with one change. Item 2's interface gains one request, the logged accept, which answers the Server's session and the ephemeral it generated; the client keeps the log beside the Beacon owners, appends each logged ephemeral, and answers the Server read by the ordinary reveal request of the Server's identity slot, returned together with the log. Everything after the challenge (the post-challenge phase, the prefix and the clients of item 2's stages) is the classical construction on the logged cut. The two-slot world `laterSlotGame`, the loss `slotLossL` and the coin bill `rootBillL` are the classical ones for these clients (the bill is literally the classical bill). Two target statements are written as propositions: the general one, the logged counterpart of item 2's slot theorem for every logged program within a source budget, and its instance at the compiled LQ-F program; a proved lemma shows that the general one implies the instance. At the LQ-F budget the first term of the loss is `(qAccept + qFinish + qHmac + qHmac₂)/2^256`, so the post-run HMAC queries are charged once, in the same guessing term. The premises are those of the classical theorem (the random-oracle split R1, the HMAC-SHA-512 PRF game, the Extract game on uniform inputs, `SourceFullCorrect` and the source budget). The caveat on R1 is sharper here: after the run the adversary knows the DH coordinates of both hidden entries exactly, so their unpredictability and independence rest on R1 alone, whereas classically those coordinates also contain DH values the adversary cannot compute (which item 2 never uses).

For the compile lemma (module `PqxdhDeploymentIdealLaterGame`), the later ideal game runs the LQ-F later game with CE-11b's ideal registration, the same drawn parameters and the real post phase; the target statement equates item 2's two-slot world of the compiled LQ-F program with the probability that this game ends with the event and the designation of the target, as CE-11b's second compile lemma does classically. The proved bridges show that the ideal registration answers the post-run HMAC queries exactly as the real Server does, so the later ideal game can be written in the form that the existing join with the later record world takes.

What this means: the unit is bookkeeping for the later-quantum lane, and nothing is claimed about LQ-F security until the target statements are proved. LQ-F claims confidentiality only; no authentication theorem is used on the compiled LQ-F program. If a later proof needs a different target, the frozen definitions are not edited: a new definition with a comparison lemma is added. A contamination scan finds no reference to the fixed-HKDF items item 2 excludes, and a closure check finds that the new clients reach, even indirectly, none of the definitions that are given the KEM candidate (a fixed list of candidate-carrying definitions); the candidate-freedom condition (item 2's T7 condition) is itself structural, because the candidate is drawn after the prefix and passed only to the hidden reads. The scan and the check are scratch metaprograms whose results the receipt records, not committed checks.

Review. An independent review in two parts (semantic and hygiene) found no error in the Lean statements or proofs and approved with nits. Its main finding concerned the reason given for the absence of a post-run budget in the compile-lemma target.
