After the run the adversary's coin, HMAC and hash queries read no stored field of any owner; this follows from the cost table of those commands, not from the lemma that was cited, which bounds only the Server read. The review also pointed out a consequence for the unit that will prove this target: without a post-run budget the post-run queries have no fixed cap, and in the later mode the compiled program reads every owner's identity at the end, so the classical lemmas that cut the run at the selected accept, which need a cap on every kind of query and no identity read, cannot be reused as they stand. The proof will bound each kind of query separately, as the existing later-mode lemmas do; should that fail, a second target that also takes the post-run budget can be added beside the frozen one at no cost to the final composition, which already carries that budget. The other findings concerned names and records: the new loss is the logged form of an existing classical loss, which is now named; the name "design-v2" denoted two different designs and is now qualified; one new lemma shares its short name with an older lemma of a different statement; a name opened but never used in one module is dropped; and the clean-tree checks of the reviewed commit and the scratch status of the two scans above are now recorded. The fix pass changed only docstrings and records; no Lean statement, definition or proof changed. A confirming review of the fix pass found every finding resolved and no statement weakened, and rebuilt both modules and the root import with results identical to the recorded ones; its two remarks concerned the effort estimate of the unit that will prove the compile-lemma target and a count in the records, and both are corrected. The commit that records the confirming review is the one integrated into the central branch (by fast-forward, after a merge of the central branch if it moved in between).

## Common deployment experiment, LQ-F upstream unit C: CE-11b's ideal-game chain, the slot invariance and the designation range in the later-quantum game

In the exact later-quantum profile (LQ-F), the experiment has a second phase: after the run, the adversary receives every honest Beacon secret of the profile, the Server's identity seed and every Server ephemeral, and may keep querying fresh coins, the public HMAC and the public hash. Unit D fixed the later ideal game, the counterpart of CE-11b's ideal game in which the Server's registration is replaced by its idealized form while the post-run phase stays real. Unit C carries three classical results to this later game. It adds four modules and 53 theorems, and no assumption or contract.

First, CE-11b's chain (modules `PqxdhDeploymentIdealLater` and `PqxdhDeploymentIdealLaterEnv`). Classically, a sequence of exact rewrites turns the ideal registration into a form that an environment of the record-lift model can run, and the record world with that environment then has the same law as the ideal game. Each rewrite changes hidden state or, in one step, the CTX cache inside the deployment state: it forgets an unused entry of that cache, represents the hidden 108-byte outputs differently, moves the hidden seeds, or draws a seed later. Unit C shows that every rewrite survives the post-run phase, for two reasons. The post-run phase runs only on the deployment state of the protocol (the registration state with its caches). The rewrites either leave that state alone, so the post-run phase is unaffected, or change only its CTX cache, and completing an entry of that cache before or after the post-run phase gives the same result. And what the adversary receives after the run (the Beacon secrets, the Server seed and the ephemerals) includes neither the hidden state nor the CTX cache. The unit proves this once, as a general transport lemma, and then repeats CE-11b's steps with it. It also extends the join with the record world to an environment that first draws the challenger's parameters, which classically needed a separate lemma. The result is that the later ideal game and the later record world with the ideal environment of the target have the same law of the post-run adversary's output, the run-phase ledger and the produced frames. They also agree on the Server's public data, the record view, the Beacon-side reveal and the Server's ephemeral log. The Server seed, which is revealed too, is not among these components, as in the existing public comparison for a general environment; the post-run adversary receives it in both worlds, and the equal laws of its output already account for it. In particular, the decision of the later second compile lemma, whose statement unit D fixed, has the same probability in both. Once unit B proves that lemma, this gives the later form of CE-11b's hand-off. One check concerns item 2: the environment's reveal function does not read the hidden-slot material or the shared HMAC cache, so item 2's idealized random-oracle slice is never handed over directly. The slice can still affect the reveal through the course of the run (for example, whether a Beacon's challenge finish succeeds decides whether its one-time secret is captured in the snapshot that the reveal reads), which item 2's argument allows.

Second, the slot invariance U-L4 (module `PqxdhDeploymentIdealLaterSlots`). CE-11b showed that, on the run phase, each record handle is tied to a hidden slot only as the ideal game intends, unless a public anomaly occurs in the transcript; CE-12 bounds that anomaly by a ciphertext-guessing term. In the later game the post-run phase could in principle install new kernels and so change which handles hold hidden slots. Unit C shows that it does not. In the ideal environment, the post-run queries become only coin draws and public hash requests, and these leave the record lift's control state, which contains the handle-to-slot map, unchanged. Hence the same statement holds at the end of the later game. The anomaly reads only the run-phase transcript, so it has the same probability in the later game as after the run, and the existing bounds apply unchanged.

Third, the designation range (module `PqxdhDeploymentLaterTargetRange`). A claim designates a target, a pair of an accept ordinal and a KEM creation index, through the public transcript of the run. Classically every designation lies below the accept and creation budgets. The question whether a designation lies out of range reads only the transcript, which the post-run phase does not change, so the existing comparison between the later game and the classical game moves the classical fact over. Every designation in the later game lies in range, and the last column of the headline's target domain is never designated. The two-sided KEM transfer of the later game therefore sums over the tight domain, with one IND-CCA advantage and one correctness error per target, the terms of the existing transfer, and none for the never-designated column.

What this means: unit C supplies the parts of the later-quantum composition that do not depend on item 2 over the logged source or on the later second compile lemma. The later-quantum headlines still need units A2 (item 2's theorem for the compiled later program) and B2 (the later compile lemma), and then their composition. The premises are those of the classical results: the approved codec read-back contracts, the run-phase budget, and, for the KEM transfer only, the existing functional-decapsulation contract of the KEM hop. LQ-F claims confidentiality only; no authentication theorem is used. A contamination scan finds that the unit uses no DH-keyed component. Its one reference outside item 2's allowed list is the functional-decapsulation contract of the KEM transfer, which item 2 itself must not use and the KEM transfer always has.

Review. An independent review in two parts (semantic and hygiene) found no error in the Lean statements or proofs and approved with nits. Its one minor finding concerned this entry: it said that the post-run adversary learns nothing from item 2's idealized slice through the reveal, which is more than the Lean fact shows. That fact says only that the reveal function does not read the slice; the slice can still influence the reveal through the course of the run, as item 2's argument allows, and the entry now says so. Two further findings also corrected this entry: one rewrite does change the deployment state, in its CTX cache, with which the post-run phase commutes and which the reveal does not see; and the public comparison covers the Beacon-side reveal and the Server's ephemeral log, not the Server seed. The other findings concerned names and records: three names opened but never used are dropped; the four parts of the unit are now called "unit C1" to "unit C4", to keep them apart from the hand-off obligations C1 to C7; the clean-tree checks of the reviewed commit are recorded; a remark on source hygiene now says that no declaration is opaque rather than that the word never occurs; and a broader contamination scan by the review, which gives the same result as the unit's, is recorded. The fix pass changed three `open` lines, one module docstring and the records; no Lean statement, definition or proof changed. A confirming review of the fix pass found every finding resolved, no statement weakened and no new defect, and rebuilt the four modules and the root import with results identical to the recorded ones; it required no change. The commit that records the confirming review is the one integrated into the central branch (by fast-forward, after a merge of the central branch if it moved in between).

## Common deployment experiment, LQ-F upstream unit A1: item 2's first stages over the logged later-quantum source

Item 2 relates the KEM-ideal world of a registration (the world in which the shared secret of the selected accept is replaced by a uniform value) to a world in which the hidden root material is drawn independently of everything the adversary sees. Its first stages remove analysis bookkeeping from that world, hide the KEM secret behind opaque handles, and then split the random-oracle table that derives roots, so that the reads that depend on the secret go to a separate table. In the exact later-quantum profile (LQ-F) the compiled program differs from the classical one in two ways: every Server accept also returns the ephemeral it generated, which is kept in a log, and after the run a Server read returns the Server's identity seed together with that log. Unit D fixed the definitions for item 2 over this logged program; unit A1 proves item 2's stages S0a, S0b, S1b and S1c for it (three modules, 49 small theorems, no new assumption); stage S1a, the random-oracle lemma G1, is generic and is reused unchanged.

What is proved. First, the logged KEM-ideal world equals a world in which no write-only record of the analysis is kept and the post-challenge router holds a fixed public value instead of the KEM secret; the secret is then an argument only of two private root computations. Second, that world is exactly the "shared" game of the random-oracle lemma G1: a prefix that stops at the selected accept and returns the table built so far, a secret drawn afterwards, and a client without the secret that reads the table either at full inputs or at hidden coordinates completed by the secret. Everything the logged program reveals, including the Server read and the log, is computed by that client from the answers it receives, which is the condition item 2's main theorem needs. Third, the shared game and G1's "split" game, in which the hidden entries come from an independent table and no secret is drawn, differ by at most the number of table-reading requests the source budget allows (raw accepts, Beacon finishes and public HMAC queries) divided by 2^256. In the later-quantum profile the compiled program stays within caps whose HMAC cap is the sum of the HMAC budgets of the run and of the phase after it, so that number includes the adversary's HMAC queries after the run, which are therefore paid for once, in the same term.

How. The logged program is written as the classical source client with one extra request, the logged accept, on top of the classical command layer with one extra handler. A general lifting lemma then turns each per-request fact of the classical proof into the same fact for the logged client, provided the two layers agree on the logged accept and on the Server read; the classical facts are reused as they are, and only the logged accept needed new arguments (it reads no bookkeeping, never asks for the challenge decapsulation, reads the table at most once and adds at most one table entry). Three cases arise for the selected accept. If it is reached, encapsulates and carries the challenger's key, the program continues after the cut, and each HMAC query after the run reads the table at most once, which the bound counts. If it is reached and encapsulates under another key, the branch stops at once with the answer false: nothing after the cut runs and nothing is read. If it is never reached, or rejects before encapsulation, the whole program, including everything after the run, finishes inside the prefix; nothing then depends on the secret, and the charge for that outcome is zero, within the same bound.

What this means. These are the steps of item 2 that the later-quantum composition needs before the root expansion and the key schedule (unit A2). The bound rests on modelling the 192-byte zero-key Extract slice as a random oracle (route R1), as classically, and the caveat recorded with unit D applies: after the run the adversary knows the Diffie-Hellman coordinates of both hidden entries, so their unpredictability and independence rest on that model alone. Only confidentiality is claimed for LQ-F; no authentication theorem is used on the compiled program, no component keyed by Diffie-Hellman secrecy is used, and no claim is made against quantum queries to the random oracle. A contamination scan, a closure check showing that the clients reach none of the definitions that are given the KEM secret (a fixed list of candidate-carrying definitions), and a scan for name clashes, all scratch metaprograms, found nothing; the condition itself is structural, because the secret is drawn after the prefix and passed only to the hidden reads.

Review. An independent review in two parts (semantic and hygiene) found no error in the Lean statements or proofs and approved with nits. The semantic part also proved, in a scratch file, that at the compiled later-quantum program the bound is the accept, finish and HMAC budgets over 2^256, with the HMAC budget after the run counted once and no further premise. Its findings concerned the precision of the explanations: the account of the HMAC queries after the run left out the case in which the selected accept carries a key other than the challenger's (the branch then stops and runs nothing after the cut), and called those queries table reads when each makes at most one; the statement that they are paid for once cited only the lemma that adds up the caps, not the lemma showing that the compiled program stays within them; this entry overstated what the closure check shows (as did unit D's entry, whose wording is corrected the same way) and called the lifted stages "the first four"; and one module description said that no per-request proof is repeated, although the logged accept's facts are re-proved. The hygiene part found thirteen names opened but never used, which are dropped, a sentence that said "imported" where "referenced" is meant, two instances missing from the receipt's lists and a misattributed section number. The fix pass changed only descriptions, the unused names and records; no Lean statement, definition or proof changed. A confirming review of the fix pass found every finding resolved and no statement weakened, and rebuilt the three modules and the root import with results identical to the recorded ones; its two remarks concerned the wording of one sentence of unit D's entry and the record of what the hygiene review's own reference scan showed, and both are corrected. The commit that records the confirming review is the one integrated into the central branch (by fast-forward, after a merge of the central branch if it moved in between).

## Common deployment experiment, CE-12 P2: symbolic eligibility, the gap and collision terms, and the symbolic corollaries

The classical headlines of CE-12 P1 measure events on handles that the experiment's public designation assigns to a target. The ProVerif models state their conclusions for a different kind of party: a Server peer that accepted the registration of an honest Beacon, and a Beacon that registered with the experiment's Server. This stage connects the two notions. It proves that the conclusions also hold on the ProVerif-shaped parties, at the cost of a small number of extra terms. Six new modules hold 120 checked theorems. Every theorem depends only on Lean's standard axioms, and no new assumption or contract is used. An independent review in three parts (semantic, composition, hygiene) found no error in the composition of the bounds; its findings (two missing Server-side forms, an incomplete injective event, an incorrect explanation of why one term stays open, and an owner notice that named only one of two open terms) are fixed. A confirming review of the fixes found every finding resolved; its two remaining remarks concerned the wording of the accompanying implementation guide (how many of the bills to be collected are already proved, and the phrasing of the step for a root drawn before the hidden key) and are taken. The stage was not yet integrated when this explanation was written. Two of the extra terms are not yet bounded by closed advantages, as explained below; the owner is to be told before publication.

Symbolic eligibility. A Server peer is symbolically eligible when the session that built it accepted a Phase 1 candidate that the source verification accepts with the identity key of an honest Beacon, and that Beacon never had a bundle request rejected in its fresh state. An owner (a Beacon) is symbolically eligible when it completed its registration, was created pinned to the experiment's Server identity and protected key ID, and never had a bundle request rejected in its fresh state. These conditions read the Beacons' real identity keys and the constructed Server, so they are not public functions of the transcript. They appear on the left-hand sides of the bounds below; the intermediate forms that list events instead of numbers also show them on the right-hand side, inside the two gap events, which are built from them.

The two gaps. A symbolically eligible handle can fail to be designated. For a Server peer, this means that an accepted candidate carries an honest Beacon's identity key with a key tuple other than the one that Beacon published, which is the published-tuple forgery of CE-A2pub. Its probability is at most `ε_A2pub`, a sum of joint-use signature-forgery advantages. For an owner, either no session matched it before its acceptance with its pin (the CE-A1 failure, at most `ε_A1`, the Server-authentication bound of CE-A1), or a session matched it but carried a different KEM ciphertext than the one the Beacon decapsulated (the "ciphertext gap"). Two facts read from the Rust code enter these proofs. A Beacon's registration finish succeeds only in the InitSent state, so its first successful finish is the one that established it; this is proved as a new invariant of the experiment. Session handles are positional.

The ciphertext gap stays an explicit term. The design planned to close the ciphertext gap with a statistical bound in the ideal world (`ctgap_world`), behind a half-day spike with a stop rule. The spike stated the bound and estimated the proof at three to six days, above the rule, so the rule fired. The bound itself is sound. Its core step says that each root the experiment draws yields the hidden key the argument tracks with probability at most `2^-256`; this holds by averaging over the uniform distribution of that key, because the Beacon's sequence-one key is a fixed function of the root alone (in the Rust code the initial chain derivation takes only the root), whether the root is drawn before or after the key, even though the key is not independent of what the adversary sees (it seals the Server's sequence-one record in the build response). What is missing is Lean machinery: a lemma for this averaged union bound over the ideal world's dynamically filled root table, and several invariants of the ideal environment. No random-oracle model and no new idealization is needed. (The first version of this entry said the opposite; the review corrected it.) Every Beacon-side bound therefore carries the probability of the public ciphertext-gap event (`ctGapTerm`) explicitly. This is weaker than the planned Beacon-side corollary, because the term is a probability in the real experiment rather than a closed advantage. (Added by CE-12 D-ct: the ciphertext-gap term is now bounded by a closed term made of attacker advantages and a statistical term, and every headline that carried it is restated with that term in its place; see the entry "Common deployment experiment, CE-12 D-ct: the ciphertext-gap term closed". It was not yet integrated when this note was written; its birthday term was reported to the owner on 2026-10-10 and accepted under the owner's 2026-10-07 delegation of proof-internal choices.)

The collision terms. Two further events can make the designation move between symbolically eligible handles. The first is an identity collision, two Beacons with the same identity public key. Its probability is at most `ε_inj`, a sum of forgery advantages of a fixed reduction that signs with the colliding seed. The second is a ciphertext collision, two sessions that carry the same KEM ciphertext to the same Beacon's published KEM key. The KEM-level half of its bound is proved: two independent encapsulations to a fresh key collide with probability at most the IND-CCA advantage of a fixed attacker, which encapsulates once more and compares, plus twice the ML-KEM correctness error, plus `2^-256`. No minimum-entropy property of ML-KEM is assumed. The game-level step that would turn the collision probability in the experiment into that quantity is not proved, so the ciphertext-collision probability (`ctCollTerm`) also stays explicit, again a probability in the real experiment rather than a closed advantage. The owner is to be told about both explicit terms.

The symbolic corollaries, Server side. For records the Server accepted (b2s), the probability that the Server accepts, on a symbolically eligible peer, a decoded frame that no Beacon publishing the accepted identity had sent before is at most the CE-OR b2s bound plus `ε_A2pub`. Fresh-message secrecy of a message sent on a symbolically eligible Server peer costs the Server-side CE-APP bound plus `ε_A2pub`, and key transfer for a claim on a symbolically eligible Server peer costs the one-sided CE-KT bound plus `ε_A2pub`, without CE-A1's premises. None of the Server-side forms carries `ε_A1` or either explicit term.

The symbolic corollaries, Beacon side. For records a Beacon accepted (s2b, record positions from 2), the probability that a symbolically eligible Beacon accepts a decoded frame that no Server peer built for its identity had sent before is at most the CE-OR s2b bound plus `ε_A1`, the ciphertext-gap term and the ciphertext-collision term. The sender form of unknown-key share has the same structure: an eligible Beacon's record accepted on a handle that is not one of its symbolic partners. Fresh-message secrecy of a message sent on a symbolically eligible Beacon costs the CE-APP bound plus `ε_A1` and the ciphertext-gap term, and so does key transfer for a claim on a symbolically eligible Beacon (with the one-sided CE-KT bound). For a message or claim whose side is not fixed in advance, the forms add `ε_A2pub`, `ε_A1` and the ciphertext-gap term. Each corollary is a union bound: on every run, the symbolic event is the classical event or one of the gap and collision events.

Injectivity. ProVerif's injective conclusions add that no two accepts are matched to one send. The theorems bound named failure modes of injectivity; that these are all the failure modes is argued in prose, not proved. For records the Server accepted, the modes are a registration replayed under one Beacon's identity (two Server peers accepting one Beacon's send both accepted that Beacon's identity) and a Server peer accepting a sequence number twice, which never happens. The Server-side injective form costs no more than the plain one (one `ε_A2pub`, because the replay is again a published-tuple forgery). For records a Beacon accepted, the modes are two Beacons matched to one session, two Beacons with the same identity key (two Beacons accepting one Server peer's send: key IDs are unique in the Rust Server, so that peer is one session, whose accepted identity is both Beacons'), and a Beacon accepting a sequence number twice. The Beacon-side form costs `ε_A1` plus the identity-collision term `ε_inj`, together with the two explicit terms; including the identity collision costs nothing extra, because a shared match is already an identity collision.

Left-or-right secrecy. The symbolic form is restricted to runs where no bundle request was rejected in a fresh state, the condition the owner approved for this purpose. A run is symbolically eligible when a test session exists and every admitted test query was sent on a symbolically eligible handle. The classical form uses the same restriction as a public filter. Every classically eligible run is symbolically eligible. A run that is symbolically but not classically eligible has an undesignated test handle (a gap) or a designation that moved after a test was admitted. Admitted tests share the first test's session at admission, and a designation moves only when a Beacon with a smaller index later publishes the same identity (an identity collision) or a smaller session later becomes linked to the same Beacon (a ciphertext collision). Since the two eligibility events are nested, the two advantages differ by at most half the probability of the difference: at most half of the sum of `ε_A2pub`, `ε_A1`, `ε_inj` and the two explicit terms. With the classical bound this gives the symbolic left-or-right bound. When every admitted test is on a Server peer (the Server-to-Beacon secrecy rows), the difference can only be a Server-side gap or an identity collision, so the two advantages differ by at most half of `ε_A2pub + ε_inj`, with no explicit term, and the classical Server-side bound has no anomaly term.

Premises. Every statement holds for every adversary within its budget, in the experiment with a generated Server seed, under the approved Phase 1 and Phase 2 read-back contracts. The bounds with `ε_A2pub` add the condition that the signature verification rejects short inputs. The bounds with `ε_A1` add CE-A1's premises: the frame read-back and writer laws, the two X25519 laws, full correctness of the source key schedule, the verification adapter and the KEM cost bound. The corollaries add the premises of the classical headline they extend. The collision bound needs functional decapsulation.

Bills. The new encapsulate-and-compare attacker makes only the queries of one encapsulation after the challenge and no query before it. The record-lift reductions behind the integrity and secrecy terms of the classical headlines are stated with their query bills at each target's resource input.

What is not claimed. There is no closed bound for the ciphertext-gap and ciphertext-collision terms; the bounds that contain them are therefore not yet bounds by advantages alone. The uniform-query bill of the first phase of the anomaly attacker, whose IND-CCA advantage enters every bound with the anomaly term, is not proved, and neither is the collection of all bills into one statement; publication of the bounds with the anomaly term waits for it, and publication of the bounds with the ciphertext-collision term waits for its game-level step. There is no agreement of the b2s publisher pin or of the full-reply-mode (mode O) plaintext, which stay symbolic-only. Beacon-side statements cover only Beacons pinned to the experiment's Server identity and protected key ID. The origin events cover raw receives only, and there is no unknown-key-share form linked to plaintexts. The later-quantum versions are a later unit. The remaining work and its estimates are listed in the guide's section "CE-12 P2: open points and the rest of P2". (Added by the CE-12 P2b review fix pass: P2b step 1 proves the anomaly attacker's bill and the collection of all bills, step 2 the closed ciphertext-collision bound and the bounds restated with it, and step 3 the agreement fact in the ideal record world, without its lift to the deployment experiment; see the three CE-12 P2b entries below. The ciphertext-gap term stays explicit.) (Added by CE-12 D-ct: the ciphertext-gap term is now bounded by a closed term made of attacker advantages and a statistical term, and every headline that carried it is restated with that term in its place; see the entry "Common deployment experiment, CE-12 D-ct: the ciphertext-gap term closed". It was not yet integrated when this note was written; its birthday term was reported to the owner on 2026-10-10 and accepted under the owner's 2026-10-07 delegation of proof-internal choices.)

## Common deployment experiment, LQ-F upstream unit A2: item 2's confidentiality stages over the logged later-quantum source and the slot theorem

Unit A1 carried item 2's first stages to the logged program of the exact later-quantum profile (LQ-F), in which every Server accept also returns the ephemeral it generated (kept in a log) and, after the run, a Server read returns the Server's identity seed with that log. It ended with a world in which the hidden root material comes from an independent random-oracle table. Unit A2 proves the remaining stages of item 2 that LQ-F needs for this program (S2, T, S3b, S7 with T7, and the S8 bills; not T8 or the key-first stage S6) and so the theorem that unit D fixed in advance (U-L1): the KEM-ideal world of the compiled LQ-F program and item 2's two-slot world, in which the first two hidden 108-byte key-schedule outputs are drawn uniformly and kept in two slots, differ by at most the frozen loss. It adds six modules and 87 small theorems, and no assumption or contract.

What is proved. First, the root expansion: after unit A1, every hidden root is the HMAC-SHA-512 expansion of a uniform hidden block, so it can be replaced by a uniform root at the cost of one HMAC pseudorandomness advantage per root that the program actually derives. Second, that number is at most two, for every logged program and without any premise: one root for the Server's resumption of the selected accept, and at most one for a Beacon finish carrying the challenge marker. The reason is the one of the classical argument: a Beacon finishes only once and every Beacon generates its own ML-KEM key pair, so at most one Beacon can hold the selected key, and none before the key router has handed it out. The logged accept and the Server read change nothing here: the accept derives no hidden root and creates no Beacon, and the Server read is an ordinary reveal of the Server's identity slot. Third, the first hidden root is read only through its 108-byte key-schedule output, so the uniform-root world is the key-schedule game on a distinguisher built from the program. Fourth, a hybrid replaces the first and then the second hidden output by uniform bytes, at the cost of four key-schedule advantages each; with only two hidden reads, the result is exactly the two-slot world. Adding the three parts, with unit A1's guessing term, gives the frozen loss term by term. At the compiled LQ-F program the guessing term is the accept, finish and HMAC budgets over 2^256, where the HMAC budget is the sum of the budgets of the run and of the phase after it, so the adversary's HMAC queries after the run are paid for once, in that term. Theorem T7 for the logged program (the corresponding bound, with the four key-schedule advantages of the first hidden output only, against the world in which only that output is uniform) is proved on the way.

The bills. The reductions behind the advantages (two pseudorandomness reductions and four key-schedule reductions per hidden output) run the whole logged program, including the phase after the run, so their resource bounds grow with the post-run budget but their simulation stays exact. The unit bounds every reduction's queries by bills built from the frozen coin bill of unit D (the classical bill at the logged budget) plus fixed constants; the post-run coins, HMAC queries and hash queries enter through that budget, and the Server read costs nothing. The bounds take a cap on the number of Server reads only because the counting method needs a cap for every kind of request; the read weighs nothing, so the cap does not appear in any bill, and the compiled program reads the Server at most once.

What this means. With unit A1, item 2's confidentiality transfer (T7 and S7 with their bills) now holds for the program that the later-quantum game compiles to, so the later-quantum headlines need only the later form of the second compile lemma (unit B) and their composition. Item 2's theorem T8 (the composite of the authentication theorem T5 with T7, in its `authenticated_*` forms) and the key-first stage S6 are deliberately not carried to this program, because the later mode claims confidentiality only and nothing uses the key-first form there. The premises are exactly those of the classical theorem: the random-oracle model of the 192-byte zero-key Extract slice (route R1), the HMAC-SHA-512 pseudorandomness game, the Extract game on uniform inputs, the functional contract `SourceFullCorrect` of the key-derivation source, and the source budget. The caveat recorded with unit D applies in full: after the run the adversary knows the Diffie-Hellman coordinates of both hidden entries exactly, so their unpredictability and independence rest on the R1 model alone, whereas classically those coordinates also contain values the adversary cannot compute (which item 2 never uses). Only confidentiality is claimed for LQ-F; no authentication theorem is used on the compiled program, no component keyed by Diffie-Hellman secrecy is used, and no claim is made against quantum queries to the random oracle. A contamination scan, a closure check showing that the new definitions reach none of the definitions that are given the KEM secret (a fixed list of candidate-carrying definitions), and a scan for name clashes, all scratch metaprograms whose results the receipt records, found nothing. The candidate-freedom condition (item 2's T7 condition) is itself structural, because the secret is drawn after the prefix and passed only to the hidden reads.

Review. An independent review in two parts (semantic and hygiene) found no error in the Lean statements or proofs and approved with nits. The semantic part checked that the main statements are exact logged counterparts of the classical ones with the classical premises and that the two proved theorems have exactly the frozen statements of unit D as their types. A scratch scan of the complete proof terms showed that every component of item 2's sensitive modules that the new proofs reach is also reached by the classical proof, apart from six data definitions of the signature module (fields of a candidate record and a signature splitter) reached through the compiled program's ledger; no game or advantage keyed by Diffie-Hellman secrecy, no authentication theorem (T5) and no key-transfer theorem (T8) is reached, so the unit adds no idealization beyond R1 and no hidden assumption. A scratch proof confirmed that at the compiled later-quantum program the guessing term is the accept, finish and HMAC budgets over 2^256, with the HMAC budget after the run counted once. Its findings concerned this entry's precision: it said that the unit proves "the rest of item 2" and that "item 2 now holds", although only the confidentiality stages are carried over; it called the bound of T7 for the logged program "the same bound", although that bound has the key-schedule advantages of the first hidden output only; it said that the compiled program reads the Server once, where the Lean fact is at most once, and that every reduction's queries are bounded by the frozen coin bill, where the bills add fixed constants to it; and its closure-check sentence lacked the qualification that the entries of units D and A1 carry. The other findings, from both parts, concerned two theorems without a description, which now have one, and imprecise records: a relation and the congruence lemmas Lean generates were misnamed in the guide, the commit recording the clean-tree checks was not listed, the receipt said that the central branch did not move during the unit although it moved before the documentation commit, and the designs the guides cite existed only in scratch; both designs are now committed as snapshots. The fix pass changed two descriptions in Lean and the records; no Lean statement, definition or proof changed. A confirming review of the fix pass found every finding resolved and no statement weakened, and compiled the changed module again without error or warning; its remarks concerned a record of the planned merge with the central branch, which named two files as conflicting that merge without a conflict, the two different names this entry gave theorem T8, and this entry's title, which still spoke of item 2's remaining stages, and all are corrected. The central branch moved after the unit was built, so it is merged into the commit that records the confirming review, the checks are repeated on that merge, and the central branch is fast-forwarded to it.

## Production boundary PB-01: Server birth and Beacon creation in source order

`PqxdhBoundaryBirth` writes down the order in which the Rust constructors work and proves that the common deployment experiment's two constructors follow it exactly. The Server is born as in `Server::try_new` without a supplied seed: runtime initialization first, and only if it succeeds one generated identity seed; a failed initialization keeps whatever it did to the runtime and draws nothing. A Beacon is created as in `Beacon::try_new` after the experiment's approved deviation D1 (no second runtime initialization): the pinned Server identity key must have exactly 32 bytes, otherwise nothing happens; then the identity seed, the prekey and the ML-KEM key pair are drawn in that order and the new Beacon is added at the next handle, with every other part of the experiment's state unchanged. Both equalities hold for every state and survive every continuation, so the later whole-program join can use them directly. Two bill statements carry the existing query counts over: the Server birth costs the declared initialization bill plus 32 uniform bytes, and a creation costs two 32-byte draws plus the declared ML-KEM bill (nothing for a rejected pin). ## Common deployment experiment, LQ-F upstream unit B: the later second compile lemma

The second compile lemma of the classical composition (CE-11b) says that item 2's view of the compiled deployment program and the ideal game of the common deployment experiment agree: the probability that item 2's decision accepts in its two-slot world equals the probability that the event happens with the designated target in the ideal game, in which the Server's registration is replaced by its idealized form. In the exact later-quantum profile (LQ-F), the experiment continues after the run: the adversary receives every honest Beacon secret, the Server's identity seed and every Server ephemeral, and may keep querying fresh coins, the public HMAC and the public hash. The compiled program grows accordingly: every Server accept also records the ephemeral it generated in a log, and after the run the program reads every owner's fields, reads the Server's seed with the log, and runs the post-run adversary. Unit D fixed the statement of the later second compile lemma for this program; unit B proves it exactly as fixed (eight modules, 145 small theorems, no new assumption, contract or budget).

What is proved. Under the approved codec read-back contracts and the run-phase budget, and for every post-run adversary, the probability that item 2's decision accepts in its two-slot world of the compiled later-quantum program equals the probability that the later ideal game ends with the later-quantum event and the designation of the target. No budget for the post-run adversary is needed: after the run, the compiled program makes no Server accept, creates no owner and reads no KEM key, whatever the post-run adversary does.

How. The proof follows the classical one step by step. First, both sides draw the challenger's parameters (the selected KEM key pair, the other key pairs and the challenge ciphertext) up front. Second, both sides are cut at the selected Server accept: before it, item 2's world and the ideal game run the same program on the same state, so they can be compared through one common prefix; the ideal game also keeps two pieces of bookkeeping that the post-run phase reads, the snapshot of the Beacon secrets taken at each finish and the Server's ephemeral log, and the comparison carries them along. Third, every branch in which the selected accept is never reached, fails, or carries a key other than the challenger's accepts nothing on either side. Fourth, in the remaining, active branch, both sides are written as functions of one execution: the rest of the compiled program run by a single source that answers the hidden steps as the ideal game does and every other request as the real source does. Item 2's layers simulate that source request by request; the classical steps are reused as they are, and the new requests are handled separately: an accept after the selected one (which logs its ephemeral the same way on both sides), the reads of the owners' identity seeds after the run (which go to the identity pool, where the seeds are stored), and the read of the Server's seed. On the other side, the ideal game's run is the image of the same execution under the merge of the compiled program's local copies into the shared state, with the snapshot and the log carried exactly; after the run, the reads and the post-run phase of the compiled program give the same values as the ideal game's post-run phase, which reads the merged state, the snapshot and the log. Finally, the two decisions read the same output, ledger and produced frames, and whether the selected accept returned a session. Unit D's entry expected that this proof would bound each kind of query separately, because the classical lemmas that cut the run at the selected accept need a cap on every kind of query and no budget is given for the post-run adversary. The proof does not do that: it applies those lemmas, in their logged form, only to the run phase of the compiled program, whose queries the run-phase budget caps in every kind, and what follows the run phase needs no cap, because where the selected accept is never reached it is discarded on both sides, and otherwise it only has to read no KEM key and create no owner.

What this means. With unit C's result that the later ideal game and the later record world with the ideal environment of the target have the same law on what the decision reads (the post-run output, the run-phase ledger and the produced frames), this lemma completes the later form of the classical hand-off between item 2 and the record lift; the composition is a short step for the later-quantum headlines (P3). The lemma is an equality of probabilities: it charges nothing and makes no security claim by itself. Its premises are those of the classical lemma, the approved codec read-back contracts and the run-phase budget. LQ-F claims confidentiality only; no authentication theorem is used on the compiled program, and a contamination scan finds that the unit uses no component keyed by Diffie-Hellman secrecy.

Review. An independent review in two parts (semantic and hygiene) found no error in the Lean statements or proofs and approved with nits. The semantic part checked that the main theorem is exactly the frozen statement with no hidden premise, that every definition and theorem of the eight modules rests only on the three standard axioms of Lean's logic, and, in a scratch file, that the composition with unit C's result needs no new proof. Its main finding was that unit D's prediction of how this proof would treat the query budget, recorded in unit D's guide and analysis entry and in the description of the frozen statement, had become wrong without the documents saying so; the guide now records the route taken and closes unit D's open point, this entry corrects unit D's, and the frozen description is left unedited. The other findings concerned records and wording: the documents named an older state of the central branch than the one at the time; two lists of where the premises are used were incomplete; the sentence on unit C's result did not say on which observations the two worlds agree; three places said that every theorem uses exactly the three standard axioms, although one uses only two of them; the account of the contamination scan was narrower than the scans that support the claim; one theorem had no description; twenty-eight opened names were never used (the fix pass drops them and ten more found by a scan that respects the scope of each opening); and the single review cycle for both halves of the unit was not recorded as a deviation from the design. The fix pass changed only descriptions, the unused names and records; no Lean statement, definition or proof changed, and the rebuilt modules and the inventory check pass. A confirming review of the fix pass found every finding resolved and no statement weakened, and rebuilt the eight modules without error or warning into files identical to the fix pass's; its remarks concerned the lists of the direct references into modules named after Diffie-Hellman or key derivation, which left out the description of the HMAC oracle and some byte types (one list also the type of the ephemeral scalar, and a scan made for this record found one more byte type), and the wording of one record of the closure comparison, and both are corrected. The central branch moved after the unit was built, so it is merged into the commit that records the confirming review, the checks are repeated on that merge, and the central branch is fast-forwarded to it.

## Production boundary PB-D: one source step for every deployment command

`PqxdhBoundaryDeploymentStep` puts the published per-command boundary results together into one step of the whole deployment: for each command the adversary can issue, it runs the source program that the earlier boundary modules proved equal to that command (Beacon creation, the Phase 1 bundle over the extracted unsigned builder, the raw acceptance, the extracted Server build with its pending token, the Beacon's registration finish, the two record sends and the two raw record receives), and leaves coins, the public HMAC and the BLAKE2b oracle as the experiment's own model oracles. These commands are the experiment's approved interface, not every Rust entry point: its approved deviations D1-D5 (listed in the survey's deviation table and to be collected in the final ledger) stay the model's scope; in particular Beacon creation is `Beacon::try_new` without its second runtime initialization (D1), failures of the native key generators are not modeled, and the build payload is the adversary's choice (D4). It then proves, for every command and every complete state of the experiment, that this step is exactly the common deployment experiment's own command handler, with the same reply and the same complete state afterwards. Each command's case is one citation of an equality that was already published for every state, so no extra invariant, success assumption or new contract is needed, and the `checks` parameter stays free. The equality holds at the production frame codec, the one whose frame reader is the source's complete-frame decoder over the abstract message reader and whose Server route reads the same frame header, because that is where the published raw-receive and finish results live; three small lemmas record what this means for item 8's final composition: the route agrees with the decoder on every successful decode (already proved), and the Phase 1 and Phase 2 read-back laws are the same at the production codec as at the original one. The frame read-back and read-writable laws stay codec contracts that item 8 carries. Whether a record or finish command could return a Rust failure is also settled for the source model: in the source model, every outcome is a normal return (a fact about the extracted local steps and the reviewed adapter transcriptions, not a panic-freedom result for the Rust code). All fifteen statements have exact axiom guards and both contamination scans with their failing controls pass. Two independent fresh-context reviews approved the module with minor documentation corrections, which are applied: the commands' scope under the experiment's deviations is stated, a remark on which cited results hold for every codec is corrected, and the wording above now says that the normal-return result and the decoder are facts about the source model. A confirming review found them applied. See `doc/impl/production-boundary-deployment-step.md` and `doc/impl/proof-receipts/production-boundary-deployment-step.json`.

## Production boundary PB-D: the whole classical deployment game runs the source programs

`PqxdhBoundaryDeployment` lifts the per-command step to the whole common deployment experiment. Its source game first creates the Server in source order (runtime initialization, then one generated identity seed) and then lets the adversary, wrapped in the experiment's own secrecy layer for the left-or-right tests and fresh messages, issue its commands one after another, each answered by the source program of that command (a Rust failure would stop the run; the theorems below show that none occurs in the source model). As in the step module, the commands are the experiment's approved interface under its deviations D1-D5, not every Rust entry point; for example, Beacon creation omits Rust's second runtime initialization and failures of the key generators are not modeled. The main theorem says that this source game is exactly the published common deployment experiment at the production frame codec: the same created Server, the same adversary output, the same secrecy ledger, the same complete final state with every counter and every produced record, and the same runtime, for every identity index, every setting of the `checks` parameter, both observation modes and every adversary. The only difference is bookkeeping: the source side reports the adversary output and the ledger inside a Rust success value, which a fixed map adds and a fixed inverse removes. Consequences proved for item 8: the index-0 instance that the headline theorems use, that the source game never returns a Rust failure, that any continuation sees the same value, and that every observation and every event has the same distribution or probability on both sides, both in the evaluation-measure form that the headline theorems use and in the older probability notation that the library is retiring, so the CE-12 headline bounds can be read on the source game without depending on that notation. One scan exception is recorded: like the experiment itself, the source game hands the setup's functional record cryptography to the experiment's secrecy layer, which the contamination scan would otherwise flag; the exception is limited to the record-cryptography parameter of that secrecy layer in this module, and the contamination scan now checks this on every run (64 occurrences today, all that parameter), so any other use would fail the scan. All nine statements have exact axiom guards and both contamination scans with their failing controls pass. The later-quantum game is the next increment. Two independent fresh-context reviews approved the module with minor corrections, which are applied: besides the scope sentence and the per-run scan check above, a counting slip in the guide is fixed and the evaluation-measure transfer is new. A confirming review found them applied; its one remark, that the guide should also name the evaluation-measure transfer as a way to read the headline bounds on the source game, is addressed. See `doc/impl/production-boundary-deployment.md` and `doc/impl/proof-receipts/production-boundary-deployment.json`.

## Production boundary PB-D: the later-quantum deployment game runs the source programs

`PqxdhBoundaryDeploymentLater` does for the later-quantum version of the common deployment experiment what the previous module did for the classical one. In that version the experiment keeps two extra pieces of bookkeeping during the run, which exist only so that secrets can be handed to a second adversary afterwards: a snapshot of a Beacon's prekey and one-time secrets taken just before each registration finish, and a private log with one entry per registration accept, holding the Server ephemeral secret when one was generated. The source game creates the Server in source order and answers each command of the first adversary with the source program of that command: a registration finish first records the snapshot from the state before the command and then runs the source finish, a registration accept runs the source acceptance that also writes the log entry (the logged acceptance boundary of increment A), and every other command runs the classical source step and leaves both pieces of bookkeeping alone. As in the classical module, the commands are the experiment's approved interface under its deviations D1-D5, not every Rust entry point, so the snapshot and the reveal are complete relative to that command set; for example, Rust's public Beacon helpers `delete_onetime_keypair` and `delete_pq_keypair`, which can abort a Beacon that is waiting for its registration finish and drop its secrets without a finish (so no snapshot is taken), are omitted under D3. If the run succeeds, the game hands the second adversary the run's output together with the modeled reveal (each created Beacon's identity seed and current or snapshotted secrets, the Server's identity seed and the ephemeral log) and lets it query fresh coins, the public HMAC and the hash oracle on the final state. The main theorem says that this source game is exactly the published later-quantum game at the production frame codec: the same created Server, the same output of the second adversary, the same secrecy ledger, the same snapshot, the same complete final state, the same ephemeral log and the same runtime, for every identity index, every setting of the `checks` parameter, both observation modes and every pair of adversaries; nothing that the reveal could depend on is dropped. As before, the only difference is bookkeeping (the output and the ledger sit inside a Rust success value), and the same consequences are proved for item 8: the index-0 instance, that the source game never returns a Rust failure in the source model, that any continuation sees the same value, and that every observation and every event has the same distribution or probability on both sides. The proof needs no new assumption: it reuses the classical per-command step, the logged acceptance boundary and two lemmas of the published later-quantum game, all of which hold for every state. The reveal and the second phase are the experiment's approved model of a later disclosure, not a claim about erasing memory, and the queries after the run are classical. Where the Rust code actually generates or holds each revealed secret (the Server seed at birth, the Beacon keys at creation, the one-time secret of a bundle, the snapshot point (the state that the Beacon's registration finish reads on entry, before it drops both secrets), the Server ephemeral, and the two approved exceptions) stays a reviewed reading of the source, with the proposed pinning check not implemented. The same scan exception as for the classical game is recorded and limited to the one place where the source game hands the setup's record cryptography to the experiment's secrecy layer (29 occurrences today, all that parameter, checked on every scan run). All seventeen statements have exact axiom guards and both contamination scans with their failing controls pass. Two independent fresh-context reviews approved the module with small documentation remarks, which are applied without any change to the Lean code: this paragraph now states the scope of the commands, that the log holds one entry per accept and that the normal-return result is a fact about the source model, and the guide records that the post phase reaches the experiment's native handler only for its HMAC and hash commands (the run phase reaches no handler of the experiment), the exact Rust point of the finish snapshot and the reviewers' audit of the import closure. A confirming review found them applied; its one remark, that the guide named the wrong arms of the experiment's native handler as the route to the native acceptance and build, is corrected. See `doc/impl/production-boundary-deployment-later.md` and `doc/impl/proof-receipts/production-boundary-deployment-later.json`.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-12 P3: the later-quantum headline theorems

This stage proves the later-quantum headline theorems of the common deployment experiment. In the later-quantum game (LQ-F) the adversary first runs the whole deployment as in the classical experiment; afterwards it learns every honest Beacon secret of the profile, the Server's identity seed and every Server ephemeral, and a second, post-run adversary keeps querying the public coin, HMAC and hash functions and produces the final output. The later mode claims confidentiality only: the stage proves key transfer, fresh-message secrecy and left-or-right secrecy of the test session (CE-KT-L, CE-APP-L, CE-LOR-L) with their symbolic-eligibility forms and bills, and nothing about origin, binding or authentication after the reveal. Seven new modules hold 91 checked theorems; every theorem depends only on Lean's standard axioms, and no new assumption or contract is used. They compose the finished later-quantum upstream (the per-target KEM transfer for the later game, item 2 over the logged source, the later second compile lemma, CE-11b's later pieces and the record lift's later forms) with the classical headlines' events and containments. Independent reviews checked the statements against the design, re-derived the composition hop by hop from the cited statements, and checked the guards, the inventory and the import and reference scans. They found no defect in the Lean statements; their findings concerned the precision of this explanation and of the stage's records (the premises of the symbolic forms, the scope caveats of the classical headlines, where the post budget enters, the bills, and the description of the identity-collision term), and are fixed; in the Lean modules only docstrings changed. A confirming review found every finding resolved and the published modules untouched; its one remark, that the sentence below on the scan of direct references claimed more than the scan checked (it looks for the provenance theorem and item 2's authenticated key-transfer theorems, while the Server-authentication bound CE-A1 is cited, through CE-12 P2's bounds), is taken. The stage was not yet integrated when this explanation was written.

How the claims are measured. The events read the post adversary's output, the run's ledger (transcript, test session, fresh messages) and the produced frames. As in the classical headlines, these are the experiment's own records, not a public view: the transcript includes replies that the adversary does not see in the private-reply mode, and the produced frames include frames of failed writes that were never published. A claim names a record handle; its target `g` is the Server session and Beacon KEM key that the handle's public designation on the run's transcript names, exactly as in the classical headlines. Every bound is a sum over all targets with coefficient one. The reductions behind the loss terms run the later game, including the post adversary, and evaluate the event and the claim (for CE-LOR-L also the filter and the guess); the claim and the guess are read from the post adversary's output. The advantage terms are therefore small under the contracts only when these functions are efficiently computable and the post adversary is efficient. The run-phase adversary must respect the experiment's budget, and the post adversary must respect a separate post budget on every input (numbers of post coin, HMAC and hash queries). The post budget enters the bounds in three places: the random-oracle guessing term of the key-schedule term, which counts the post HMAC queries once; the query bills of the KEM, PRF and key-schedule reductions, which are evaluated at caps that include the post coin, HMAC and hash queries; and the record layer, whose integrity loss contains a hash term computed from a hash bill that includes the post phase's hash work, and whose reductions' bills include the post budget.

CE-KT-L (key transfer). For any event and claim, the probability that the later game ends with the event and the claim designating `g` differs from the probability of the same in the later ideal game of `g` by at most the KEM term plus the key-schedule term. The later ideal game runs the same two phases, but the target's two hidden registration values come from a lazily sampled uniform table keyed by their Diffie-Hellman coordinates, as in CE-KT; the post phase is the real one. The KEM term is one ML-KEM IND-CCA advantage of an explicit adversary built from the later game plus the ML-KEM correctness error. The key-schedule term is `(qAccept + qFinish + qHmac + qHmac₂)/2^256` (the random-oracle guessing term, which charges the post-run HMAC queries once) plus two HMAC-PRF advantages and the key-schedule bounds of the two hidden entries. Summed over the targets, the probability of the event with a designated claim differs from the sum of the ideal-game probabilities by at most the sum of these terms; the same holds with the later record world of the target's ideal environment in place of the ideal game. Premises: functional decapsulation of the KEM, the approved read-back laws of the Phase 1 and Phase 2 codecs, the full source correctness of the key schedule, the run budget and the post budget. Because the post adversary knows both hidden entries' Diffie-Hellman coordinates exactly, the randomness of the hidden values rests on the random-oracle model of the 192-byte Extract slice (route R1) alone. This is a transfer, not a statement that the root key stays secret.

CE-APP-L (fresh-message secrecy, private-reply mode). The probability that the post adversary, after the reveal, names a fresh message that the experiment chose during the run on a designated handle and guesses it exactly is at most the sum over targets of the KEM term, the key-schedule term, the anomaly term `β_g` of the run-phase adversary, the later record-layer term and 2^-min (min the shortest admitted fresh-message length in bytes); a fresh message on a Server peer needs no anomaly term. The anomaly term is the classical one: the anomaly is an event of the run's transcript, which the post phase does not change, so it is bounded on the run-phase adversary exactly as in CE-12 P1 (one IND-CCA advantage of a predict-then-compare adversary, the correctness error and 2^-256). The later record-layer term is the loss of the explicit reductions of the later record lift (key-chain hops, AEAD integrity and privacy), whose hash bills include the post phase's hash work. Premises: those of CE-KT-L, the KEM cost bound and the runtime initializer's query bound.

CE-LOR-L (left-or-right secrecy of the test session, private-reply mode). Eligibility is as in CE-LOR: a test session exists, a public filter `F` of the run's transcript view holds, and every admitted test was sent on a handle designating the target of the first admitted test. The post adversary wins when its output bit equals the hidden test bit. The advantage, the winning probability minus half the eligible probability, is in absolute value at most the sum over targets of the KEM, key-schedule and later record-layer terms for the winning event, half of the same for the eligibility, and half of `β_g`; with every admitted test on a Server peer the anomaly term is dropped. The final step uses the later record lift's fact that, after any reveal of environment-only data and any post phase, a test bit used only on hidden handles is independent of everything public, so that the winning probability in the later ideal record world is exactly half the eligible probability. Premises: those of CE-APP-L.

Symbolic eligibility. Each headline also has a form in which designation is replaced by the ProVerif-shaped eligibility of CE-12 P2 (a Server peer whose accepted keys are an owner's, or a Beacon pinned to the experiment's Server and key ID), read on the later game's run ledger and final state. The difference between the two forms consists of gap and collision events of the run (an eligible handle that is not designated, two owners with one identity key, two sessions with one ciphertext); these read only the constructed Server, the run's ledger and the owners' identity keys, which the post phase does not change, so their probabilities in the later game equal their probabilities in the classical experiment of the run-phase adversary. Hence the key-transfer and fresh-message forms add exactly CE-12 P2's terms of the run-phase adversary: `ε_A2pub` on the Server side, `ε_A1` with the explicit ciphertext-gap probability on the Beacon side, and all three for the forms that cover both sides. The left-or-right form adds half of the sum of all its terms: `ε_A2pub`, `ε_A1`, the ciphertext-gap probability, the explicit ciphertext-collision probability of the run-phase adversary, and `ε_inj`; its Server-side form adds half of `ε_A2pub + ε_inj`. `ε_inj` is not a term of the adversary: it is the collider advantage of the setup, a sum over the possible identity indices of the signature contract's advantage of explicit zero-query collision reductions, which depends only on the setup and the number of registrations and bounds the probability that two owners share an identity key. Premises: the Server-side forms add that signature verification under an identity key rejects every signature shorter than 64 bytes; the Beacon-side forms add CE-A1's premises (the KEM cost bound, which the key-transfer headline itself does not need, the frame read-back law, the codec's read-writable law, the two X25519 laws and the attached verification adapter); the forms with both sides and the left-or-right form need both sets. For the left-or-right form the stage also shows that every outcome of the later game corresponds to an outcome of the classical experiment with the same Server, the same ledger and the same state up to caches, so that CE-12 P2's facts about the classical experiment's outcomes hold for the later game too. CE-A2pub, CE-A1 and the collision bounds are applied only to the classical experiment of the run-phase adversary, never to the program the later game compiles to; a scan of the direct references of all 113 constants of the stage's modules confirms that they cite neither the provenance theorem A2 nor item 2's authenticated key-transfer theorems T5 and T8; CE-A2pub and CE-A1 enter only through CE-12 P2's bounds on that classical experiment. (Added by CE-12 D-ct: the ciphertext-gap term is now bounded by a closed term made of attacker advantages and a statistical term, and every headline that carried it is restated with that term in its place; see the entry "Common deployment experiment, CE-12 D-ct: the ciphertext-gap term closed". It was not yet integrated when this note was written; its birthday term was reported to the owner on 2026-10-10 and accepted under the owner's 2026-10-07 delegation of proof-internal choices.)

Bills. Every reduction has an explicit query bill on central except one: the KEM adversary's queries at the later game's transported caps (the post budget enters only the uniform allowance), the PRF and key-schedule reductions' coin bills at the same caps, the later record lift's reductions at a bill input that includes the post budget, and the hash routes of every later record-world outcome within `qHash + S + R + qBuild + qFinish + qHash₂`. The exception is the uniform and base-query bill of the first phase of the anomaly term's adversary: it is CE-12 P2b's `ptc_bills`, proved on P2b's branch and not yet on central. This stage proves that phase's decapsulation count (at most the budget's number of finishes plus one), and P2b's bill applies unchanged to the anomaly term of the run-phase adversary once P2b is integrated.

What is not claimed. No later origin, unknown-key-share, binding or authentication statement. The adversary is classical with a post-run reveal; nothing is claimed about quantum adversaries or quantum random-oracle access, and the ProVerif passive-quantum rows are matched by correspondence, not by a soundness theorem. The classical limits stay: claims about owners need the Beacon's pin to be the experiment's Server and key ID; the left-or-right claim concerns the single test session and counts only eligible runs; key transfer is not root secrecy. The ciphertext-gap and ciphertext-collision terms of the symbolic forms stay explicit probabilities. All losses are explicit advantages of explicit reductions or explicit statistical terms; that they are small rests on the stated contracts (ML-KEM IND-CCA, HMAC-PRF, Extract-on-uniform, the random-oracle models of R1 and BLAKE2b, the modified-nonce AEAD's IND$ and INT-CTXT security, and for the symbolic forms the signature and Gap-DH contracts behind CE-A1 and CE-A2pub), as recorded in the trusted boundary.

## Common deployment experiment, CE-12 P2b: the bills of the headline reductions

Every advantage in a CE-12 bound is the success measure of an explicit attacker (a reduction) built from the deployment adversary. Such a bound is meaningful only if each reduction is as efficient as the deployment adversary, up to a stated overhead; the overhead is the reduction's "bill", the number of random coins, calls to the primitives' base oracle and decryption-oracle calls it makes. One bill was missing: the bill of the attacker behind the anomaly term `β_g`, which predicts the challenge ciphertext of a key-encapsulation game and is built from a simulation of the whole deployment experiment. Until that bill was proved, the bounds that contain `β_g` were held back from publication. This step proves it, collects the bills of all CE-12 reductions in one statement, and restates every bound with `β_g` together with the bills of its reductions. Four new modules hold 71 checked theorems; every theorem depends only on Lean's standard axioms, no new assumption or contract is used, and none of the published CE-12 modules is changed. Steps 1 to 3 were reviewed independently together (see "Review" at the end of the step 3 entry); they are not yet integrated.

The cost of one step of the simulation. The attacker behind `β_g` runs the deployment adversary against a simulated deployment in which one Beacon's KEM key is the challenge key, and it answers that Beacon's registration finishes through the key-encapsulation game's decryption oracle. Every other operation it performs on its own coins. The first new theorem bounds, for each kind of deployment command, the coins one simulated step can draw, from every state of the simulation: one for a coin request; the Beacon's identity and prekey plus, beyond the pre-drawn pool, one key generation for a create; 32 for a bundle; for the selected accept while it is active, the Server's 32-coin ephemeral key and one read of a hidden key-schedule value (108 coins), and for every other accept the ordinary accept's ephemeral key (32 coins), its encapsulation and one further 64-coin value of the key-schedule root table; for a build, one hidden-value read, one BLAKE2b digest and one 64-byte seed for the hidden Server install; for a finish, the ordinary finish's cap of 69 callbacks, which also covers the challenged Beacon's finish (one decapsulation, one hidden-value read and one digest), plus one seed for the hidden Beacon install; 64 (one value of the Extract table) for an HMAC request; and 64 (one BLAKE2b digest) for a hash request and each record send or receive. The design had expected these numbers to be read off the existing cost bounds of the ideal environment, but those bounds concern a different presentation of the same game, which is equal to this one only as a probability distribution; query counts do not carry over along such an equality, so the bounds were proved again on the simulation itself, from the same building blocks.

The bill of the anomaly attacker. Each query of the deployment adversary costs the simulation at most the step costs of the commands the experiment's secrecy layer issues for it: the command itself, or, for a challenge (`test`) query, one coin and one send, and for a fresh-message query, one coin per message byte and one send. Summed over the adversary's budget, the attacker before the challenge makes at most `guessBill` uniform queries: one key generation for its own stand-in key pair and one for each of the other `qCreate` pool keys, the runtime initialization and the Server's 32-byte seed, and the sum over the fourteen query classes of the class's cap times its per-query cost. Written out, the per-query costs are 1 per coin, `64 + keygenCost` per create, 32 per bundle, `140 + encapsCost` per accept, 236 per build, `69·max(64, decapsCost) + 64` per finish, 64 per HMAC, hash and record command, 129 per challenge query (a send is charged as both a Server and a Beacon send, because its side is not fixed in advance) and the maximum fresh-message length plus 128 per fresh message. It makes no call to the primitives' base oracle (all its randomness is its own coins) and at most `qFinish + 1` decryption-oracle calls (one per simulated finish of the challenged Beacon, and one to check its prediction); after the challenge it makes no call at all. The premises are those of the existing key-encapsulation bill: a cost bound on the KEM programs and the base interpreter, a bound on the runtime initialization, and an adversary that stays within its budget.

All bills in one statement. `HeadlineBills` collects, at the deployment budget, the bills of every reduction behind the CE-12 terms: the key-encapsulation attacker of the key-transfer term, the HMAC and key-schedule attackers of the slot term, the anomaly attacker above, the record-layer attackers of the integrity and secrecy terms, the Server-authentication attackers of the CE-A1 term, the signature attackers of the published-tuple term, the identity-collision attackers, and the encapsulate-and-compare attacker of the ciphertext-collision bound. All of them were proved before except the anomaly attacker's; this statement instantiates them at the budget and proves them together. The Server-authentication bills were previously stated only alongside the CE-A1 bound, under its security premises; here they are derived from the resource premises alone, as they should be, since a bill does not depend on whether the attack succeeds. The statement needs the cost bounds, the initialization bound, the adversary's budget and, for the record-layer bills, full correctness of the key schedule (the premise under which the record-layer theorems state their bills).

The billed bounds. For each of the fifteen published bounds that contain `β_g` (origin authentication of the records a Beacon accepts, the sender form of unknown-key share, fresh-message secrecy and left-or-right secrecy, each per target and summed, and the seven symbolic and injective forms built on them), a new theorem states the same bound under the same premises together with the bills of exactly the reductions whose advantages appear in it. With these, every advantage in those bounds cites an attacker whose resources are proved, so the hold on publication for the anomaly term is lifted. The bounds themselves are unchanged: each new theorem is the published one, restated word for word, combined with the bills.

What is not claimed. The two explicit terms of P2, the ciphertext-gap probability and the ciphertext-collision probability, are probabilities in the real experiment rather than advantages of attackers; they have no bill, they are still to be reported to the owner, and the bounds with the ciphertext-collision term remain held back until its game-level step is proved. (Added by the CE-12 P2b review fix pass: step 2 proves that step and restates those bounds with the closed term; see the next entry. The ciphertext-gap term stays explicit and is still to be reported to the owner.) The bills count random coins and oracle calls, the cost model of every earlier bill, not running time; deterministic local work such as parsing, key derivation, encryption and frame writing is not counted. They are worst-case caps on every execution path and are not tight (for example, every finish is charged the ordinary finish's cap; and every create is charged a key generation beyond the pre-drawn pool, although the attacker's pool holds `qCreate + 1` key pairs, so a create within the budget always takes its key pair from the pool and `guessBill` over-charges by `qCreate` key generations). The agreement fact for the publisher pin and plaintext, the closed ciphertext-gap bound and the later-quantum versions are later steps, listed in the guide's section "CE-12 P2b: open points and the rest of P2". (Added by the CE-12 P2b review fix pass: step 3 proves the agreement fact in the ideal record world but not its lift to the deployment experiment; see the third CE-12 P2b entry.) (Added by CE-12 D-ct: the ciphertext-gap term is now bounded by a closed term made of attacker advantages and a statistical term, and every headline that carried it is restated with that term in its place; see the entry "Common deployment experiment, CE-12 D-ct: the ciphertext-gap term closed". It was not yet integrated when this note was written; its birthday term was reported to the owner on 2026-10-10 and accepted under the owner's 2026-10-07 delegation of proof-internal choices.)

## Common deployment experiment, CE-12 P2b: the ciphertext-collision bound

The symbolic corollaries of CE-12 P2 compare the deployment's public designation of a session with ProVerif's symbolic eligibility. On the Beacon side the designation can move between sessions when two distinct Server sessions send a Beacon the same KEM ciphertext, encapsulated to the Beacon's published key. P2 bounded this only by an explicit probability in the real experiment, `ctCollTerm`: the probability that the final transcript shows two sessions whose build responses carry one ciphertext and whose accepted candidates name one owner's published post-quantum key.
